cases.title: `^build` builds every dependency before the project that needs it
cases.why: A project’s build reads what its dependencies built, so each dependency must finish first. Started early, app concatenates a lib or ui output that is missing or left over from an older build. The run can still exit 0, so the bad bundle ships without anyone seeing an error.

cases.title: Running one project's task runs what it depends on, and nothing else
cases.why: Asking for one project’s task means that task done right, which needs what it depends on built first. Skipping the dependencies builds ui on a missing or stale lib. Running unrelated projects as well spends CI minutes on work nobody asked for and can fail the run on code the user did not touch.

cases.title: A bare name in dependsOn waits on the same project’s task
cases.why: A bare name in dependsOn points at a task in the same project, the usual way to say test needs build. If the runner ignores it or looks elsewhere, test reads a `dist` that is missing or from the last build. The test then passes or fails on old code, which is worse than no test.

cases.title: `lib#build` in dependsOn runs that task first, with no package dependency
cases.why: An edge like `lib#build` states an order the package manifests do not show. site publishes lib’s output, so lib must be built first even though site does not list lib as a dependency. Ignoring the edge publishes a missing or stale file, and the order would hold only by luck of timing.

cases.title: A dependency two projects share builds once per run
cases.why: When two projects depend on the same library, one run needs that library built only once. Building it twice wastes time, and a second build can rewrite files while the first consumer is reading them. Each task in a run is one unit of work, however many paths lead to it.

cases.title: `^build` reaches a dependency’s dependency when the middle project has no build
cases.why: app reads lib’s output, reached through mid, which has no build of its own. A project without the task does not cut the chain; its own dependencies still have to be built. Stopping at mid leaves app reading a missing or stale lib, and the build of app still exits 0.

cases.title: Running a library’s task does not run the projects that depend on it
cases.why: Dependencies run first because the task needs them; dependents do not, because the task does not read them. Building lib should not rebuild ui and app, which only consume lib. Pulling them in turns a quick library build into a workspace build and can fail it on code the user never asked to touch.

cases.title: A task only some projects declare runs in exactly those
cases.why: Running a task by name runs it where it is declared and nowhere else. A project without that task has nothing to run, and should not be swapped for some other task it does have. Running `build` in place of a missing `lint` does work nobody asked for and reports it as lint.

cases.title: A project whose directory holds spaces builds, caches and restores
cases.why: A directory name with spaces is a valid path and must work like any other. A runner that splits paths on spaces misses inputs, writes outputs to the wrong place or fails to restore them. The project then looks cached while its `dist` stays empty, or never caches at all.

cases.title: A task named `test:unit` runs as its own task
cases.why: A colon is a common part of task names such as `test:unit`, not a separator the runner may reinterpret. Reading it as project and task, or as a prefix of `test`, runs the wrong command. The user asked for unit tests and gets the whole suite, or nothing, under the same green exit.

cases.title: `^gen` runs the dependencies’ gen first, and not their build
cases.why: `^gen` asks for one specific task in each dependency, here the code generation app reads. Running lib’s build in its place leaves `gen/g.txt` missing or stale, and app builds on it. Running both wastes time on a build nobody asked for; the caret names a task, not a whole project.

cases.title: `^build` over a dependency that declares no build runs the project alone
cases.why: `^build` means build each dependency that has a build. A dependency without one has nothing to wait for, so the project runs on its own. Failing the run would make every project declare an empty build, and running some other task of lib in its place does work nobody asked for.

cases.title: A five-project chain builds strictly from the bottom up
cases.why: Each project in the chain reads the one below it, so the order must hold at every step, not only the first. If any build starts early it reads a missing or older output, and the error carries silently up to the top. A long chain is where a scheduler that only checks direct edges or races ahead shows it.

cases.title: Two selected projects over one dependency build it once, before both
cases.why: Two selected projects that share a dependency need it built once, and before either of them. Building it twice wastes time and can rewrite its output while one of them reads it. Starting either project before the shared build finishes gives it a missing or stale input.

cases.title: `test` on `build` and `^build` waits for both the project’s and its dependency’s build
cases.why: Two edges on one task both have to hold: the project’s own build and its dependency’s build. Honouring only one lets test start while the other build is still writing, so it checks a missing or half-written output. The test result then says nothing reliable about the code.

cases.title: Selecting a project and its dependency runs the dependency once, first
cases.why: Selecting a dependency by name does not make it independent of the project that needs it. lib must still build once and before app, as it would if only app were asked for. Running it twice or alongside app wastes time and lets app read a missing or stale lib.

cases.title: `^build` follows a dependency by package name when its directory is named otherwise
cases.why: Projects depend on each other by package name, and the directory a package lives in can be named anything. Matching dependencies by directory name drops the edge from app to ui. app then builds before ui, or on an old ui, and the run still exits 0.

cases.title: `@acme/core#build` in dependsOn runs that scoped project’s build first
cases.why: Scoped names such as `@acme/core` are ordinary package names and must work in an explicit edge. A runner that misreads the `@` or the `/` cannot find the task and either fails or drops the edge. Dropping it lets site build first and copy a missing or stale core output.

cases.title: A project nested in another runs its own task in its own directory
cases.why: A project inside another project’s directory is still its own project with its own task. Running it from the outer directory, or folding it into the outer project, writes outputs to the wrong place or skips it. Each task must run where its project lives, or its paths mean something else.

cases.title: Projects that depend on each other run a task that names no dependency
cases.why: Packages that depend on each other form a cycle only for tasks that wait on dependencies. A task that names no dependency has no order to keep, so nothing stops it. Refusing the run would block checks like lint in any workspace with a package cycle, for no reason the tasks give.

cases.title: `^build` across projects that depend on each other fails before any build runs
cases.why: When each build waits on the other, no order is right: whichever runs first builds on a dependency not built yet. Running anyway gives an output that depends on timing and is never reproducible. Failing before any build runs names the cycle so the user can break it.

cases.title: A project listing itself as a dependency is no cycle: `^build` runs its build
cases.why: A package cannot be its own dependency, so a self entry in its manifest orders nothing. Treating it as a cycle fails a run that has a clear and valid order. The right reading ignores the self edge and runs the build once. A package that lists itself is a common slip in a manifest, and it should not block every build of that package.

cases.title: Two projects’ tasks naming each other fail the run before either runs
cases.why: Two tasks that each wait on the other can never both run after their dependency. Running them anyway breaks the order the user wrote, so one of them reads a missing or stale output. Failing before either runs points at the cycle instead of producing a build that depends on timing.

cases.title: A task that depends on itself fails the run
cases.why: A task cannot run after itself, so a self dependency is a mistake in the config. Running the task anyway hides that mistake and ignores an order the user wrote, perhaps meaning another task. Failing the run makes the bad edge visible while it is cheap to fix.

cases.title: A workspace package named only as a peer is built first, and an edit to it runs the consumer again
cases.why: The workspace links the peer in, so the consumer’s build reads it as it reads any dependency. Naming it as a peer only changes who installs it outside the workspace. Building the consumer first, or replaying it after the peer changed, leaves it built against code that is no longer there.

cases.title: Selecting a project by name runs its task and no other project’s
cases.why: Selecting a project by name is the most basic way to say what a run should do. Running other projects as well spends time on work nobody asked for and can fail the run on code the user did not touch. Running fewer drops the one task the user wanted checked.

cases.title: A `*` in a name selects every project it matches
cases.why: A `*` in a project name is a pattern, so `u*` means every project whose name starts with u. Treating it as a literal name selects nothing, and matching too loosely pulls in projects the pattern excludes. Either way the user runs a different set than the one they wrote.

cases.title: A name matches whole: `foo` never selects `foo-e2e`
cases.why: A name without a wildcard must match a project name in full. Matching it as a prefix makes `foo` also run `foo-e2e`, which may be slow or need services the user did not start. The user would have no plain way left to select just `foo`. Wildcards are there for when the user wants more.

cases.title: A `.` in a name is a dot: `socket.io` never selects `socketxio`
cases.why: Package names often contain dots, and a dot in a selector means a dot. Reading it as a pattern that matches any character selects `socketxio` too, a different package. A selector that matches more than its text runs work the user never named.

cases.title: Two selectors run the union of what each selects
cases.why: Several selectors each add projects to the run, so the result is everything any of them selects. Keeping only the last one, or only the projects all of them match, silently drops work the user asked for. CI then reports green for checks that never ran.

cases.title: Selecting a project with its dependencies takes every transitive one
cases.why: Selecting a project with its dependencies means the whole chain below it, not only the direct ones. Stopping at ui leaves utils out, though app builds on it through ui. Unrelated projects like lib must stay out, or the selection means nothing.

cases.title: Selecting a project with its dependents takes every transitive one
cases.why: Selecting a project with its dependents means everything that could break when it changes, at any depth. app uses utils only through ui, but a change to utils still reaches it. Leaving app out lets a breaking change pass the check that was meant to catch it.

cases.title: Selecting only a project’s dependents leaves the project out
cases.why: Asking for only the dependents is a way to check what a change could break without rerunning the project itself. Including utils runs work the user excluded on purpose. Dropping the transitive app misses a project the change can still break.

cases.title: Selecting only a project’s dependencies leaves the project out
cases.why: Asking for only the dependencies prepares everything a project builds on, without the project itself. This is common before working on app locally. Including app runs what the user left out, and stopping at ui leaves utils, which ui needs, unprepared.

cases.title: Dependents with their dependencies takes what each dependent builds on
cases.why: To test the dependents of ui, each dependent needs everything it builds on, not only ui. app needs kit as much as ui, so leaving kit out runs app against a missing or stale dependency. lib is unrelated and must stay out, or the selection grows to the whole workspace.

cases.title: An exclude alone selects every project but the one it names
cases.why: An exclude on its own means everything except that project. Treating it as an empty selection runs nothing and lets CI pass having checked nothing. Treating it as a no-op runs the project the user asked to skip, which may be slow or broken for known reasons.

cases.title: `*` and an exclude select every project but that one
cases.why: `*` with an exclude is the explicit form of every project but one. The exclude must win over the wildcard, or the project the user named is run anyway. Common uses are skipping a slow or known broken package while still checking the rest.

cases.title: An exclude given before an include still removes what the include adds
cases.why: An exclude names a project the user does not want run, wherever it appears on the command line. Applying selectors in order, so a later include adds utils back, makes the result depend on argument order. Scripts and CI configs build these lists in any order and expect the same set.

cases.title: Excluding a project with its dependencies removes them all
cases.why: Excluding a project with its dependencies removes the project and everything below it. Removing only ui leaves utils in the run, though the user excluded the whole subtree. The rest of the workspace, app and lib here, must still run. This is how a user leaves out a whole stack, such as a library and its private helpers.

cases.title: `*` selects scoped and unscoped projects alike
cases.why: `*` means every project, and a scoped name like `@acme/core` is a project like any other. A wildcard that stops at the `/` drops every scoped package from the run. In workspaces where most packages are scoped, that is most of the checks, gone without a warning.

cases.title: `@acme/*` selects exactly that scope
cases.why: `@acme/*` is the usual way to select one npm scope. It must take every package in that scope and nothing outside it. Missing scoped names runs nothing, and matching unscoped ones runs projects the user did not ask for. Scopes often group a team’s or a product’s packages, so this selection is used a lot in CI.

cases.title: A glob matches across the scope’s `/`: `*core*` selects `@acme/core`
cases.why: Users think of a scoped package by its name, and `*core*` should find `@acme/core`. A wildcard that cannot cross the scope’s `/` silently skips it. The selection then runs fewer projects than the pattern plainly matches, with no sign anything was missed.

cases.title: Excluding `*utils` takes out the scoped `@acme/utils`
cases.why: An exclude pattern must match the same names an include would. If `*utils` cannot match `@acme/utils`, the package the user meant to skip runs anyway. Include and exclude have to read patterns the same way, or one of them lies. Scoped names are common enough that this mismatch would surface in most workspaces.

cases.title: A bare `core` selects `@acme/core` when only that package carries the name
cases.why: When only one package is named `core` under any scope, a bare `core` can only mean that package. This is how the common package manager filter grammar reads it, which users already know. Selecting nothing instead runs nothing the user asked for, and may pass CI having checked nothing.

cases.title: A directory glob selects the projects directly under it
cases.why: A directory glob such as `packages/*` selects the projects directly under that path. It must not reach projects nested deeper, which a `**` is for, and must not reach other folders. Users rely on this to run one area of the repo, such as every app or every library.

cases.title: A `**` directory glob reaches a project nested in another
cases.why: `**` in a directory glob means any depth, so it takes a project nested inside another. Stopping at one level drops the nested project without warning. Other top level folders such as `apps` must still stay out. Nested projects are common in repos that keep examples or fixtures inside a package.

cases.title: A directory that is a project selects that project, not one nested in it
cases.why: Naming a project by its path means that project. The project nested below it has a path of its own and is not part of it. Pulling it in runs work the user did not ask for, and makes a single project impossible to select by directory. Directory selectors exist so a user can point at exactly one folder.

cases.title: A directory does not select a sibling that shares its prefix
cases.why: A directory names a path, and `packages/app` is not a prefix of `packages/app-extra`. Matching by string prefix runs a sibling the user did not name. A selection that runs more than asked reports nothing wrong; it only costs time and can hide a failure behind someone else’s.

cases.title: A directory glob minus one directory selects every other project there
cases.why: A directory exclude must remove a project selected by a directory glob, just as name excludes do. Skipping docs while checking the other apps is a common need. If the exclude is ignored, the project the user wanted left out runs and may fail the run for them.

cases.title: A name and a directory select the union
cases.why: Selectors by name and by directory may be mixed, and each adds its projects to the run. Keeping only one kind silently drops what the other selected. Projects neither selector names must stay out. Users mix the two when one project is easier to name and another easier to point at by path.

cases.title: Selecting by name in a package graph with a cycle runs that project alone
cases.why: A cycle among packages does not change what selecting one project by name means. Only that project runs, since its task depends on nothing. Failing the run or pulling in the whole cycle punishes a workspace for a shape that does not affect this task.

cases.title: Walking a package cycle takes each project in it once
cases.why: A walk over dependencies in a package cycle reaches each project in the cycle. It must take each one once and stop, not loop or fail. Unrelated projects stay out, so the run is the cycle and nothing more. Cycles do occur in real workspaces, often through test or tooling packages, and must not crash a selection.

cases.title: A project whose task names another project’s task counts as its dependent
cases.why: A task that names another project’s task depends on that project, even if no package manifest says so. e2e needs app’s check, so it is a dependent of app. Leaving it out of the dependents of app skips the project that tests app, and a breaking change passes.

cases.title: A selector that matches no project fails the run
cases.why: A selector that matches nothing is almost always a typo or a renamed package. If the run exits 0, CI passes having checked nothing, and no one notices until something broken ships. Failing the run names the selector that went wrong, while it is cheap to fix.

cases.title: A tag selects exactly the projects carrying it
cases.why: A tag is a label the user put on projects so they can be picked as a group, such as every service or every library. Selecting by it must take exactly those projects. Taking more runs work nobody asked for; taking fewer skips a project the user believes was built or tested.

cases.title: A `*` in a tag selects the projects carrying any tag it matches
cases.why: A pattern in a tag picks every tag it matches, as a pattern in a name picks every name. Users group tags by prefix, such as scope:web and scope:api, to select a family at once. Matching only the literal text selects nothing, so the run passes while it built none of them.

cases.title: A tag excluded takes the projects carrying it out of the selection
cases.why: Excluding a tag says to leave out every project carrying it, such as slow end-to-end suites. The rest of the selection must still run. A tool that ignores the exclusion runs the work the user just opted out of; one that drops too much skips projects the user expects checked.

cases.title: A tag and its dependencies select the tagged projects and what they depend on
cases.why: Selecting a tag with its dependencies means the tagged projects and everything they need to build. A tagged app cannot build without its libraries, even untagged ones. Leaving them out fails the run or builds against stale output; adding unrelated projects runs work nobody asked for.

cases.title: Skipping dependencies runs the selected task and not what it depends on
cases.why: Skipping dependencies is an explicit request to run just the selected task against what is already on disk. It saves time when the user knows the dependencies are current, such as rerunning one app after a full build. Running lib anyway ignores the flag, and not running app at all drops the work that was asked for.

cases.title: A task the full run built replays when its dependencies are skipped
cases.why: Skipping a dependency changes the schedule, not the task: app reads the same lib output and sources as in the full run. Its result is already cached, so it should replay. Rebuilding it just because the dependency was skipped wastes the cache exactly when the user is trying to save time.

cases.title: With dependencies skipped, a dependency rebuilt since still reruns its dependant
cases.why: app reads lib’s output, so a new lib must give app a new cache key even when lib is not scheduled. Here lib was rebuilt on its own since app last ran. A key that leaves out the skipped lib replays app built on the old lib, and the stale bundle ships under a green run.

cases.title: With dependencies skipped, a change two dependencies down still reruns the dependant
cases.why: base reaches app through lib’s output, so a change to base must change app’s key even with both skipped. The key has to fold the skipped lib and everything lib itself folds. Stopping one level down replays app with the old base inside it, which no error will ever point out.

cases.title: What a run builds on a skipped, out-of-date dependency never replays in a full run
cases.why: When dependencies are skipped, app may build on a lib output older than lib’s sources. That result is valid for this run only and must not be stored under the key a full run will look up. Otherwise the next full build rebuilds lib but replays app with the old lib baked in.

cases.title: Skipping dependencies with a dependency also selected replays both
cases.why: Selecting app and lib with dependencies skipped asks for both, and nothing either reads has changed since the full run. Both should replay from cache. Rebuilding either one only because the skipped base was left out of the schedule wastes the time the flag exists to save.

cases.title: Two selected tasks keep their order when the task between them is skipped
cases.why: app builds on base through lib, so when both base and app are selected, base must finish first even though lib between them is skipped. Run side by side, app reads whatever base left on disk last time, or a half-written file. Skipping a task drops it from the run; it does not drop the order between the tasks that remain.

cases.title: `lint.*` in dependsOn runs every task it matches and none it does not
cases.why: A pattern in dependsOn promises that every task it matches runs first, and only those. Missing one match lets the dependant run before a check it was meant to wait for, so a failing lint step can pass unseen. Pulling in a task the pattern does not match, like `build` here, spends time on work nobody asked for and writes files the run should not touch.

cases.title: `^build.*` waits for every matching task of each dependency
cases.why: `^build.*` means every matching task in each dependency finishes before the dependant starts. A dependant that starts after only some of them reads a half-built dependency: here one of the two files could be missing or old. The result then depends on scheduling, so a failure shows up on one machine and not on the next.

cases.title: A task on `build.*` reruns when a matched task’s input changes
cases.why: A task that depends on a pattern depends on what each matched task produced. `top` copies the file `build.x` wrote, so a change to `build.x`’s source must change `top`’s key too. Replaying `top` after that source changed ships the old bytes under a green run, and nothing in the output says so.

cases.title: `*` alone in dependsOn fails the run
cases.why: A dependency pattern that matches every task, the task itself included, is almost always a typo for a name. Accepted, it makes the task wait on itself, a cycle, or quietly runs every task in the project before it. Failing the run costs one edit; guessing what was meant hides a config mistake that later shows up only as slow or odd builds.

cases.title: `^*` alone in dependsOn fails the run
cases.why: A dependency pattern that matches every task, the task itself included, is almost always a typo for a name. Accepted, it makes the task wait on itself, a cycle, or quietly runs every task in the project before it. Failing the run costs one edit; guessing what was meant hides a config mistake that later shows up only as slow or odd builds.

cases.title: `**` alone in dependsOn fails the run
cases.why: A dependency pattern that matches every task, the task itself included, is almost always a typo for a name. Accepted, it makes the task wait on itself, a cycle, or quietly runs every task in the project before it. Failing the run costs one edit; guessing what was meant hides a config mistake that later shows up only as slow or odd builds.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 1, independent tasks run one at a time
cases.why: A concurrency of 1 is how a user says tasks must not overlap, often because they share a port, a database or a lock file. Running two at once anyway breaks that promise and gives failures that come and go with timing. The limit has to hold exactly, not on average.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 2, no more than two tasks run at once
cases.why: The concurrency limit caps how many tasks run at once, so a run fits the machine’s memory and cores. Going over it can run a CI machine out of memory or slow every task down. The cap must hold at every moment, including when one task ends and the next ones start.

cases.title: Tasks that fail still count against the concurrency limit while they run
cases.why: A failing task is still a process using its slot until it exits. Freeing the slot when the failure is first noticed, or starting the next task early, lets more tasks run than the limit allows. The limit exists for the shared resources, and those are still in use until the process is gone.

cases.title: A concurrency far above the number of tasks runs them all and ends
cases.why: A concurrency higher than the number of tasks simply means no limit in practice. Every task should run and the run should end normally. Hanging while waiting for work that will never come, or refusing the setting, breaks a common choice such as a large fixed value in CI.

cases.title: A failure at the bottom of a chain runs nothing above it
cases.why: When a dependency fails, everything that builds on it would read a missing or broken output. Running lib and app anyway wastes time and can produce output that looks fine but is built on nothing. Skipping them keeps the failure in one place, where the user can see its real cause.

cases.title: A task behind a replayed task still waits for what the replayed one depends on
cases.why: app’s test reads lib’s output as well as app’s, so it must wait for lib’s task, not only for app’s build. When app’s build replays from cache it finishes at once, but that says nothing about lib being done. Starting the test then makes it read lib’s old output, and it passes or fails on the wrong code.

cases.title: A failed dependency stops the task behind a replayed one from running
cases.why: app’s test reads lib’s output, and this time lib failed, so that output is missing or old. A replay of app’s build does not make lib’s failure go away. Running the test anyway checks stale code and can report a pass for a tree that does not build.

cases.title: A server starts when one of the tasks that need it must run, though another replays
cases.why: When any task that needs a server has to run, the server must start for it. Here web’s test replays from cache, but docs changed and its test must run against the server. Skipping the server because one dependant replayed leaves docs testing against nothing, so it hangs or fails for no reason in its own code.

cases.title: A server whose own build fails never starts, nor does what needs it
cases.why: A server that depends on a failed build would serve a missing or old output. Starting it anyway, and the tests behind it, checks the wrong code and can pass. Stopping both keeps the failure visible and avoids a long running process nobody can use.

cases.title: A project without the requested task runs none of the tasks it would need
cases.why: A task’s dependencies run only because that task needs them. docs declares no verify, so nothing in this run needs docs’ build. Running it anyway wastes time and can fail the run on a project that had no part in what was asked. Only tasks reachable from the ones requested belong in the run.

cases.title: Asking for two tasks, one of which no project declares, fails the run
cases.why: A task name that no project declares is a typo or a removed task. If it is dropped silently because the other name was found, the run exits 0 having skipped part of what was asked. CI then reports a check as passing that never ran. Failing names the unknown task, so the fix is a one word change.

cases.title: Two tasks in one run each run where declared, though one project lacks one
cases.why: Asking for two tasks runs each one where it is declared. b has no lint, which is no reason to skip b’s build or to fail the run. Each requested task is looked up on its own; unrelated tasks such as check must not run. Projects rarely declare the same set of tasks, so this mix is the normal case.

cases.title: Two tasks one project declares both run in one run
cases.why: Naming two tasks in one run is a request for both. Running only the first, or only the last, silently drops work the user asked for. CI scripts often combine tasks this way and read the exit code as covering all of them. Every named task has to be found and run, or the run must fail.

cases.title: Asking for a task in a project that does not declare it fails the run
cases.why: The user asked for typecheck in a, which does not declare it; only b does. If the run exits 0, it reports a type check that never happened. Running b’s typecheck in its place is also wrong, since b was not selected. Failing points the user at the missing task before anyone relies on the result.

cases.title: Excluding one member keeps the workspace-root project’s task
cases.why: The exclude names b alone, and the workspace root is a project like any other. Dropping the root along with the excluded member removes checks the user never asked to skip. Root level tasks often guard shared tooling, so losing them hides real failures.

cases.title: Selecting the workspace-root project by name runs its task and not its members’
cases.why: The members live inside the root’s directory, but each is a project of its own. Selecting the root by name means the root’s task only. Treating the root as containing its members runs every project in the workspace when one was asked for. Scope is by project, not by folder nesting.

cases.title: A selection its excludes leave empty, beside a selector matching nothing, fails the run
cases.why: Here nothing is left to run, and one selector matches no project at all. That selector is almost always a typo, and exiting 0 lets CI pass having checked nothing. A selection the user empties on purpose with excludes is different, but the unmatched name is still an error to report.

cases.title: Projects under a dot directory, under underscored names, and two of one base name each run
cases.why: Every listed project must be found and run, wherever it lives. Skipping directories that start with a dot or look like generated code drops real projects silently. Two projects in folders with the same base name are still two projects, and merging them loses one.

cases.title: A project whose directory holds spaces and parentheses runs there, caches and restores
cases.why: Spaces and parentheses are valid in directory names, and tasks must run in their own directory with their files found and restored. A runner that passes such paths through a shell unquoted breaks the command or writes outputs elsewhere. The cache must also restore into the same odd path, or a hit leaves `dist` empty.

cases.title: A change selects a project whose task names the changed project’s task
cases.why: app declares that its build needs lib’s build, so a change to lib affects app even without a package dependency. An affected run that follows only package manifests leaves app out. app then goes untested on the new lib, and the breakage shows up later, after merge.

cases.title: Selecting a project’s dependencies follows a task it names in another project
cases.why: e2e’s test names app’s build, so app is one of e2e’s dependencies even though no manifest says so. lib is app’s dependency, so it counts too. Following only package manifests finds none of these, and the user gets an empty run instead of the projects e2e builds on.

cases.title: A project’s dependents reach through a package dependency and then a task another project names
cases.why: A change to lib reaches app through the package graph, and reaches e2e because e2e’s test names app’s build. Dependents must be followed across both kinds of edge, in any order. Stopping at the first kind leaves e2e untested on a change that can break it.

cases.title: A cached test behind a dev server runs again when the server’s sources change
cases.why: A test behind a server checks the server as much as its own code. When the server’s sources change, the old pass says nothing about the new server. Replaying it vouches for a server the test never saw, and a broken server ships under a green run.

cases.title: With dependencies skipped, a test behind an unchanged server replays and no server starts
cases.why: Nothing the test or its server reads changed since the full run, so the test’s cached result is still valid. With dependencies skipped, it should replay and no server should start. Starting the server anyway costs its whole start up time for a test that will not run.

cases.title: With dependencies skipped, each selected task reruns on any of its rebuilt dependencies
cases.why: A task’s key must cover every dependency it reads, skipped or not. app reads both lib and base, and top reads tool, so a new base or tool must rerun them. Keying on the first dependency only replays app or top built on the old one, and nothing in the run shows it.

cases.title: Args forwarded to a run reach a requested server’s command
cases.why: Arguments after `--` are how a user passes options such as a port to the command a task runs. A server task is still a task, so `dev -- --port 3000` must start the server with that port. Dropping them starts it on the default port, where the test or the developer then talks to the wrong server or none.

cases.title: Args forwarded to a run reach a requested server that prints a ready line
cases.why: A server the run waits on until it prints a ready line is started like any other task. Its forwarded arguments must reach it, so `dev -- --port 3000` does not lose the port. Starting it a different way when a ready line is declared would make the same command behave differently for a setting about timing.

cases.title: Args forwarded to a server reach it as typed, never expanded by a shell
cases.why: The user’s own shell already parsed and quoted the arguments, so each must arrive as one literal string. Passing them through a second shell expands `$(...)` and backquotes, which runs commands the user never asked to run. It also splits `a b` in two, so the server gets different arguments than typed.

cases.title: A closed terminal lets a process a task backgrounded run its cleanup
cases.why: Closing a terminal sends a hang-up, and processes a task started in the background often trap it to clean up, such as removing a lock or stopping a container. The run must pass the signal on and give them time to finish. Killing them outright, as a run that dies of the hang-up does, skips that cleanup and leaves the machine in a broken state.

cases.title: A `dependsOn` edge added to a task orders and keys it: an edit to the dependency then runs it again
cases.why: Adding a dependsOn edge says the task now reads what the dependency produces. From then on the dependency must run first, and its changes must reach the task’s key. A tool that orders the new edge but keys only on the old config replays a stale result after the dependency changes.

cases.title: A member’s task that depends on a workspace-root task runs after it
cases.why: A member’s task may depend on a task of the workspace-root project, such as code generation over shared tools. That dependency must be honoured like any other edge, with the root task finishing first. Running the member first reads a missing or stale generated file, or races the generator.

cases.title: Editing a root file a workspace-root task reads runs it again
cases.why: The workspace root can be a project with its own tasks, reading files no member owns. When such a file changes, the root task’s key changes and the task must run again. Replaying the cached result would ship output generated from the old file.

cases.title: Editing a member’s file leaves a workspace-root task over `**` replayed
cases.why: A project owns the files under it except those inside a nested project. For the workspace-root project, every member is nested, so a root task over `**` does not read the members’ files. Rerunning it on every member edit would rebuild the root on nearly every change in the workspace.

cases.title: An edit inside a nested repository a workspace-level input glob covers runs the task again
cases.why: The outer git records a nested repository as one path, or not at all, so it never lists the files inside. A task whose input glob covers them still reads those files. A key built only from the outer repository misses the edit and replays output built from the old content.

cases.title: A changed root file no member owns selects the workspace-root project
cases.why: A file at the workspace root that no member owns belongs to the workspace-root project. A change to it must select that project’s tasks, like a change in any member. Treating root files as nobody’s skips root tasks such as code generation that read them.

cases.title: A changed member file selects the member, not the workspace-root project holding it
cases.why: A member file lies under the workspace root, but the member owns it, not the root project. An edit there selects the member alone. Also selecting the root project would rerun root tasks on nearly every change, since every member file is under the root.

cases.title: dependsOn naming a task the project lacks fails the run
cases.why: A dependency the user wrote is a promise that something runs first. If the named task does not exist and the run goes on, the task runs without the input it waits on and may read a missing or stale file. The typo never surfaces, so a green run hides that the order was never kept.

cases.title: dependsOn naming a project that does not exist fails the run
cases.why: A dependency on another project names work that must finish first. If that project does not exist, perhaps renamed or misspelt, running anyway builds on whatever its old output left behind. Failing the run points at the bad name at once, instead of letting CI pass on an order nobody enforced.

cases.title: dependsOn naming a task another project lacks fails the run
cases.why: Naming `lib#gen` says lib produces something this task reads. When lib declares no such task, nothing produces it, and a run that carries on reads a missing or stale file. Refusing the run turns a silent wrong build into an error that names the bad edge.

cases.title: Selecting a project without the task, with its dependencies, runs the task in those dependencies
cases.why: The selection is mid and everything below it, and the task exists in lib, so lib’s build is what was asked for. mid lacking the task removes only mid from the run, not the projects reached through it. Failing, or running nothing, leaves lib unbuilt for the user who wanted mid’s dependencies ready, and app above the selection must stay out.

cases.title: A dependency named in both `dependencies` and `devDependencies` is built once, before its dependant
cases.why: Listing a package in two dependency fields of one manifest still makes it one dependency. `^build` must build it first, and once: two edges to the same task are one edge. Missing the edge builds app against a missing lib; running lib twice wastes the work and can rewrite its output while app reads it.

cases.title: A `PATH=…` prefix on a command decides where that command’s program is found
cases.why: In sh, `PATH=dir tool` looks `tool` up in `dir`: the assignment holds for that one command, lookup included. A runner that resolves the program itself, with the PATH it was started with, finds no `tool` or a different one. The task then fails, or runs a program the command never named, though the same line works in a terminal.

cases.title: A second run over an unchanged tree replays instead of running
cases.why: When nothing a task reads has changed, its last result is still right, so replaying it is safe. Running it again spends CI minutes and local time on work whose answer is already known. Across a monorepo of many tasks, this is what lets a run with no changes finish in seconds instead of taking the full build time.

cases.title: Editing an input runs the task again
cases.why: A changed input means the stored result was computed from source that no longer exists. Replaying it would ship output built from the old code under a green run. Seeing every edit to a declared input is the most basic promise a cache makes, and every other saving depends on it.

cases.title: A same-size edit right after a commit runs the task again
cases.why: Change detection must rest on content, not on size and timestamps alone. An edit that keeps the file’s length and lands in the same second as a commit can look untouched to a check based on file stats. A tool that trusts such a check replays the old output, and the edit never reaches the build.

cases.title: A new file under an input glob runs the task again
cases.why: A glob names a set of files, and adding a file changes that set. A build that concatenates, bundles or tests everything under `src/` gives different output once a new file exists. Keying only on the files seen before would replay a bundle that is missing the new module.

cases.title: Deleting an input runs the task again
cases.why: Removing a file changes the input set just as editing one does. A task that bundles a directory must stop including the deleted file. Replaying the old result would ship code that is gone from the tree, such as a removed module or a test that should no longer run.

cases.title: Renaming an input runs the task again
cases.why: A file’s path is part of what a task reads, not only its bytes. A rename can change order, module names or import paths, so the output can differ even when no content changed. A key built only from the set of content hashes sees the same bytes and replays output that still names the old file.

cases.title: An edit deep in a nested input directory runs the task again
cases.why: A recursive glob covers every depth, and a change at any depth counts. A tool that stops walking early, or trusts a directory’s own timestamp, can miss an edit several levels down. Real sources nest deeply, so missing such an edit replays stale output for ordinary work.

cases.title: An edit to an input named with spaces, `$` and quotes runs the task again
cases.why: File names with spaces, quotes or `$` are legal and occur in real repos, for example among assets and fixtures. If such a name is mangled when it is listed, quoted or passed through a shell, the file drops out of the key. Edits to it then never rerun the task, and the build ships its old content.

cases.title: An edit to an input with a non-ASCII name runs the task again
cases.why: Non-ASCII file names are ordinary on every current file system and must map to the same path every time. git escapes such names in its plain output; a reader that does not undo the escaping loses the file from the key. Edits to it then replay the old output.

cases.title: Undoing an edit replays the first run’s outputs, not the edited ones
cases.why: A key must depend only on the current inputs, so going back to old inputs must give back the old outputs. After an undo, the tree must hold what the first run produced, not the edited run’s output. A tool that keeps whatever it wrote last leaves output from code that is no longer in the tree, under a green run.

cases.title: A file outside the task’s inputs changes nothing
cases.why: Declared inputs are the contract: only those files can change the result. Rerunning a build because a README or another unrelated file changed wastes time on every docs edit. Explicit inputs are what let a cache stay warm across changes that cannot matter to the task.

cases.title: A file a `!` input pattern takes back changes nothing
cases.why: A `!` pattern is the user stating that a file does not affect the task. Notes, another tool’s fixtures or generated docs often sit inside a source folder. Ignoring the exclusion reruns the task on edits the user has said cannot change its output, and the cache loses its value for that folder.

cases.title: A gitignored file under an input glob changes nothing
cases.why: Files git ignores are local state such as logs, editor files and caches, not part of the source. They differ between machines and change on their own. Keying on them gives every machine a different key, so the cache misses on every CI runner and laptop even when the committed source is identical.

cases.title: A new file git does not track yet is an input
cases.why: A task reads what is on disk, not what git has recorded. A developer adds a file and builds before committing, and the new file belongs in the output. A tool that keys only on tracked files replays the old result until the next commit, hiding the new file from local builds.

cases.title: Making an input executable runs the task again
cases.why: The file mode is part of what a task reads: a build that copies a script ships it runnable or not. A key that hashes content alone sees no change after `chmod +x`. The cache then replays an output whose script is not executable, and the failure shows only when someone tries to run it.

cases.title: Making the file an input link points at executable runs the task again
cases.why: The link itself is unchanged; only the mode of the file it points to moved. The task reads that mode, so its output can change, as a script that checks whether a file is runnable does. A key that looks only at the link, or ignores modes, replays the old result under the new tree.

cases.title: Two dependencies that swap contents, at the same output path, run the project built on them again
cases.why: After the swap each dependency holds what the other had, so the set of files is the same but which name holds which is not. The consumer reads them by name and builds a different result. A key that folds the dependencies without their order sees nothing new and replays the old output.

cases.title: Editing a dependency rebuilds the projects that read its output
cases.why: A project built from a dependency’s output must rebuild when that dependency changes. Otherwise the app keeps bundling the old library while the library itself is new, and the two disagree inside one green build. The mismatch is hard to spot because each project looks up to date on its own.

cases.title: Editing one project does not rerun a project that does not depend on it
cases.why: A change can only affect projects that read it, directly or through their dependencies. Rebuilding unrelated projects on every edit makes CI time grow with the size of the repo rather than the size of the change. In a large monorepo that is the difference between checking one package and rebuilding everything.

cases.title: An edit to a file outside a dependency’s build inputs does not rebuild its dependents
cases.why: A dependant is affected only when something its dependency’s build reads has changed. A test file in a library does not change the built library, so the app built from it stays the same. Rebuilding the whole chain on every test edit throws away cached work whose result is already known.

cases.title: A project nested inside another keeps its files out of the outer project’s inputs
cases.why: A project nested in another’s folder owns its own files. If the outer project’s `**` also counts them, every edit inside the inner project reruns the outer one too. Project boundaries are what keep one team’s change from invalidating another team’s cache.

cases.title: Pointing an input symlink at another file runs the task again
cases.why: A task reads the file behind a link, so pointing the link somewhere else changes the input. A key built from the link’s own path, or from what it pointed at once, misses the change. The cache then replays output built from the old target while the tree points at the new one.

cases.title: A task that lists no inputs never replays a stale result when a file it reads changes
cases.why: When a task lists no inputs, any default is a guess at what it reads. Here the command reads a file outside its project; when that file changes, a guessed key does not, and the cache replays the old bytes under a green run. Not caching such a task, or rerunning it, is right. Declaring inputs is how a task earns caching.

cases.title: A task that lists no inputs never replays a stale result when a variable it reads changes
cases.why: A task that lists no inputs gives the tool no way to know which variables it reads. A cache keyed on files alone replays the output of a value the command no longer sees: `MODE` moves from dev to prod and a dev build ships as prod. Rerunning the task, or hiding the variable from it, both keep the output true.

cases.title: A task that lists no inputs runs again when its project’s sources change
cases.why: Whatever a tool does with a task that declares no inputs, it must not miss an edit to the project’s own sources. Running such a task every time is correct, and so is keying it on a default set that covers the edit. Replaying the result from before the edit would ship old code after a plain source change.

cases.title: An edit deep under a brace alternative ending in `**` runs the task again
cases.why: A brace stands for its alternatives, so `{src/**,lib/**}` means `src/**` and `lib/**`, each at full depth. A tool that matches `**` inside a brace only one level deep misses nested files. An edit deep under `src` then replays output built from the old file.

cases.title: An input `{src,lib}` keys every file under both directories
cases.why: Each brace alternative here names a directory, and a directory input keys its whole tree. `{src,lib}` should mean the same as listing `src` and `lib`. A tool that matches only the directory entries keys nothing inside, and edits under them replay stale output.

cases.title: An input `{./src,lib}/**` keys files under `src`
cases.why: `./src` and `src` name the same directory, inside a brace or not. A tool that compares the alternative to paths without dropping the `./` matches nothing. Edits under `src` then change no key, and the old output replays. Writing `./` is a style choice and must not change which files are keyed.

cases.title: An input `{.,src}/*.txt` keys a `.txt` file at the project’s top
cases.why: `.` is the project directory, so `{.,src}/*.txt` covers `.txt` files at the project’s top and in `src`. A tool that drops or mismatches the `.` alternative misses the top-level file. Edits to it then replay a stale result. The pattern is valid and common in shell-style globs.

cases.title: A file no brace alternative names changes nothing
cases.why: A brace limits the inputs to the paths its alternatives name. A file in a directory no alternative names is not what the task reads. Keying it anyway reruns the task on unrelated edits, wasting work on every developer machine and in CI. The brace is how the user narrows the set.

cases.title: A `,` inside a class in a brace alternative is part of the name, not a cut
cases.why: Inside a character class, a `,` is a character to match, not a brace separator. A parser that splits on it first breaks `a[,]b` into two broken alternatives. The file `a,b.txt` then matches nothing, and edits to it replay stale output. Classes are parsed before alternatives are cut.

cases.title: A `{` inside a class in a brace alternative is part of the name
cases.why: Inside a character class, `{` is a character to match, not the start of a nested brace. A parser that reads it as syntax mangles the pattern. The file `a{b.txt` drops out of the key, and its edits replay a stale result. Classes are parsed before braces, so their contents are plain characters.

cases.title: A `!` brace alternative with a `,` in a class takes that file back
cases.why: A negation is parsed the same way as a positive glob, so `a[,]b` still names `a,b.txt`. If the negation is split at the comma, it matches nothing and the file stays an input. Every edit to it then reruns a task the user said it does not affect. Negations follow the same grammar as the globs they narrow.

cases.title: An input `src/\{b\}.txt` keys the file named with the braces
cases.why: A backslash escapes a brace, so `src/\{b\}.txt` names the file `{b}.txt` literally. Braces in file names are rare but legal. A tool that drops the escapes keys `b.txt` instead, and edits to the real file replay a stale result. The escape is the only way to name such a file in a glob.

cases.title: An input `src/\{b\}.txt` does not key `src/b.txt`
cases.why: An escaped brace is literal text, not an alternative, so `src/\{b\}.txt` does not name `src/b.txt`. The escape is how the user says exactly which file they mean. Keying the other file reruns the task when nothing it reads changed. Reading it as a brace undoes the escape.

cases.title: An input written `./src/**` keys the files under `src`
cases.why: `./src/**` and `src/**` name the same files; the `./` prefix is a common way to write a relative path. A tool that matches the glob against paths without `./` finds nothing. The key then never moves, and every edit under `src` replays the old output.

cases.title: A negation written `!./gen/**` takes `gen` back out of the inputs
cases.why: A negation written `!./gen/**` takes back the same files as `!gen/**`. If the `./` makes it match nothing, `gen` stays in the inputs. Every regeneration then reruns a task the user said does not read it. Generated files are often the very thing such a negation is written to exclude, so the rerun repeats on every generator run.

cases.title: Outputs written `./dist/**` are stored and restored
cases.why: Output globs are project-relative paths, and `./dist/**` names the same files as `dist/**`. If the `./` makes the glob match nothing, the cache stores an empty entry. A later replay then counts as a hit and restores nothing, leaving `dist` missing for the next step.

cases.title: An input `*/.` names each top directory’s whole tree
cases.why: `src/.` is the directory `src` itself, so `*/.` names each top directory and its whole tree. A tool that treats the trailing `.` as a literal file name matches nothing. The task’s key then ignores every source edit and replays the old output. `.` means the directory in any path.

cases.title: A negation `!gen/.` takes the whole `gen` tree back
cases.why: A negation `!gen/.` names the directory `gen` and takes its whole tree back. If the trailing `.` makes the negation match nothing, generated files stay in the key. Every regeneration then reruns a task the user excluded them from. Its positive form keys the whole tree, so its negation takes the whole tree back.

cases.title: An input `src/**/` (a trailing slash) keys the files under `src`
cases.why: A trailing slash marks a pattern as a directory, so `src/**/` covers the directories under `src` and the files in them. A tool that matches only directory entries keys no file. The key never moves, and edits under `src` replay stale output. The slash narrows the match to directories; it does not empty it.

cases.title: An input naming a directory, `src`, keys every file in its tree
cases.why: A user who names a directory, `src`, means the files in it. A tool that treats the name as a glob matching only the directory entry keys nothing inside. Every edit under `src` then replays the old output, with no warning. Naming a directory is the simplest input there is, so it must mean its contents.

cases.title: An input naming a directory with a trailing slash, `src/`, keys its tree
cases.why: `src/` is a common way to name a directory, and it means every file in its tree. Read as a bare glob, it matches no file and the key never moves. Every edit under `src` then replays the old output under a green run. The slash only says the path is a directory; it does not change which files are in it.

cases.title: A negation naming a directory, `!gen`, takes its whole tree back
cases.why: A negation naming a directory, `!gen`, takes back every file in that tree, just as the positive form keys it. If it only removed the directory entry, the generated files would stay in the key. Each regeneration would then rerun a task the user excluded them from.

cases.title: An output naming a directory, `dist`, stores and restores its whole tree
cases.why: An output naming a directory, `dist`, means everything the task wrote there. A tool that stores only the directory entry restores an empty `dist` on a replay. The next step then finds no build output, though the run reported a cache hit. A hit that restores nothing is worse than a miss, because nothing looks wrong.

cases.title: A dotfile under an output glob is restored with the rest
cases.why: An output glob covers every file the task wrote under it, dotfiles included. Dotfiles in build output often carry metadata, manifests or config. Leaving them out of the stored entry restores a tree that differs from a fresh build. A replay must leave the same tree a fresh run does.

cases.title: An input `app/[ab]/*.js` keys the directories the class names
cases.why: A character class `[ab]` matches one of the listed characters, as in any glob. `app/[ab]/*.js` therefore covers `app/a` and `app/b`. A tool that reads the brackets literally keys nothing, and edits to those files replay stale output. Classes are part of every common glob syntax.

cases.title: An input `app/[ab]/*.js` does not key a directory the class leaves out
cases.why: A character class matches only the characters it lists, so `app/[ab]/` leaves `app/c` out. A file outside the class is not what the task reads. Keying it reruns the task on edits that cannot change its output. The class is how the user narrows the set, and the cache should honour it.

cases.title: An input `app/\[id\]/**` keys the route directory named `[id]`
cases.why: File-system routers name directories with brackets, such as `app/[id]`, and an escaped `\[id\]` names that directory literally. Read as a class, the pattern matches `app/i/…` and never the route. An edit to the route then replays the old output. Without the escape, a bracketed route cannot be named at all.

cases.title: An input `app/\[id\]/*.js` does not key the sibling `app/i` a class would match
cases.why: An escaped `\[id\]` names the literal directory `[id]`, not a class of the letters i and d. A sibling `app/i` is not what the task reads. Keying it reruns the task on edits that cannot change its output. The escape is how the user says the brackets are part of the name, and the match should honour that.

cases.title: An output `app/\[id\]/page.js` restores the route and leaves the sibling `app/i` alone
cases.why: An escaped output `app/\[id\]/page.js` names the route file literally. Read as a class, it matches `app/i/page.js` instead, so a restore can overwrite or delete that sibling and miss the route. A replay must bring back the route and leave unrelated files alone.

cases.title: A `!` input listed before the glob it narrows still takes its file back
cases.why: Inputs are a set, not an ordered ignore file: the position of a negation in the list carries no meaning. A tool that applies a negation only to globs listed before it ignores this one. The excluded file then keys the task, and edits to it rerun the task for nothing.

cases.title: A task whose inputs cover its own outputs still replays on the next run
cases.why: A broad input such as `**` often covers the task’s own output directory. Keying a task on what it wrote moves its key after every run, so it never replays. The cache then fills with entries nothing uses, and every run does the full work. Declared outputs are what the task makes, never what it reads.

cases.title: A committed file under a nested `node_modules` is an input like any other
cases.why: Ignored files are local state, but a file committed to the repository is source, whatever directory it sits in. An install under `node_modules` is untracked; a committed test fixture there is not. Skipping it by directory name replays tests against the old fixture.

cases.title: A committed file under a dot directory (`.github`) is an input of `**`
cases.why: A committed file under a dot directory like `.github` is part of the repository, and `**` covers it. Shell-style globbing skips dot directories unless asked. A task that reads such a file would then replay stale output after it changes. `**` in an input means every file under it.

cases.title: A dotfile under an input glob (`src/.env`) is an input
cases.why: A dotfile such as `src/.env` under an input glob is a file the task can read. Shell-style globbing skips dotfiles by default, and a tool that copies that rule drops it from the key. Editing it then replays output built from the old values. Dotfiles are often config, the files most likely to change the output.

cases.title: A file whose name sorts after every other is still an input

cases.title: Projects named like `pkg-b`, `pkg.c` and `pkg0` keep their files out of `pkg`’s inputs

cases.title: Creating a named input file that did not exist runs the task again

cases.title: Input globs into directories that do not exist are no error

cases.title: Two tasks of one project with different negations each key their own set

cases.title: A sibling task keying a file does not pull it into a task that takes it back

cases.title: Editing a declared file at the workspace root runs the task again

cases.title: A root file no root input names changes nothing

cases.title: A root input reaching into another project’s directory keys that file

cases.title: A gitignored file under a root input glob changes nothing

cases.title: A file keying a same-project dependency reruns the task that depends on it
cases.why: A dependency’s key carries its inputs to the tasks after it, inside one project as across projects. Here `test` lists only `package.json` and reads the fixtures through the `fixtures` task’s output. Only that dependency’s key can carry the fixture edit; without it, tests replay against old fixtures.

cases.title: A file outside a same-project dependency’s inputs does not rerun its dependant
cases.why: A file outside the dependency’s inputs, like `fixtures.txt` beside `fixtures/`, changes neither the dependency’s key nor the dependant’s. Both should replay. Rerunning on a name that only resembles an input wastes the run. Inputs are matched by path, not by name likeness, and the dependant inherits only the dependency’s key.

cases.title: A committed file another task declares as its output stays readable while that task runs
cases.why: A tool that clears a task’s outputs before running it must not delete a committed file another task reads in parallel. Here `index.json` is both committed source and a declared output. Deleting it mid-run makes the reader fail or read nothing, a failure that depends on timing and is hard to reproduce.

cases.title: A task rewriting its own input ahead of a reader leaves the reader’s output current
cases.why: The reader’s key must see the bytes the formatter wrote in this run, not the ones it found before. A runner that hashes every input up front keys the reader on the old `a.txt` and stores the new output under that key. A later run with the old source then replays output built from the new one, so the build ships text the source no longer holds.

cases.title: A task depending on another project’s named task rebuilds when that task’s output changes
cases.why: A task that depends on another task builds on what that task produced. When the upstream output changes, the dependant must run again, even though none of its own files changed. A runner that only looks at the dependant’s own inputs replays its old output, and the app ships with a generated file from an earlier seed.

cases.title: A result built from an input another task edited mid-run is not replayed once the input is put back
cases.why: A key taken over the old bytes must not be stored with an output built from the new ones. Here another task edits `src/a.txt` while the reader runs, so the reader’s output reflects the edit but its key does not. Once the file is put back, that key matches again and replays the edit that is gone. A runner must re-check its inputs before storing.

cases.title: Tasks built over a dependency whose input was edited mid-run are not replayed once it is put back
cases.why: A stale key does not stay in one task: it flows down the chain. Each dependant folds the dependency’s key from before the edit, while its output carries the edit itself. If the dependency’s entry is not dropped, every task built on it is stored wrong too, and putting the file back replays the whole chain from a state that no longer exists.

cases.title: A change in what a key command prints runs the task again
cases.why: A key command is how a task declares an input that is not a file, such as a tool’s version or a generated value. Its printed answer is part of the key, so a new answer must run the task again. Otherwise the runner replays output built for the old answer, for example a build made with a compiler version that is no longer installed.

cases.title: A key command printing the same as before lets the task replay
cases.why: A key command makes its answer part of the key, not a reason to always run. If it prints the same as before, nothing the task depends on has changed, and the stored result is still right. A runner that treats any key command as uncacheable rebuilds on every run, and the declared input buys only wasted time.

cases.title: A key command that exits non-zero fails the run without running the task
cases.why: Without its answer the key is unknown, so the task can neither replay nor run safely. Running it and storing the result under a guessed key, or replaying an old entry, is how stale bytes reach a green build. A command that fails also often means a tool is missing or broken. The run must stop and say so.

cases.title: A key command two projects share is run once per run
cases.why: A key command reads the state of the machine, which does not change during a run. When two projects declare the same command, its answer is the same for both, so running it twice only costs time. A slow command, such as asking a toolchain for its version, would otherwise be paid once per project on every run.

cases.title: A gitignored `.env.local` keyed through a command’s output reruns the task when edited or removed
cases.why: A gitignored file is local state and is no input by default, which is right. A user who wants such a file to count can say so through a key command, and that explicit choice must hold. Editing or removing `.env.local` must then run the task again; otherwise the build keeps an old API address or a value from a file that no longer exists.

cases.title: A key command reading a dependency’s output answers after that dependency ran
cases.why: A key command must answer for the state the task will run in. If it reads a dependency’s output before that dependency has run, it answers for the previous run. The task then builds from the new output but is stored under the old answer, and a later run replays the wrong result. The command must wait for the dependencies.

cases.title: A task reading a same-project dependency’s output, its inputs excluding it, rebuilds when the source changes
cases.why: A task may leave its dependency’s output out of its own inputs, since that output follows from the dependency’s inputs. Its key must then fold in the dependency’s key. When `src/a.txt` changes, the build runs and the test must run too. Otherwise the test result replayed is for the old source, and a broken change passes.

cases.title: A task reading a same-project dependency’s output replays when nothing changed
cases.why: When nothing changed, both the build and the task that reads its output have results already stored. Folding the dependency’s key, rather than hashing its output after each run, lets the reader replay. A runner that cannot replay here reruns a test suite on every run though no source moved.

cases.title: An input list holding only a `!` pattern never replays a stale result

cases.title: An input `!!vendor/**` never turns the rest of the inputs off

cases.title: A project nested several directories down keeps its files out of the outer project’s inputs

cases.title: A nested project named `pkg*` does not take its sibling `pkg-b` out of the outer inputs

cases.title: An output glob climbing out of the project, `../../victim/**`, never deletes what is there
cases.why: A task owns only the files in its project, and an output glob that climbs out with `..` must not give it more. Tools clear outputs before a run and before a restore. Following `..` there deletes another directory’s files, which may be source or another team’s work. Ignoring or refusing such a glob is safe; deleting is not.

cases.title: An output glob into a sibling whose name extends the project’s, `../a-extra/**`, deletes nothing
cases.why: A sibling whose name starts with the project’s, like `a-extra` beside `a`, is still another directory. A boundary check that compares paths as text prefixes thinks `packages/a-extra` lies inside `packages/a`. The clean before a run or a restore then deletes files the task does not own.

cases.title: An output directory that is a link out of the project never has the link’s target emptied
cases.why: Clearing an output directory must not follow a link out of the project. If `dist` points elsewhere, clearing `dist/**` through the link deletes another directory’s files, which may be the only copy of something. Refusing the run is acceptable; emptying the link’s target is not.

cases.title: A link a task leaves in its output directory is cleared, and the file it points at survives
cases.why: A link the task wrote is the output, not the file it points at. Clearing outputs must remove the link itself and leave its target alone. A tool that follows the link while cleaning deletes a file elsewhere in the repo that the task never wrote, and no later run brings it back.

cases.title: An output under a directory whose name holds a backslash is restored
cases.why: A backslash is an ordinary character in a file name on Linux and macOS. A tool that reads it as a path separator or an escape stores or restores the file under the wrong path, or not at all. The replay then leaves a tree missing an output the task wrote, under a green run.

cases.title: A file under an output directory that no output pattern matches survives a rebuild and a replay
cases.why: `dist/**/*.js` names the build’s files; other files under `dist` are not the task’s to delete. A user may keep notes, fixtures or another tool’s files there. Clearing the whole directory before a run or a replay deletes them, and nothing brings them back.

cases.title: An output naming a directory with a trailing slash, `dist/`, stores and restores its tree
cases.why: Writing a directory as `dist/` is a common way to say the whole tree. A tool that reads it as a pattern matching nothing stores an empty entry. The next replay then restores nothing, so the task has to run again for work that was already done, or the tree is left without its build.

cases.title: A root output naming a directory, `generated`, stores and restores its tree
cases.why: A root output that names a directory, like `generated`, means everything under it. If the tool stores only the directory, or nothing, a later run cannot restore the files. The task then runs again for work already done, or a replay reports success while `generated` stays empty.

cases.title: A root output inside the task’s own project is not its own input, though its inputs cover it
cases.why: A file the task writes is its output, never its input, even when an input glob such as `**` covers it. If the key includes it, each run changes the key of the next, so the second run misses. The task then reruns on every run and the cache never helps it.

cases.title: A key command printing a different byte that is not UTF-8 runs the task again

cases.title: Colour, short status and quoted paths in the repository’s git config still let an edit rerun
cases.why: Repository git settings are the user’s to choose and must not change what a task runner sees. cases.title: An edit to a committed file inside the task’s own output directory runs it again
cases.why: A committed file the task reads is an input, even when it sits inside a directory declared as output. Left out of the key as an output, an edit to it changes nothing the tool sees. The run then replays the old build and writes the old generated file over the new data.

cases.title: A committed edit to a file under the outputs, outside the inputs, is not reverted by a replay
cases.why: A replay writes back what the task produced, not the committed state of every file under its output glob. Here `out/LICENSE` is committed source the task never writes. cases.title: A committed file under the outputs made executable is not made plain again by a replay
