cases.title: A file force-added to git under ignored outputs, then edited and committed, is not reverted by a replay
cases.why: Git tracks the file although its folder is ignored, because the user added it on purpose and then edited and committed it. A replay that writes the cached copy over it destroys committed work. The tree must keep what version control holds, not what an older run left behind.

cases.title: A generator rewriting its committed output leaves the new bytes, and a later run brings them back
cases.why: A generated file that is also committed must end up matching what the generator makes now. After the user resets it to the committed version, the next run must bring the new output back, by running or by replay. A tool that sees the committed bytes and calls it done leaves a stale route table in the tree.

cases.title: A committed file under a root output glob survives a run that no longer writes it
cases.why: A committed file under an output glob is source the repository holds, not something this task made. A task that stops writing it does not own it. Clearing every match before the run deletes it, and the user finds a tracked file missing after a build.

cases.title: A skip-worktree input absent from disk, as a sparse checkout leaves it, reruns the task once it appears
cases.why: A sparse checkout leaves some tracked files off disk; that is not a change by anyone. When the file appears, the task reads new content and must rerun. A tool that trusts git’s skip-worktree flag never looks at the file and replays the build made without it.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, changing an input from CRLF to LF runs the task again
cases.why: Under `* text=auto`, git normalises line endings, so a CRLF file and its LF version are one blob to git. The task reads the bytes on disk, and those differ. A tool that keys on git’s blob id sees no change and replays the CRLF build, here a wrong byte count. Windows checkouts and editors switch endings all the time.

cases.title: A root `.gitattributes` text rule reaches a run of one project: CRLF to LF runs it again
cases.why: A root `.gitattributes` applies to every project, also when a run selects only one. git compares the file after that rule, so CRLF and LF read as one blob while the task reads different bytes. A tool that trusts git here, or reads attributes only from the selected project, replays the build made from the CRLF file.

cases.title: A text rule in the user’s global git attributes file: CRLF to LF runs the task again
cases.why: Text rules can also come from the user’s global git attributes file, outside the repo. Under such a rule git sees CRLF and LF as one blob, while the task reads different bytes. A tool that trusts git’s view replays the old build, and only on machines with that setting, which makes the stale result hard to reproduce.

cases.title: With `core.autocrlf` set, changing an input from CRLF to LF runs the task again
cases.why: `core.autocrlf` makes git convert line endings, so it reports no change when CRLF becomes LF. The task reads the file on disk, whose bytes did change. A tool that trusts git here replays the CRLF build, and whether a developer gets a stale result depends on their own git config.

cases.title: With git's `core.trustctime=false`, a same-size edit that keeps its mtime runs the task again
cases.why: With `core.trustctime=false` git ignores the change time, so a same-size rewrite that keeps the mtime looks clean to git. The task reads new bytes all the same. A tool that trusts git’s clean answer replays the old output. The setting is common where backup or indexing tools touch the change time.

cases.title: With git's `core.checkStat=minimal`, a same-size edit that keeps its mtime runs the task again
cases.why: With `core.checkStat=minimal` git compares only size and whole-second mtime. A same-size edit with the same mtime then looks clean to git while the bytes differ. A tool that trusts git’s answer replays the old output. Such edits come from tools that restore timestamps, such as archive extractors and sync tools.

cases.title: A consumer reading what its dependency writes into it as a root output builds each version
cases.why: A file one task writes into another project mid-run must be keyed as it is when the reader runs. Keyed before it lands, the consumer’s key reflects the previous version, and the run replays a build made from another version. Cycling through versions shows the mismatch. A tool may refuse an input over another task’s output instead.

cases.title: Renaming an input and back leaves only the outputs that name produces
cases.why: Renaming a file can change which output files a task writes, even with the same bytes. Each name’s entry holds its own outputs, and switching back must leave only that name’s files. A replay that adds to the old tree leaves `a.js` and `b.js` side by side, and a bundle or test picks up a file with no source.

cases.title: An edit to a committed input whose name is not UTF-8 never replays the old build
cases.why: File names on Linux are bytes and need not be valid UTF-8. Committed, such a name reaches a tool through git, which escapes it in its plain output; a tool that cannot decode it may drop the file from the key, and its edit replays the old build. Refusing the name is acceptable; ignoring the file is not.

cases.title: An edit to an untracked input whose name is not UTF-8 never replays the old build
cases.why: File names on Linux are bytes and need not be valid UTF-8. Untracked, such a name is found only by walking the disk; a tool that cannot decode it may drop the file from the key, and its edit replays the old build. Refusing the name is acceptable; ignoring the file is not.

cases.title: An edit to a root input whose name is not UTF-8 never replays the old build
cases.why: Root inputs are matched like project inputs, and a name that is not UTF-8 must count there too. Shared files at the root are often read by many tasks. A tool that drops the odd name from the key replays old builds in every task that reads it. Refusing the name is acceptable; skipping it is not.

cases.title: A name that is not UTF-8 in one project does not stop another project’s task
cases.why: A problem in one project’s files must not stop unrelated projects. A tool that fails the whole workspace on one odd file name blocks every build until someone renames it. Refusing the project that holds the name, or keying the name as bytes, both let project `b` build.

cases.title: An input whose name holds U+FFFD as a character is an input like any other
cases.why: U+FFFD is a valid character that a file name can hold, not a sign of a broken name. A tool that uses it to mark bytes it could not decode, and then drops such names, loses a real file from the key. Edits to it then replay the old output, under a green run.

cases.title: An output whose name is not UTF-8 is there after the next run, replayed or rebuilt
cases.why: Outputs whose names are not UTF-8 must be stored and restored like any other. An entry saved without such a file restores a tree missing an output the task wrote. Anything that later reads that file fails, or ships without it, under a green run. Rebuilding instead of replaying is also correct.

cases.title: A file dropped by hand into a dependency’s output directory does not rerun its dependants
cases.why: A dependant keys on what its dependency is built from, not on every file sitting in the dependency’s output directory. A stray file dropped there by hand does not change what the dependency produces. Rerunning the whole chain for it wastes time, and the dependency’s replay restores its own outputs anyway.

cases.title: A new file under a root input glob runs the task again
cases.why: A root input glob names a set of files, and adding a file to it is a change. A new file under shared `config/` often changes how every task that reads it builds. A tool that keys only the root files it saw before replays the old output without the new config.

cases.title: A task whose inputs cover another task’s output never replays a build of that output’s old bytes
cases.why: When one task’s inputs cover another task’s output, the key must see that output as it is when the reader runs. Keyed before it lands, the reader’s key reflects the previous contents, and the run replays a build of old generated code. Switching the seed back and forth shows it. A tool may refuse the overlap instead.

cases.title: In projects that depend on each other, editing one reruns only its task
cases.why: Projects that depend on each other through their manifests still own separate files. A task that reads only its own sources, with no task dependency, need not rerun when the other project changes. Treating the cycle as one unit reruns both on every edit, or refuses a workspace the package manager accepts.

cases.title: An input a dependency deletes before its dependant starts lets the dependant run
cases.why: A file a dependency deletes before the dependant runs is simply absent when the dependant reads its inputs. The right key treats it as gone. A tool that hashed the inputs up front fails on the missing file, or keys content that no longer exists and later replays a listing that still names it.

cases.title: Edits behind an input directory that is a link, and behind a linked root input directory, rerun
cases.why: A task reads through a linked directory to the files behind it, and shared code is often linked into a project this way. A tool that keys on the link itself, or skips links while walking, sees no change when the files behind it are edited. The run then replays the old build.

cases.title: Edits behind links below a glob’s fixed directory, one of them never committed, rerun
cases.why: Links can sit anywhere below a glob’s fixed part, and some are made after the last commit. The task reads through all of them. A tool that walks only the fixed directory, or lists only what git tracks, misses edits behind these links and replays the old build.

cases.title: An edit behind a brace alternative’s directory that is a link reruns
cases.why: A brace pattern like `{lib,src}/**` expands into several directories, and any of them can be a link. A tool that follows links for plain globs but not for brace alternatives misses edits behind a linked one. The run then replays old output for files the task reads.

cases.title: An edit behind a link inside a gitignored input directory reruns
cases.why: Naming an ignored directory in the inputs opts it in, and links inside it still lead to files the task reads. Generated folders often hold links to shared code. A tool that walks the ignored folder but does not follow its links misses edits behind them and replays the old build.

cases.title: A committed edit to a tracked file an input link out of the project points at reruns
cases.why: A link that points outside the project still names a file the task reads. Committing the edit behind it must not hide it: git sees the link itself unchanged, since only the target’s content moved. A tool that keys on git’s record of the link replays the build made from the old target.

cases.title: An edit behind an input link to a file outside the project reruns
cases.why: A task reads the contents behind an input link, wherever that file lives. A tool that keys on the link’s own text sees the same target path after an edit. The run then replays output built from the old contents, though the file the task reads has changed.

cases.title: An edit to a gitignored file an input link points at reruns
cases.why: A link listed as an input makes its target an input, even when the target is gitignored: explicit inputs beat ignore rules. A tool that keys only on tracked or unignored content misses the edit behind the link. The run then replays the build made from the old target.

cases.title: An edit, and then a new file, behind a linked input directory rerun
cases.why: Files behind a linked input directory count like files in a real one, including new ones. A tool that records the directory’s content once, or only what git tracks, misses a file added behind the link. The task’s glob reads it, so the replayed output is missing it.

cases.title: An edit behind a link found inside a linked input directory reruns
cases.why: Links can chain: a linked directory may itself hold links. The task follows every one of them when it reads. A tool that resolves only the first level keys a link it cannot see through, and edits behind the second link replay the old build. Shared folders linked from several places often look like this.

cases.title: A dangling input link reruns its task once the file it names appears
cases.why: A dangling link is an input whose target is missing, and that missing state belongs in the key. When the target appears, the task reads new content and must rerun. A tool that skips dangling links keys the same before and after, and keeps replaying output that says the file is absent.

cases.title: Input links that point at each other are no error, and an unchanged tree replays
cases.why: Links that point at each other are legal on disk and turn up in real repos by mistake. A tool that follows them without a limit hangs or crashes, and one that treats them as an error fails a build that runs fine. Keying them as unresolved links lets an unchanged tree replay like any other.

cases.title: A stray file under an output glob the task never wrote to is gone after a replay
cases.why: A replay must leave the output tree as the task left it, and here the task wrote nothing. A tool that skips the clean when the entry is empty leaves a stray file in place. That file then ships, or gets tested, as if this build had made it, and the next clean build disagrees.

cases.title: A stray file under a root output glob the task never wrote to is gone after a replay
cases.why: A root output glob is cleaned on replay like a project one, even when the task wrote nothing under it. Otherwise a stray file, left by hand or by an older build, stays in a directory the task owns. Later steps then read it as if this build produced it.

cases.title: Changed files named in CJK, Cyrillic or with an emoji select their projects
cases.why: Changed files with CJK, Cyrillic or emoji names are ordinary changes. git escapes such names in its plain output; a tool that reads that output without undoing the escaping maps the path to no project. Those projects are then left out of an affected run, and CI skips the very code that changed.

cases.title: A committed change in a project whose directory is named `café` selects it
cases.why: A project’s directory may have a non-ASCII name like `café`, and a change inside it must select it. If git’s escaped path is compared with the decoded directory name, the two never match. The changed project is then left out of an affected run, and CI goes green without testing it.

cases.title: An input made unreadable after an edit fails the task or rebuilds it, never replays
cases.why: A file the tool cannot read cannot key the task, so the tool must not act as if nothing changed. Leaving it out of the key replays the build from before the edit. Failing the run or rebuilding are both honest outcomes the user can see; a replay hides the edit.

cases.title: Editing an input git was told to assume unchanged runs the task again
cases.why: `--assume-unchanged` is a promise to git’s status, used to make it faster, not a statement about the build. The bytes on disk are what the task reads. A tool that trusts the flag and keys the committed blob replays stale output after every local edit to that file.

cases.title: Editing an input git was told to skip in the work tree runs the task again
cases.why: `--skip-worktree` tells git to stop looking at a file, often for local config overrides or sparse checkouts. It says nothing about what the build reads. Keying the committed blob instead of the bytes on disk replays output built from content that is not there.

cases.title: A same-size edit that keeps the file’s modification time runs the task again
cases.why: Size and modification time are a hint for when to look again, not the content. Copying with `cp -p` or `touch -r` can leave both as they were after a real edit. A tool that trusts them alone replays output built from the old bytes under a green run. The content is what the task reads.

cases.title: A same-size edit within the same whole-second stamp as the first write runs the task again
cases.why: ext3, HFS+, FAT and some network mounts keep only whole seconds. Two writes in one second then carry one stamp, and a same-size edit looks untouched. A tool that trusts the stamp replays stale output, a bug that only shows after quick edits such as a script or a fast save.

cases.title: An input edited while the task runs is not replayed under the key of the bytes before
cases.why: The output was made from bytes edited during the run, not the ones read when the key was taken. Stored under the first bytes’ key, undoing the edit later replays the edited result. The tool must notice the change and not file the output under a key it does not match.

cases.title: An edit to a project inside a nested repository (a submodule) runs its task again
cases.why: A submodule is held by the outer repository as one entry, a commit id, not as files. None of the project’s files are the outer git’s to list. A tool that keys the project from the outer index sees nothing change, and edits inside the submodule replay stale output.

cases.title: An edit to a project inside a nested repository (untracked) runs its task again
cases.why: A nested repository the outer one does not track is invisible to the outer git’s listing, yet its files are still the project’s sources. A tool that relies on the outer git alone keys none of them. Every edit then replays the old output, and the project never rebuilds until its cache is cleared.

cases.title: An edit inside a nested repository (a submodule) under a project’s input glob runs its task again
cases.why: The outer git holds a vendored submodule as one path pinned to a commit, but its working files can still change. Those files are what the task reads. Keying the gitlink alone misses edits made inside it, which replay stale output until someone commits the submodule.

cases.title: An edit inside a nested repository (untracked) under a project’s input glob runs its task again
cases.why: An untracked nested repository under a project’s input glob is a directory of files the task reads. The outer git skips it as a separate repository. A tool that relies on that listing drops the files from the key, and their edits replay a stale result.

cases.title: A file a nested repository tracks despite its own ignore rule is an input
cases.why: An ignore rule only stops untracked files: one a repository force-added is source like any other. That holds inside a nested repository too. A tool that applies the nested `.gitignore` without checking that repository’s index drops the file, and edits to it replay stale output.

cases.title: An input glob over a nested project never replays a stale result
cases.why: Another project’s files belong to it, so a glob reaching into a nested project is a boundary question. A tool may refuse the glob, or key on those files. Silently dropping them while the command still reads them replays a stale result, which is the one wrong answer.

cases.title: An input naming a file of a nested project never replays a stale result
cases.why: An input that names one file of a nested project is explicit, but the file belongs to that other project. A tool may refuse the path or key on it. Accepting the name and then keying nothing replays output built from the old file, with no sign that anything was skipped.

cases.title: A brace input reaching a nested project never replays a stale result
cases.why: A brace alternative can reach a nested project as easily as a plain glob. A tool must apply the same rule to it: refuse it, or key the file. Expanding the brace without that check lets the nested file change unseen and replays a stale result.

cases.title: A committed file in an output directory survives a run when git cannot read its index
cases.why: A git that cannot read its index lists nothing, which looks like nothing is committed. A tool that clears outputs before a run must refuse when it cannot tell what is committed, not delete. Losing a user’s committed file is worse than any failed build.

cases.title: A committed file reached through a linked output directory is never deleted
cases.why: A link such as `public -> static`, made by a setup script, is the output’s path; the committed files behind it are the user’s source. A tool that clears or restores outputs through the link must not delete them. Doing so destroys files in the repository during a routine build.

cases.title: A `!` input takes its files back from every positive glob that matched them
cases.why: A negated input removes its files from the task’s whole input set, not only from the glob listed next to it. If the exclusion applied to one positive glob only, a spec file matched by another glob would still key the build. Every edit to a spec file would then rebuild output that never reads it.

cases.title: An input `src/*` keys the dotfile `src/.env`
cases.why: An input glob lists the files a task reads, so `src/*` covers every file in `src`, dotfiles included. Shell-style globbing hides dotfiles unless asked, and a `.env` the task reads would then change no key. Editing it would replay output built from the old values under a green run.

cases.title: A cached task declaring empty inputs replays after a project file changes
cases.why: Empty inputs is an explicit statement that the task reads no file, so it is keyed on its command and config alone. It differs from listing no inputs at all, which says nothing and is not cached. Rerunning it on every project edit would ignore what the user declared and waste the run the cache was meant to save.

cases.title: An input `src/*:*.txt` keys a file whose name holds a colon
cases.why: A colon is a plain character in a POSIX file name, so a wildcard must match it like any other. A tool that reads it as a drive or scheme separator drops the file from the key. Edits to that file then replay the old output, and the build ships content that no longer matches the source.

cases.title: An input naming `src/a:b.txt` outright keys it, untracked or committed
cases.why: An input that names a file outright asks for exactly that file, whatever characters its name holds and whether git tracks it yet. A colon must not be parsed as a separator. Skipping the file lets edits to it replay a stale result, both before and after it is committed.

cases.title: A `!src/a:b.txt` input takes the file with the colon back
cases.why: A negated input names a file the user said does not affect the task, and that holds for a name with a colon too. If the negation fails to parse, the file stays in the key. Every edit to it then reruns work that cannot change the output, on every machine and in CI.

cases.title: An input named with a backslash and a double quote is keyed
cases.why: A file name can hold a backslash or a double quote, and it must be keyed by its real bytes. Listed without `-z`, git C-quotes such a name, and a tool that reads the quoted form looks up a path that does not exist. The file drops out of the key, so edits to it replay a stale result.

cases.title: An input whose name opens with a byte-order mark is keyed, untracked and committed
cases.why: A file name is the exact bytes on disk, including a leading U+FEFF byte-order mark. A decoder that strips the mark loses the name, so the file drops out of the key. Every edit to it then replays the old output, whether the file is untracked or committed.

cases.title: A file in a new untracked directory is an input; an ignored install inside it is not
cases.why: A new file under an input glob is part of what the task reads, even in a directory git has never seen. Missing it replays output built without that file. An ignored `node_modules` install inside the same directory is local state, not source, so it must not key the task and rerun it after every install.

cases.title: Pointing a dangling input link at another missing target runs the task again
cases.why: A symbolic link is an input in its own right: its target string is what it holds, with or without a file behind it. A command can read that string, as `readlink` does here. A tool that skips dangling links keeps the same key after the target changes and replays output naming the old target.

cases.title: A directory link back into its own input tree neither hangs nor fails the run
cases.why: A directory link that points back into its own tree is legal, and it turns up in vendored and generated layouts. A walker that follows links without tracking where it has been loops forever or fails on an endless path. A hung CI job or a crash over a harmless link blocks every build in the repository.

cases.title: Named pipes under the input and output globs neither hang the run nor stop a replay
cases.why: A named pipe holds no bytes to hash or store, and opening one to read blocks until something writes. A tool that reads every matched path as a file hangs the run on the first pipe. Pipes under input or output globs must be passed over, so the build still runs, replays, and reruns on a real edit.

cases.title: A committed input replaced by a directory keys what the directory holds
cases.why: When a committed file becomes a directory of the same name, the task now reads the files inside it. A tool that trusts git’s record of the old file, or skips the path as a type mismatch, keeps the old key. Edits inside the new directory then replay output built from a file that is gone.

cases.title: A project nested in `foo` keeps its files out of `foo`’s inputs beside a sibling `foo-bar`
cases.why: A nested project’s files belong to it alone, so an edit there must not rerun the project around it. Here `foo-bar` sorts between `foo` and `foo/`, and a sorted scan that stops at it never sees `foo/inner` as nested. An edit in `inner` then reruns `foo` too, work nothing asked for.

cases.title: A same-size edit is seen after `git read-tree` leaves the index without file stats
cases.why: An index entry with no stat data says nothing about the file on disk. `git read-tree` leaves the index that way, and a tool that reads it as a sign of a clean file keys the committed blob, not the edited bytes. A same-size edit then replays the old output under a green run.

cases.title: An edit made before `git read-tree` wiped the index stats still runs the task again
cases.why: An edit made before `git read-tree` is still an edit: the bytes on disk differ from the last build. Reading the tree drops the index’s stat data, so a tool comparing stats against the index cannot tell. It must look at the file itself, or the next run replays output built from the old bytes.

cases.title: A gitignored input named outright keys its creation, each edit, and its removal
cases.why: Naming an ignored file such as `.env.local` in the inputs asks for it, even though broad globs skip ignored files. Its creation, each edit and its removal all change what the task reads. Skipping any of them replays a result built from other values, such as a bundle pointed at the wrong API.

cases.title: An input `gen/**` keys every file under the gitignored directory `gen`
cases.why: A glob whose fixed prefix is an ignored directory asks for that directory by name. Generated sources often live in an ignored `gen/`, and the build reads them. Skipping its files replays output built from the old generated code after every regeneration.

cases.title: An input `gen/*.js` keys a matching file in the gitignored directory `gen`
cases.why: An input `gen/*.js` names files in the ignored directory `gen`, so the matching files are inputs. The ignore rule decides what git tracks, not what the task reads. Leaving the match out replays a stale result after the generator rewrites it. The glob still limits the key to the files it matches.

cases.title: An input `gen/*.js` over a gitignored `gen` does not key a JSON file beside the match
cases.why: Naming an ignored directory with a narrow glob asks only for what that glob matches. A JSON file beside the `.js` match is outside it and stays local state. Keying the whole ignored directory would rerun the task on every unrelated generated file. The narrow glob is how the user says which generated files matter.

cases.title: An input naming a generated client under `node_modules` keys it
cases.why: A generator such as `prisma generate` writes its client under `node_modules`, and a build that compiles against it reads it. Naming that path asks for it even though `node_modules` is ignored. Skipping it replays output checked against the old client, and the mismatch shows up only at runtime.

cases.title: An input `gen/**` over a gitignored `gen` keys a `node_modules` inside it
cases.why: An entry naming an ignored directory asks for the whole directory; nothing under it is dropped by name. A `node_modules` inside `gen` is part of what was asked for. Skipping it by its usual meaning replays a stale result after that code changes. Explicit config beats the usual skip rules.

cases.title: A brace input `{gen/a.txt,gen/b.txt}` keys each gitignored file it names
cases.why: A brace of whole paths names each one outright, as its expansions written out would. Each named file is an input even though git ignores it. Treating the brace as a broad glob that skips ignored files replays output built from the old file. The brace is only shorthand for listing the paths one by one.

cases.title: A brace input `{gen,out}/**` keys the files of both gitignored directories
cases.why: `{gen,out}/**` means `gen/**` and `out/**`, and each alternative names an ignored directory outright. Both trees are what the task reads. A tool that treats the brace differently from the two separate globs keys only one of them, and edits to the other replay stale output.

cases.title: An input `gen/**` keys an ignored file beside the `.gitkeep` that keeps `gen` in git
cases.why: git lists the `.gitkeep`, so `gen` looks tracked, but the files beside it are ignored and still what the task reads. A tool that takes git’s listing of a tracked directory as complete misses them. Each regeneration of `gen/client.ts` then replays output built from the old client.

cases.title: An input `out/**` over an ignored `out` keys an untracked file beside a force-added one
cases.why: One force-added file makes git list part of the ignored `out`, but the untracked files beside it are still under the glob. A tool that trusts git’s listing for the directory sees only the committed file. Edits to the rest then replay a stale result. The glob, not git’s listing, decides what is an input.

cases.title: A task that rewrites its own input runs again once the old bytes are put back
cases.why: A task that rewrites its own input, like a formatter, made its result from the bytes before the rewrite but leaves the bytes after on disk. Stored under the old bytes’ key, a later checkout of the unformatted file replays a no-op and leaves it unformatted. The task must run again so the file really is formatted.

cases.title: An input edited and put back while the task runs does not replay the edited result
cases.why: A key describes the bytes the task read, and here the command read an edit that was undone before it finished. The bytes on disk match the key again, but the output came from the edit. Filed under that key, it replays the edited result over a source that no longer holds it.

cases.title: An input another task swaps out and puts back while a task reads it is not replayed
cases.why: Another task swapped the file while the reader ran, so the reader saw the swapped bytes. The key, taken before or after, describes the original bytes. Stored under it, the bad result replays on every later run with the good file, until someone clears the cache by hand.

cases.title: A committed input a dependency edits before the task starts is not replayed once put back
cases.why: The key must describe the bytes the command read, not the bytes before an earlier task ran. Here a dependency edits a committed input just before the task starts. A key taken before the dependency ran files the edited output under the old bytes, and putting those bytes back replays the edit.

cases.title: An untracked input a dependency edits before the task starts is not replayed once put back
cases.why: An untracked input is read the same way as a committed one, so the same rule holds. A dependency edits it just before the task starts, and the output is built from the edit. Filed under the key of the bytes before, it replays the edited result once the original bytes come back.

cases.title: A file behind a linked input directory, edited while the task runs, is not replayed once put back
cases.why: A linked directory’s target string did not change, but a file behind it did while the command ran. The output was built from the new bytes. Stored under the key of the old ones, it replays the edited result once they are put back, and the link gives no sign anything moved.

cases.title: A file behind a linked input file, edited while the task runs, is not replayed once put back
cases.why: A linked input file holds a target string, and the bytes behind it are what the command reads. Here those bytes changed while the task ran. Stored under the key of the bytes before, the output replays the edited content after the original is restored.

cases.title: A file the command adds under an input glob is not replayed once it is gone
cases.why: A key must describe what the task read. Here the command created `src/new.txt` after the key was taken and read it into the output. Stored under that key, the next run replays content from a file that no longer exists. A clean build of the same sources would not produce it.

cases.title: A file added in a directory created while the task runs is not replayed once it is gone
cases.why: The command created a new directory with a file in it after the key was taken, then read that file. The key describes the tree without the directory. Replayed under it, the output carries content from a file that is gone, and a clean build would not reproduce it.

cases.title: A named input absent when the task started, then created by it, is not replayed once gone
cases.why: A named input that is missing when the key is taken is keyed as absent. The command then created it and read it into the output. Stored under the key for its absence, the output replays content from that file the next time it is missing, which a clean build would not produce.

cases.title: A directory link added under an input glob while the task runs is not replayed once gone
cases.why: The command created a link whose name matches no `*.txt`, but the files behind it do, and the command read them. The key was taken without them. Stored under it, the output replays content from files that are no longer reachable once the link is gone.

cases.title: A task writing an ignored file, or one outside its inputs, still replays on the next run
cases.why: A task that writes a log or another ignored file, or a file outside its inputs, has not changed its own inputs. Those writes are side effects and local state, not source. Treating them as input changes would keep the task from ever replaying, so it would rerun on every build.

cases.title: Under a git hook’s GIT_INDEX_FILE, a file a nested repository force-added despite its ignore rule is still an input
cases.why: Git hooks run with `GIT_INDEX_FILE` set to the outer repository’s index. A tool that passes it on reads the wrong index when it lists a project inside a nested repository. The force-added file then drops out of the key, and a build started from a hook, such as pre-commit, replays a stale result.

cases.title: Under a git hook’s GIT_DIR, a file a nested repository force-added despite its ignore rule is still an input
cases.why: Git hooks can run with `GIT_DIR` pointing at the outer repository. Passed through to the nested repository’s listing, it makes git describe the wrong repository. A file the nested repository tracks despite its ignore rule then goes unkeyed, and a pre-commit build replays stale output.

cases.title: Under a git hook’s GIT_INDEX_FILE, a file a nested repository force-added despite its ignore rule is still an input
cases.why: A project can vendor a repository of its own under an input glob. Under a hook’s `GIT_INDEX_FILE`, a tool that lists it with the outer index loses the files that repository force-added. Edits to them replay a stale result only when run from a hook, which makes the bug hard to see.

cases.title: Under a git hook’s GIT_DIR, a file a nested repository force-added despite its ignore rule is still an input
cases.why: The variables a hook sets describe the outer repository, not one vendored inside a project. With `GIT_DIR` passed on, listing the vendored repository reads the outer one instead. A file it force-added despite its ignore rule falls out of the key, and edits to it replay old output.

cases.title: An input `src/{b}.txt` never replays a stale result for either file it could name
cases.why: A brace with one alternative reads as `src/b.txt` to one glob library and as the literal name `src/{b}.txt` to another. Whichever file a tool keys, the other can change unseen and replay a stale result. Refusing the spelling, or keying both files, is right; replaying old bytes is not.

cases.title: Listing the same declared variables in another order still replays
cases.why: Declared environment variables are a set: their order in the config says nothing about what the task reads. Reordering the list is a cosmetic edit with the same values. Treating it as a change misses the cache for every task the edit touched, on every machine.

cases.title: An output `**/*.js` never deletes or captures a nested project’s built files
cases.why: Project boundaries are hard: a nested project’s build output belongs to that project. An outer output glob like `**/*.js` must not capture it into the outer task’s cache entry or clear it before a run. Otherwise building the outer project deletes or overwrites files the inner project made, local edits included.

cases.title: An output listed twice, and one inside another, restores each file once and intact
cases.why: Output globs that list a file twice, or overlap, still describe one set of files. Storing a file twice in one cache entry has broken restores before, leaving files missing or corrupt. Each file must be stored once and come back intact, however the globs overlap.

cases.title: A replayed `app/**` leaves the route `app/[id]` a later task adds, and drops a stray beside it
cases.why: In an output glob, `app/\[id\]` is the literal directory `[id]`, as file-system routes are often named. Read as a character class, it sets aside `app/i` instead. A replay then keeps the stray file and deletes the real route a later task added, and the app ships without that page.

cases.title: Deleted outputs come back from the cache with the same bytes
cases.why: A cache hit stands in for running the command, so it must leave the files the command would have left. If deleted outputs are not restored, the run is green but `dist` is empty, and the next step, a deploy or a test, reads nothing or fails far from the cause. The bytes must match exactly, or a hit ships something no build produced.

cases.title: Deleted outputs are restored, not rebuilt
cases.why: Deleted outputs with unchanged inputs are the normal state after a fresh clone or a clean. The cache holds the exact bytes the command made, so restoring them is enough. Rerunning the command instead spends its full time on every fresh CI machine, which is the work a cache exists to save.

cases.title: An output edited by hand is put back on the next run
cases.why: The result of a run is the tree the inputs produce, not whatever is on disk. A hand edit left in an output ships bytes no build made, and the green run says nothing is wrong. Putting the cached bytes back, or rerunning, keeps outputs a function of inputs. An edit meant to last belongs in the sources.

cases.title: A rebuild leaves no output the new inputs no longer produce
cases.why: Outputs should be exactly what the current inputs produce. When a source is renamed or deleted, the file it used to produce must go too, or it ships from `dist` forever. Such leftovers are easy to miss: tests may even pass because they still import the old file. Clearing declared outputs before the rebuild avoids it.

cases.title: Restoring an older entry leaves no file a later build added
cases.why: Restoring a cache entry must give the tree that entry’s inputs produced, not that tree laid over the current one. Here a later build added `b.txt`; once its source is removed, the older entry comes back and `b.txt` must go. Leaving it mixes two builds in one directory, a tree no single run made, and it ships.

cases.title: A stray file dropped in an output directory is gone after a restore
cases.why: Declared outputs are what the task wrote, so a restore leaves exactly that. A stray file dropped into `dist` by hand or by another tool would otherwise ship in the package or the deploy. Declaring `dist/**` makes the whole directory the task’s; a file meant to stay belongs outside it or behind a `!` entry.

cases.title: Only declared outputs are restored
cases.why: Only declared outputs are stored and restored. Here the command also writes `tmp/scratch.txt`, which no output names, so a replay must not create it. Restoring undeclared files means the cache guesses, and a guess brings temp files or local state from one machine onto another. Explicit config beats inference.

cases.title: A `!` output pattern keeps that file out of the cache
cases.why: A `!` entry says a path under an output directory is not the task’s output, often local state such as a log or a machine’s settings. It must not be stored, so it is neither shared through a remote cache nor restored on another machine. Restoring it brings back a stale or private file the user excluded on purpose.

cases.title: An executable output comes back executable
cases.why: File mode is part of what a build produces. A script or binary that comes back from the cache without its executable bit fails with permission denied, though the same command run fresh works. The failure shows only on cache hits, often only in CI, which makes it slow to trace.

cases.title: A symlink output comes back as the same link
cases.why: A symlink in the outputs is part of the tree, not a copy of its target. Restored as a regular file, `latest.txt` stops following `out.txt`, and anything that relies on the link breaks or reads old bytes after the next build. Restored as nothing, the path is simply missing. A hit must give the tree the command made.

cases.title: Nested output directories and binary bytes restore intact
cases.why: Outputs are bytes, not text. Images, wasm and compiled files hold null bytes, high bytes and carriage returns that must come back unchanged, and deep directories must keep their full paths. A restore that converts line endings, stops at a null byte or drops nested files gives a broken artifact under a green run.

cases.title: A dependency’s deleted outputs are back before a rebuilding dependent reads them
cases.why: When a dependant rebuilds, its dependencies’ outputs must be on disk first, even if those dependencies hit the cache. Here `lib/dist` was deleted and `app` changed; `app` reads `lib`’s output while it builds. Skipping `lib`’s restore because `lib` has nothing to do makes `app` fail, or build against files that are not there.

cases.title: Two projects with the same command and the same sources keep their own outputs
cases.why: The cache key must include which project a task belongs to. The same command over the same sources runs in a different directory and can produce different files, here each project’s own name. A key shared across projects restores one project’s bytes into the other: a wrong tree under a green run.

cases.title: A replayed task that lists no outputs leaves a file it wrote, and the user then edited, alone
cases.why: A task that declares no outputs restores nothing on a replay. Any default would guess what the task writes, and restoring a guessed file overwrites the user’s later edit with an old copy. Here the user changed `dist/report.txt` after the run, so a replay leaves it alone. Running the command again may rewrite it; that is what the command does.

cases.title: A replayed task that lists no outputs does not bring back a file the user deleted
cases.why: A task that declares no outputs restores nothing on a replay. The user deleted `report.txt`, and nothing declared it an output, so a replay that recreates it puts back bytes the user removed on purpose. A task that wants the file restored declares it, and then the cache knows the file is the task’s.

cases.title: Empty directories a task leaves under its outputs come back with a hit
cases.why: A cache hit should leave the same tree a fresh run leaves, empty directories included. Later steps often expect those directories to exist, such as a server that writes uploads into `dist/empty` or a packager that copies the tree as is. If a hit drops them, the build passes on the machine that ran it and fails on every machine that replayed it.

cases.title: An empty output directory removed on its own comes back on the next run
cases.why: Removing one empty directory from the outputs changes the tree the task is meant to leave, so the next run must put it back. A tool that compares only files sees nothing missing and reports the task as current. Whatever relies on that directory then fails, though the run said every output was in place.

cases.title: An empty directory no output pattern reaches is not brought back by a hit
cases.why: Output patterns say exactly what a task owns, and a hit restores only that. Here the pattern is `dist/*.txt`, which matches files, not the empty directory beside them. A tool that brings back everything the task left on disk restores paths the config never claimed, and can overwrite what another step put there. Explicit config beats what the tool saw on disk.

cases.title: A file dropped into an output directory the task left empty is gone after the next run
cases.why: A directory the task left empty is part of its outputs, so a file dropped into it is a stray. If the next run keeps it, the stray ships with the build: a leftover bundle, an old secret, a test fixture. The tree after a run should be the same whether or not someone touched it in between. The empty directory itself stays, since the task made it.

cases.title: Empty directories an older build left in the outputs do not come back with a hit
cases.why: A cache entry should hold what the task made, not whatever an older build left in the output folder. These empty directories predate the run, so an entry that holds them recreates them on every hit, on every machine. Old layouts then come back long after the code that made them is gone.

cases.title: A stray empty directory under the outputs is gone after a hit
cases.why: A hit should leave the tree exactly as the task makes it, and a stray empty directory is not part of that. Left in place, it changes what a later step sees, such as a packager that ships every folder or a glob that now matches. The directories the task did make stay; only the leftover goes.

cases.title: A directory standing where an output file belongs is replaced by the file
cases.why: When something blocks an output path, the run must still end with the file the task makes. Here a directory stands where `dist/real.txt` belongs. A tool that cannot replace it either fails a build that should pass, or keeps the directory and reports success. Either way the tree is not what the task wrote.

cases.title: Output directories come back with the modes the task gave them
cases.why: Directory modes are part of what a task produces, so a hit must bring them back. A `chmod 700 dist/keys` restored as 0755 lets every user on the machine read what the task kept private. A 0555 directory restored writable lets a later step change files meant to stay fixed. A fresh run and a hit should leave the same permissions.

cases.title: Output directory modes come back when the outputs hold a large file too
cases.why: Directory modes must come back however big the outputs are. A cache may store small and large files by different paths, for example inline or as a separate blob, and one of those paths can drop the modes. The developer then finds a private directory readable only on builds that hold a large file. The result should not depend on file size.

cases.title: Restoring into a partly deleted tree gives the directories it remakes their modes
cases.why: When a restore remakes only part of a tree, the directories it recreates need the same modes a full run gives them. Here `dist/keys` was deleted and must come back as 0700. A tool that recreates it with default permissions exposes the key file inside it. A partial repair should leave the same tree as a full one.

cases.title: An edited output inside a read-only output directory is put back, and the mode kept
cases.why: An edited output must be put back even when it sits in a directory the task made read-only. Writing there means opening the directory for a moment and closing it again. A tool that skips the file leaves the hand edit in a build marked current; one that leaves the directory writable undoes a mode the task chose. Both the bytes and the mode must end as the task left them.

cases.title: A restore writes into an emptied read-only output directory and leaves it read-only
cases.why: A restore must be able to write into a read-only directory the task made, and leave it read-only after. Failing with a permission error turns a cached build red for no reason. Opening the directory and forgetting to close it changes a mode the task set on purpose. The result should match a fresh run.

cases.title: A stray file added after a hit is gone after the next hit
cases.why: Every run must check the outputs against what the task makes, even right after a hit judged them current. A file added after that hit is not part of the cache entry. A tool that trusts its last look skips the check and ships the stray with the next build. Checking the tree on each run is what keeps a hit honest.

cases.title: A brace output pattern over two directories restores both, and nothing beside them
cases.why: A brace pattern like `{dist,lib/esm}/**` names exactly two trees, and a hit restores those two and nothing else. Missing one leaves half a package behind a green run. Restoring `lib/cjs`, which the pattern does not name, brings back files the config never claimed. The pattern is the contract, read the way a shell reads it.

cases.title: A brace of two directory names restores both trees
cases.why: A pattern naming a directory means everything under it, and a brace of two names means both trees. A tool that matches only the directory entries, or only the first alternative, restores empty folders or half the outputs. The hit is green while the build is missing files. This short spelling must cache the same as the long form `{dist,lib}/**`.

cases.title: A brace whose alternative starts with ./ restores both trees
cases.why: `./dist` and `dist` name the same directory, inside a brace as anywhere else. A tool that treats the `./` alternative as a literal name finds nothing and leaves that tree out of the cache. The build then replays with `dist` missing under a green run. A harmless spelling difference should not change what is cached.

cases.title: Two output patterns under one directory restore what each matches: dotfiles and empty directories too, and nothing else
cases.why: When two output patterns cover parts of one directory, a hit restores what either one matches. That includes dotfiles and empty directories under `out/d3/**`, which glob code often skips, and excludes `out/d1/.hid/x`, which neither pattern names. Restoring less leaves a broken build behind a green run; restoring more brings back files nobody claimed.

cases.title: A `**/*.js` output leaves installed packages under node_modules alone
cases.why: `**/*.js` means the build’s own JavaScript, not the packages installed beside it. A clean or restore that reaches into node_modules deletes or reverts installed code, here a local patch to a dependency. The next build or test then runs against packages the developer never chose. Installed packages are local state unless a task names them.

cases.title: An install task that names node_modules as its output gets it restored
cases.why: When a task names node_modules as its output, that is explicit config, and it beats any default that skips the folder. An install task cached this way should get its packages back on a hit. A tool that silently drops the pattern replays a green install with nothing installed, and the next task fails. Skipping node_modules is right only when nobody asked for it.

cases.title: A replayed task that declares no outputs brings back none of the files it wrote
cases.why: A task that declares no outputs has said it leaves nothing worth keeping, so a hit restores nothing. Here the task writes `dist/out.txt` anyway, and a replay must not bring it back. Storing files the config never named means guessing what a task owns, which can replay stale bytes over files another step wrote. If the file matters, the fix is to declare it.

cases.title: A task that declares no outputs still replays on an unchanged tree
cases.why: A task with declared inputs and no outputs, such as a lint or a type check, is still worth caching. Its result is its exit code and log, and both are known for an unchanged tree. Running it again spends minutes on every build for an answer already known. Having no outputs means nothing to restore, not nothing to cache.

cases.title: An output rewritten by hand to bytes of the same length is put back
cases.why: An output edited by hand must be noticed even when the new bytes have the same length. A check of size alone, or an mtime with one-second resolution, sees an unchanged file and keeps the edit. The build then ships content no run of the task produced, under a green result. Comparing content avoids this.

cases.title: Going back to earlier sources restores that build’s output when the task pins every mtime
cases.why: Some builds pin every output mtime for reproducible archives, so two different builds can share size and mtime. Going back to earlier sources must restore that earlier build’s bytes. A tool that judges the outputs current from size and mtime keeps the newer build’s output, so the tree no longer matches its sources. Only the bytes tell the two builds apart.

cases.title: An output made executable by hand comes back with the mode the task gave it
cases.why: File modes are part of the output, so a mode changed by hand must be put back. Here the task makes `dist/out.txt` 0644 and someone marks it executable. A tool that compares only bytes calls the tree current and ships the wrong mode. Packages and deploy steps can act on the executable bit, so the run must leave the mode the task set.

cases.title: Output files named like git’s own (.gitkeep, .gitignore) restore
cases.why: Files like `.gitkeep` and `.gitignore` inside the outputs are the task’s own files, and a hit must restore them. A tool that skips git-looking names leaves them out of the cache. The replayed tree then differs from a fresh run: an empty folder drops out of a package, or an ignore rule a later step relied on is gone. The patterns decide what is an output, not the names.

cases.title: A `.git` directory a task writes inside its outputs restores where it stands
cases.why: Only the workspace’s own `.git` is git’s metadata; a `.git` directory under `dist` is just files the task wrote. A tool that skips every `.git` leaves it out of the cache, so a hit comes back without it. Tasks that build a repo fixture or a checkout then fail after a replay but pass after a run. The output patterns decide what is kept, not the name.

cases.title: A replay where a plain file stands in place of the output directory fails, and keeps the file
cases.why: No output pattern selects a plain file where the output folder should be, so it is work nothing declared. Deleting it to make room for the restore would destroy it. The task itself could not run there either, so failing and keeping the file is the only safe outcome.

cases.title: A task that exits while a child it started still writes its outputs is not replayed with the partial tree
cases.why: The task exited while a child process it started was still writing the outputs. Saved at that moment, the cache entry holds a half-written tree. Every later replay restores that half, so the build looks done and green while files are missing or cut short.

cases.title: An output symlink to a file elsewhere in the workspace comes back as the same link
cases.why: A link in the outputs comes back as a link with the same target text, even when it points outside the output directory. Storing the target’s bytes instead turns the link into a copy that no longer follows the shared file. Dropping it leaves a missing path. Either way the replayed tree differs from the one the command made.

cases.title: A symlink output beside a large file restores both
cases.why: A cache may store large files apart from small ones, but a restore must still give the whole tree. The link and the large file it points to come from one run; restoring one without the other leaves a broken link or a missing file. The file here is large and hard to compress so that such a separate path is taken.

cases.title: An output directory that is a symlink is cached through it
cases.why: The user declared `dist` as the output, and `dist` is a link to `build` inside the same project. That changes where the bytes live, not what the task writes, so outputs are stored by following the link and restored through it. A tool that skips links caches an empty result, and the next replay leaves `build` empty under a green run.

cases.title: An output directory that is a symlink is cached through it beside a `**` pattern
cases.why: The user declared `dist` as the output, and `dist` is a link to `build` inside the same project. That changes where the bytes live, not what the task writes, so outputs are stored by following the link and restored through it. A tool that skips links caches an empty result, and the next replay leaves `build` empty under a green run.

cases.title: A file pattern under an output directory that is a symlink is cached through it
cases.why: The user declared `dist` as the output, and `dist` is a link to `build` inside the same project. That changes where the bytes live, not what the task writes, so outputs are stored by following the link and restored through it. A tool that skips links caches an empty result, and the next replay leaves `build` empty under a green run.

cases.title: An output path that is a link into a nested project never deletes or overwrites that project’s files
cases.why: Project boundaries hold even through a link. Here `a/docs` is a link into the nested project `site`, which has its own build and outputs. If a clean or restore of `a` follows the link, it deletes or overwrites `site`’s files, so building one project silently breaks another. The nested project’s files belong to its own task.

cases.title: A link into .git left inside an output directory never empties the repository
cases.why: Clearing an output directory removes the links in it; it never deletes what they point to. Here a link to `.git` sits inside `dist`. A clean that follows it empties git’s metadata, and the repository, with any work not pushed, is lost. Deleting a link is always safe; deleting through it is not.

cases.title: An output directory that is a link into .git never empties the repository
cases.why: Here the output directory itself is a link into `.git`. A tool may refuse the run or write the build’s files through the link; both keep the repository. Clearing `dist/**` by following the link is never acceptable, because it deletes git’s objects and refs, and with them any work not pushed.

cases.title: A replay never writes an output through a link into .git
cases.why: A replay writes only the files the task produced, and never through a link that leads into `.git`. A file under `.git/hooks` is code git runs on the next commit, so a restore that writes there plants a hook from a cache entry, which a shared cache may have filled from another machine. Running the command itself is the user’s own action and is not held to this.

cases.title: A replay never writes an output through a link to a directory .git does not hold yet
cases.why: A replay writes only the files the task produced, and never through a link that leads into `.git`. A file under `.git/hooks` is code git runs on the next commit, so a restore that writes there plants a hook from a cache entry, which a shared cache may have filled from another machine. Running the command itself is the user’s own action and is not held to this.

cases.title: Two unordered tasks declaring the same output pattern: neither loses its file
cases.why: Two tasks that declare the same output pattern both claim every file under `dist`, with no order between them. A tool that clears a task’s outputs before running it, or restores its entry as the whole of `dist`, deletes the other task’s file. The run still reports green, and the missing file shows up only later. Refusing the pair up front is as good as keeping both.

cases.title: An output pattern that covers another task’s output file: neither loses its file

When the first task reruns or restores, a tool that resets all of `dist` to its own entry wipes `dist/app.js` without any error. The bundle then goes missing from a green build. Refusing the pair is as good as keeping both; dropping one silently is not.

cases.title: An output directory named outright that holds another task’s output file: neither loses its file
cases.why: Naming `dist` outright claims everything below it, including `dist/sub/deep.txt`, which another task writes. A tool that replaces the whole directory on a rerun or restore deletes that file, and nothing reports it. A later step that reads it fails, far from the cause. The overlap must be refused, or both files kept.

A tool that keys `b` only on its own files misses the change upstream and replays stale output after an edit, or after the edit is undone. The dependant’s key must change whenever its dependency’s inputs do.

cases.title: Outputs with paths and file names over 100 bytes restore intact, with their modes
cases.why: A cache must store and restore every path a task writes, whatever its length. Old archive formats limit names to 100 bytes, and deep package layouts or snapshot files pass that easily. A cache that cannot hold a long name drops the file on every restore, or fails a build that passed. Modes, like the executable bit on `dist/cli`, must survive too.

cases.title: Outputs with names over 100 bytes are cached: deleted, they are restored, not rebuilt
cases.why: Long output names should not stop a task from being cached. A tool that cannot store them may skip the entry and rebuild the task each time its outputs are missing. The build stays correct but pays the full cost on every clean checkout. Deleted outputs should mean a restore, not a rebuild.

cases.title: A task whose own output patterns and directories overlap restores exactly the tree it wrote
cases.why: A task’s own output patterns may overlap: `.next/standalone` and `.next/standalone/**` name the same files, as do `.next/*.json` and `.next/**/*.json`. A file two patterns match is one output, not two to write over each other. A tool that stores it twice can fail the restore or leave a half-written file. The hit should leave exactly the tree the task wrote.

cases.title: A task whose own output patterns overlap replays after a restore
cases.why: Overlapping patterns within one task, common in framework configs, should not stop it from replaying. A tool that counts a file twice may see a mismatch after its own restore and rerun the task. Then every run after a clean checkout rebuilds work that was already cached. A restore should settle the task.

cases.title: An output pattern with a brace set of extensions restores those files and no other
cases.why: `.build/**/*.{js,map,ts}` names three extensions, so a hit restores those files and not `.build/c.css`. A tool that mishandles the brace either drops every file or restores the whole tree. The first leaves a broken build behind a green run; the second brings back files the config never claimed. Explicit patterns decide what is cached.

cases.title: Output names with a space, a quote, a backslash or non-ASCII letters restore as written
cases.why: File names with spaces, quotes, backslashes or non-ASCII letters are legal and turn up in assets and tests. A cache must store and restore them exactly. A tool that passes names through a shell or an escaping step can drop, rename or split them, so the restored tree differs from the built one. A file must come back under the name the task gave it.

cases.title: Outputs with odd names are cached: deleted, they are restored, not rebuilt
cases.why: Odd file names should not stop a task from being cached. A tool that fails to store or match them may treat the outputs as missing and rebuild every time. The build stays correct, but a task that never hits costs its full run on every machine. Deleted outputs should be restored, not rebuilt.

cases.title: A large incompressible output restores byte for byte, an executable beside it kept executable
cases.why: A large output must restore byte for byte. Incompressible data, like this 6 MB file, takes the paths that compression, chunking or streaming use for big files. A cache that truncates or corrupts it replays a broken artifact under a green run. The executable bit on the script beside it must survive the same trip.

cases.title: A retried task’s reported time covers every attempt, not only the last
cases.why: A task’s reported time is how long it held up the run, and a retried task held it up for every attempt. Reporting only the last attempt hides the cost of flaky tasks. Time budgets, critical-path estimates and CI dashboards then look better than the build really is. Each attempt counts.

cases.title: A retry does not remove the root output directory a task beside it is writing into
cases.why: A retry may clean up the failed attempt’s outputs, but only the outputs that task declared. Here `p` owns `out/a.txt`, while `q` writes `out/b.txt` into the same folder at the same time. A tool that removes the whole `out` folder before the retry deletes `q`’s file mid-run. One task’s retry must never touch another task’s work.

cases.title: An output whose mode was changed by hand gets back the mode the task gave it
cases.why: A file’s mode is part of what a task produces, so a hand change to it must be undone. Here the task makes `dist/out.txt` 0644 and someone marks it 0755. A tool that compares only bytes keeps the wrong mode and ships it. Packaging and deploy steps can act on the executable bit, so the run must leave the task’s mode.

cases.title: Empty directories a task leaves under its root outputs come back with a hit
cases.why: Empty directories under a root output tree are part of the task’s result, just as under a project’s outputs. A hit must bring back `gen/empty` along with `gen/real.txt`. A tool that stores only files, or handles root outputs on a separate path, drops it. A later step that writes into it then fails only on machines that replayed.

cases.title: A file dropped into a root output directory the task left empty is gone after the next run
cases.why: A root output folder the task left empty is part of its outputs, so a file dropped into it is a stray. The next run must remove it, as it would under a project’s outputs. A tool that cleans only project trees leaves the stray at the workspace root, where it ships or leaks into later steps. The empty folder itself stays.

cases.title: Empty directories an older build left in a root output tree do not come back with a hit
cases.why: A cache entry holds what the task made, not what older builds left behind. `gen/old` predates the run, so it must not be stored or restored. A tool that captures every folder under a root output tree recreates it on every hit, on every machine. Old layouts then outlive the code that made them.

cases.title: A stray empty directory under a root output tree is gone after a hit
cases.why: A stray empty folder under a root output tree is not part of the task’s result, so a hit removes it. Left in place, it changes what a later step sees, such as a glob that now matches or a package that ships an extra folder. Root outputs should be cleaned the same way as project outputs.

cases.title: A hit puts back an edited output, a file replaced by a directory, and removes a stray tree, in one restore
cases.why: A restore must repair every kind of damage at once: an edited file, a file replaced by a directory, and a stray tree. A tool may handle each alone yet fail on the mix, for example by writing a file into a path a directory still holds. The run then goes red, or leaves part of the damage. The end tree must match a fresh run.

cases.title: Appending to an output after a build or a restore does not change what the next restore brings back
cases.why: What a cache stores for a task must not change after the task ends. A cache that hard-links or shares its stored copy with the working tree lets a later edit to the tree rewrite the entry. Every later hit then replays the edit instead of the build. Edits after a build or a restore must stay local.

cases.title: A cached task depending on an uncached one that writes into its own inputs replays by the third run
cases.why: An uncached task that writes a file inside its own inputs changes those inputs the first time it runs. Its dependants may then miss once more, since their keys follow the dependency’s inputs. After that the file is stable, so by the third run the cached task must replay. A tool that never settles reruns the dependant on every build.

cases.title: A cached task depending on an uncached one whose written file git ignores replays on the second run
cases.why: A file git ignores is local state, not a declared input, so an uncached task writing one changes no key. The cached task that depends on it should replay on the second run, its output still holding what the dependency wrote. A tool that counts the ignored file, or treats every uncached dependency as changed, reruns the dependant on every build.

cases.title: A task reading a file an uncached task before it writes builds from the bytes written this run
cases.why: A task’s key reflects the bytes it reads when it runs, not the bytes on disk when the run started. Here an uncached task rewrites `config.json` just before the reader. Keyed from the file as the run found it, the reader replays the previous seed’s output, so the build ships old config under a green run.

cases.title: A committed file an uncached task rewrites ahead of its reader keys the reader on the new bytes
cases.why: A committed, clean file can still change during a run. Here `config.json` is clean in git at the start, but an uncached task overwrites it before the reader runs. Keying the reader from git’s committed content instead of the bytes it reads replays the output of a different config, and the run stays green.

cases.title: A package.json listed as an input and rewritten by an uncached task before its reader keys the reader on the new bytes
cases.why: A `package.json` named in the inputs is an input like any other, even though a tool also reads it as a manifest. Here an uncached task rewrites it before the reader. Keying from the copy read at startup replays output built from an older manifest, so a stale version field ships under a green run.

cases.title: A root input in a dependency that an uncached task there rewrites keys the dependant on the new bytes
cases.why: An input is keyed from what it holds when the task runs, even when it lives in another project and that project’s task writes it. Here `lib`’s uncached `gen` rewrites `lib/config.json` before `app` reads it. Keying `app` from the bytes at the start of the run replays output made from a different config.

cases.title: An uncached writer reached through a task that does nothing still keys its reader on what it wrote
cases.why: Ordering passes through every task in the graph, even one that runs nothing. Here a do-nothing task sits between the uncached writer and the reader. If the reader is keyed before the writer runs because the writer is not its direct dependency, it replays output from the previous seed under a green run.

cases.title: A cached task rewriting a file two do-nothing tasks ahead of its reader keys the reader on the new bytes
cases.why: A cached task can write files too, and a reader further down is keyed on what it wrote. Here `fmt` rewrites `config.json`, and two tasks that do nothing sit between it and the reader. Keying the reader from the file as the run found it, before `fmt` ran, replays output built from the previous seed under a green run.

cases.title: Editing the inputs of an uncached task in a dependency reruns its cached dependant
cases.why: A task that is not cached still has inputs, and its dependants still see them change. Here `ui#bare` is uncached and `app#test` depends on it. Its key comes from its inputs whether it caches or not, and the dependant folds that key, so editing `ui` reruns `app#test`. Otherwise the tests replay green against code they never ran on.

cases.title: Editing a dependency’s sources reruns a cached dependant reached through an uncached task
cases.why: A chain of dependencies passes through an uncached task without breaking. Here `app#test` depends on `ui#build`, which is uncached and depends on `ui#source`. If the uncached task in the middle cuts the chain of keys, an edit to `ui`’s sources leaves `app#test` replaying a result from before the edit, and a failing test goes unseen.

cases.title: Editing a project nothing depends on lets a task with an uncached dependency replay
cases.why: An uncached dependency does not make its dependants uncacheable. Its key comes from its inputs, so only an edit those inputs see reruns the dependant. Here the edit is in a project nothing depends on. Rerunning `app#test` for it spends CI time on every change anywhere, and makes the cache useless above any uncached task.

cases.title: An output symlink to a directory comes back as the same link

Restored as a copy of the directory, the two paths split apart, so a later write to one no longer shows in the other. cases.title: A link with a 300-byte target and an empty directory 300 bytes deep come back
cases.why: Outputs can have long paths, and empty directories are part of the tree. Classic tar headers hold 100 bytes for a name or a link target; past that an archive needs an extended header. One that truncates instead restores a link to the wrong place and drops the deep empty directory: a different tree under a green run.

cases.title: An output link whose target is not there comes back as the same link
cases.why: A link whose target does not exist yet is still output: a build may leave it for a later step, or for the program at runtime, to fill. Saving only what resolves drops the link, and a replay then gives a tree without it. Restoring it with its exact target text keeps a replay equal to a real run.

cases.title: An output link pointed elsewhere by hand, at the same length, is put back
cases.why: A link output edited by hand is like a file edited by hand: the next run puts back what the inputs produce. Here the link is pointed at `b.txt` instead of `a.txt`. The two targets have the same length, so a check of size alone sees no change; only comparing the target text catches it. Otherwise the wrong file ships through the link.

cases.title: Paths a `!` output entry takes back are left in place by a run and never come back from a replay

A replay restores the real outputs but never brings back an excluded file, like the `.tmp` scratch file the command wrote. Excluded means neither cleaned nor stored.

cases.title: A replay restores the outputs and leaves an edited path a `!` entry takes back alone
cases.why: The `!` entry says the file is not the task’s output, so it belongs to the user. Here the user edits `fixture.txt` and deletes the real outputs; the replay restores the outputs and leaves the edited file as it is. A replay that cleans the whole directory or writes over the file loses the user’s bytes with no warning.

cases.title: A stray file in an output directory with `!` entries is gone after a replay

cases.title: Editing a path a `!` output entry takes back, and the inputs name, reruns the task

A tool that leaves a path out of the key because it sits under an output directory replays a result built from the old file.

cases.title: A task adding to the tree of the task before it keeps its `!` scratch file out of what a replay brings back
cases.why: When a later task adds to the earlier task’s output tree, each task’s `!` entries still apply to its own outputs. Here `types` excludes `*.tmp`, so a replay restores `a.js` and `a.d.ts` and leaves the scratch file out. Bringing back an excluded file puts local state into a tree that ships.

cases.title: Two tasks with disjoint outputs, each with a `!` entry, both run

cases.title: A stray in an earlier task’s outputs is gone after a replay, beside a later task’s narrower `!` entry
cases.why: Each task’s `!` entries speak only for its own outputs. The later task’s `!out/types/*.tmp` is about its own tree; it does not make a stray in the earlier task’s `out` anyone’s output. A replay removes the stray, or a file no task wrote ships with the build.

cases.title: A root output’s `!` entry leaves that file in place, out of the replay, and still an input
cases.why: A `!` entry on an output at the workspace root works like one inside the project. Here `gen/keep.txt` is excluded from the root output and named as an input: it stays in place on a run, never comes from a replay, and still reruns the task when it changes. Treating it as output loses the user’s file; leaving it out of the key replays stale results.

cases.title: An output directory the user made a link out of the project stays a link, and a replay writes nothing through it
cases.why: A link at the output directory that leads out of the project is the user’s setup, not the task’s output. A replay that writes through it puts files outside the project, where no run of the task asked. Replacing it with a real directory discards what the user set up. Keeping the link and writing nothing through it is the safe outcome.
