cases.title: A task writing into the root output it reads from the task before it keeps that task’s files
cases.why: A later task may read from and write into the tree the task before it wrote. Here `individual` reads `gen/a.txt` and writes `gen/b.txt` beside it. Clearing the shared tree before the later task runs deletes the file it is about to read, so the run fails or writes the wrong bytes.

cases.title: A task writing into another project’s output directory from the root, and that project’s task adding to it: a warm run keeps both files
cases.why: A task in one project may write into another project’s output directory: here `a` writes `b/dist/a.txt`, and `b` adds its own file after it. A warm run keeps both files. If restoring `b` clears `dist` first, it deletes `a`’s file, and the package ships without it.

cases.title: A task writing into another project’s output directory from the root, and that project’s task adding to it: both replay
cases.why: When nothing changed, both tasks writing into `b/dist` replay. Rerunning them because their outputs share a directory costs their full time on every run. The graph orders them, so restoring `a`’s files and then `b`’s gives the tree the cold run left.

cases.title: A file a later task deletes from an earlier task’s root output stays deleted on warm runs
cases.why: A later task may delete a file the earlier task wrote, here `tmp.js`. On a warm run, the replay of the earlier task brings that file back. The later task must then remove it again, or not be replayed, or the file ships in every warm tree but not in a cold one.

cases.title: A declared variable reaches the command
cases.why: Declaring a variable says the task reads it, so the command must see its value. A tool that filters the environment must still pass declared names through. Otherwise a build meant for production runs with its defaults, and the output is wrong though the run is green.

cases.title: Changing a declared variable runs the task again
cases.why: A declared variable is an input like a file, and a new value is a new input. Builds often switch API addresses, feature flags or modes on a variable. Replaying the dev output when `MODE=prod` ships a development build to production with nothing in the run to say so.

cases.title: Going back to an earlier value restores that value’s outputs
cases.why: A key that depends only on inputs gives back the same output for the same inputs. Switching between dev and prod is routine, and each switch must leave a tree that matches the current value. A tool that keeps the last output in place, or restores the newest entry, leaves a build for the wrong mode.

cases.title: An unset variable and an empty one are different values
cases.why: A command can tell an unset variable from an empty one, and many scripts do, for example with `${VAR-default}`. If the key treats both the same, a run with an empty value replays output made with the default. The tree then holds a result the current environment would not produce.

cases.title: `MODE` and `mode` are different variables
cases.why: Environment variable names are case-sensitive on Linux and macOS, so `MODE` and `mode` are separate values. A key that folds case can take the wrong one, or miss a change to one because the other stayed the same. Either way the output can come from a value the command never saw.

cases.title: A variable the task does not declare changes nothing
cases.why: Only declared variables key a task; the rest of the environment changes all the time. Shells and CI runners set values such as job ids, timestamps and temporary paths that differ on every run. Keying on all of them makes every run a miss, so the cache never helps. Declaring what a task reads is what keeps its key stable.

cases.title: A `.env` file at the workspace root does not set a task’s variable
cases.why: A task’s environment is the one the shell that started the run gave it. A runner that also reads a `.env` at the root sets values nobody passed, from a file the task never declared. The same command then builds one thing on a laptop that has the file and another on CI that lacks it, and a local secret can end up in a build.

cases.title: Neither `.env.local` nor the `.env.<NODE_ENV>` file sets a task’s variable
cases.why: Files such as `.env.local` and `.env.production` are a framework’s convention, not the runner’s. If the runner picks one by `NODE_ENV`, setting one variable silently swaps in a whole file of others. A developer’s local overrides then leak into builds that differ from CI for reasons no config shows. A task that wants these files can load them itself.

cases.title: A `.env` in the directory the run starts from does not set a task’s variable
cases.why: Where a run starts must not change what a task sees. If a `.env` in the current directory were read, the same task run from the root and from inside the project would build two different things. Worse, each could replay the other’s cache entry, since nothing declared says the file was read. The shell’s environment is the only source.

cases.title: With a `.env` present, the value the shell sets is the one the task sees
cases.why: A value set in the shell is an explicit request for this run; a file on disk is not. If a `.env` overrode it, `MODE=from-shell` on the command line would be silently ignored. CI jobs that set variables per job would build with whatever a committed or leftover `.env` says. The explicit value must win, whether or not the runner reads `.env` at all.

cases.title: Editing a `.env` never replays a result built from its old value
cases.why: Whatever a runner does with `.env`, it must not replay a result built from a value that has since changed. A runner that loads `.env` into a declared variable has made the file an input, so its key must change when the file does. Otherwise an edit to `.env` replays output built for the old value. A runner that never loads the file passes too.

cases.title: A bin a project’s dependency ships is on that project’s task PATH
cases.why: A project that depends on a package expects to call that package’s bins by name, as package scripts do. The package manager links them into the project’s `node_modules/.bin`, and the task’s PATH must include it. Without it the command fails with command not found, or runs a global copy of the tool at a version the lockfile never pinned.

cases.title: A dependency shipping a bin named `sh` does not become the shell that runs the command
cases.why: The task’s PATH decides what the names in its command resolve to, not which shell parses the command. If a dependency’s bin named `sh` became the shell, any package could take over every command of the projects that depend on it. The real command would not run, yet the task could still exit 0. The shell is the runner’s choice, not a PATH lookup.

cases.title: A project under a directory holding `:` does not run a file the split PATH entry names relative to it
cases.why: A directory name is data and must not change how PATH is read. Joined into PATH, `packages/x:y/node_modules/.bin` splits in two at the `:`, and the second half is relative, so it resolves against the task’s directory. A file planted at `y/node_modules/.bin` would then run in place of a real tool. A runner must leave out an entry PATH cannot express.

cases.title: Run from inside a project, its dependencies’ tasks still run first
cases.why: A task’s dependencies are part of the task, wherever the run starts. Developers often run a task from inside the project they work on. If the runner skipped the dependencies there, the task would build against a missing or old dependency output and fail or come out wrong, while the same command from the root works.

cases.title: Run from inside a project, a change in its dependency runs it again
cases.why: A task’s key folds in its dependencies, and the directory the run starts from must not change that. Run from inside the project, a change in a dependency must still reach the task. Otherwise the developer gets a replay built against the old dependency while the same command from the root rebuilds, and tests pass against code that is gone.

cases.title: A replay started from a project’s subdirectory restores each output at its own project
cases.why: Outputs belong to their project, and the directory a run starts from changes none of their paths. A replay that restored relative to the current directory would write `dist` into `packages/app/src` and leave the real `dist` missing. The next step, a bundle or a deploy, would then read nothing or old files while the run reported success.

cases.title: A run from inside a project replays what a run from the root stored
cases.why: A task’s key comes from its inputs, not from where the run started. A run from inside a project asks for the same work as a run from the root, so it should replay what the root run stored. If the current directory leaked into the key, every developer who changes directory would rebuild the same tasks and store the same result twice.

cases.title: Forwarded flags reach the command as written, never parsed and rewritten
cases.why: Forwarded args belong to the command, and the runner passes them through untouched. A runner that parses flags and writes them back merges repeated flags, re-cases `--fooBar`, and casts `0010` to `10`. The tool then gets a different request from the one typed, and fails or behaves differently with no visible cause.

cases.title: An empty arg, spaces, a newline, quotes and `$HOME` each reach the command as one arg, unexpanded
cases.why: Each forwarded arg must arrive as exactly one arg with its bytes unchanged. If the runner joins args into a shell string, an empty arg vanishes, `sp ace` becomes two args and `$HOME` expands to a path. A test filter or message passed through the runner then means something else, and text such as `&&` can even start a second command.

cases.title: Forwarded args that look like the runner’s own flags, and an inner `--`, reach the command
cases.why: Everything after the first `--` belongs to the task, and the runner reads none of it. A runner that still acts on `--filter`, `--all` or `--base` there changes which tasks run, while the tool that should get them never does. The command looks right and does something else. An inner `--` must reach the command too, since many tools give it a meaning.

cases.title: Forwarded args reach the requested task, not its dependency of the same task name
cases.why: Args are given for the task that was asked for; a dependency was not asked for, only pulled in. If `--x` also reached `b#show`, a flag meant for one project, such as a watch or update-snapshots flag, would change every dependency sharing the task name. Those tasks could fail on an option they do not accept, or write files nobody asked for.

cases.title: A project’s external dependency changing in the lockfile runs its task again
cases.why: An installed package is code the task runs or bundles, as much as its own source. When the lockfile resolves a different version for the project, the task’s output can change, so the task must run again. A runner blind to dependencies replays a build made with the old package, and an upgrade or a security fix never reaches what ships.

cases.title: A change to an external dependency of a workspace package a project links runs that project’s task again
cases.why: What a project can import through a linked workspace package includes that package’s own dependencies. Here `c` reads `y` through `b`, so a new `y` reaches `c` even though `c`’s manifest never names it. A runner that keys `c` only on its direct dependencies replays a build made with the old `y`, and the change ships in `b` but not in `c`.

cases.title: A lockfile change no part of a project’s dependencies holds replays its task
cases.why: A lockfile holds every project’s dependencies, but each task uses only its own project’s share. A change to `y`, which `a` never installs, cannot change `a`’s output. A runner that keys every task on the whole lockfile rebuilds every project after any dependency bump, and in a large repo almost no change replays at all.

cases.title: A committed dependency change selects the projects whose dependencies hold it, through a linked workspace too, and no other
cases.why: The changed project edited no file of its own; only the lockfile records that a dependency it uses moved. That dependency is what it now imports, so its result can change. Selecting by changed files alone misses it, and selecting every project on any lockfile change runs far too much.

cases.title: A catalog entry pointed elsewhere runs the task of the project that takes it, and no other
cases.why: The project’s own manifest still says catalog:, so its files do not change; only the root and the lockfile do. The package it installs is now different, and so is what its build reads. The project that takes that entry must run again, and projects that do not take it must replay.

cases.title: Installing again with nothing changed replays every task
cases.why: An install that resolves the same packages leaves every task’s dependencies as they were. A key built from what is resolved, not from file times or a fresh `node_modules`, stays the same. A runner that reruns after each install throws away the cache on every CI job, since most jobs install first.

cases.title: Swapping which packages two dependency names install runs the task again
cases.why: The same packages are installed, but the name `foo` now resolves to the other one. A key that collects only the set of installed versions sees no change, though every `import` of `foo` now loads different code. The runner then replays output built with the old mapping. Each dependency name and what it resolves to must count together.

cases.title: Swapping which packages two of the root’s dependency names install runs a task reading them
cases.why: Packages the root installs sit where every project resolves them, so a project can read them without naming them. Swapping which package the root’s `foo` and `bar` install changes what such a project loads. If the root’s dependencies are left out of the key, the task replays output built with the old packages under a green run.

cases.title: An edit inside a local directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: A `file:` dependency is a local directory, and the lockfile names only its path. So when a file inside it changes, the lockfile stays the same while the installed code does not. A runner that keys on the lockfile alone replays the old build. The directory’s content is the dependency’s version and must be part of the key.

cases.title: An edit inside a local directory dependency replays the projects that do not depend on it
cases.why: A local directory dependency belongs to the projects that install it, not to the whole workspace. `other` does not depend on it, so an edit there cannot change `other`’s output. Treating the edit as a change for every project reruns unrelated builds each time the vendored code moves, which wastes CI time with nothing gained.

cases.title: A file added to a local directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: A new file in a local directory dependency is installed with the rest and can be imported, globbed or bundled. The lockfile still names the same path, so only the directory’s file list shows the change. A runner that hashes only the files it saw before replays a build that misses the new file.

cases.title: An edit to a file a local directory dependency links to runs the task depending on it
cases.why: A symlink in a local directory dependency installs as the file it points to, so that file is part of the dependency’s content. Editing it changes what the task reads, even though no file inside the directory changed. A runner that hashes the link text rather than its target replays output built from the old file.

cases.title: A change in a local directory dependency’s own node_modules replays the task depending on it
cases.why: An install copies a local directory dependency without its `node_modules`, so files there never reach the project. A change inside it changes nothing the task reads. A runner that hashes it reruns the task whenever the dependency’s own tools install or update, which can be on every run.

cases.title: An edit inside a `link:` directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: A `link:` dependency is a symlink to a directory, so an edit there is live in the project at once, with no install. The lockfile does not change, and the project’s own files do not either. A runner must still key on the linked directory’s content, or it replays the old build while the code it imports has changed.

cases.title: A committed edit inside a local directory dependency selects the project depending on it
cases.why: A changed-projects check must follow the same edges a key does. The edit lies under `vendor/`, which belongs to no project, but `lib` installs that directory. If the check only maps changed paths to the project holding them, it finds nothing and CI skips `lib`, so a broken dependency merges untested.

cases.title: An edit to a local dependency kept inside another project’s directory runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: A local dependency kept in another project’s directory is still the dependency of the project that installs it. When its content changes, `lib`’s installed copy changes, and `lib`’s build must run again. A runner that counts the files only for the project holding them replays `lib`’s old build.

cases.title: A committed edit to a local dependency kept inside another project’s directory selects the project depending on it
cases.why: The edit is under `other`’s directory, but `lib` is the project that installs it. A changed-projects check that maps a path only to the project holding it selects `other` and skips `lib`. CI then never tests the project the change reaches, and a pull request that breaks `lib` shows green.

cases.title: A committed edit beside a local dependency, in the project that holds it, selects only that project
cases.why: Installing a local dependency from another project’s directory claims that directory, not the whole project. An edit to `other`’s source, next to it, reaches only `other`. Selecting `lib` too, or every project, makes each pull request touching `other` run tests that cannot fail from it.

cases.title: A change to the dependencies of a workspace package linked under another name runs the linking project’s task again
cases.why: `"y": "link:../b"` installs `b` itself, so what `a` imports through `y` is everything `b` reaches. When `b`’s dependency `ms` changes, `a` loads the new `ms` too. A runner that does not follow a link into a workspace package treats `y` as opaque, and replays `a`’s build made with the old `ms`.

cases.title: A workspace package linked under another name is a dependency: its build runs first
cases.why: `"y": "link:../b"` installs the workspace package `b`, just as `"b": "workspace:*"` does. `a` reads `b`’s build, so `b` must build first. A runner that only treats `workspace:` as a link between projects may build both at once, and `a` then reads a missing or old `dist`, failing or shipping stale code.

cases.title: A dependency change of a workspace nested in another’s directory runs the nested project’s task again
cases.why: A workspace package can sit inside another project’s directory, and it keeps its own dependencies. When `n`’s dependency changes, `n`’s installed code changes, and its task must run again. A runner that finds a project’s dependencies by directory may give them to the outer project, and replay `n`’s old build.

cases.title: A dependency change of a workspace nested in another’s directory replays the outer project’s task
cases.why: A project inside another’s directory is a project of its own, with its own dependencies. A change to the nested project’s dependency does not touch the outer one, so the outer task should replay. A runner that folds nested manifests into the outer project reruns it on every change of the nested one.

cases.title: An override that forces a different transitive dependency runs the task of the project reaching it
cases.why: An override in the root manifest can swap a package deep in a project’s dependency tree. Here `b` reaches `z` through `yy`, and the override replaces it. The project’s own manifest is unchanged, so a runner that keys only on direct dependencies replays `b`’s build with the old `z`. The resolved tree is what the task loads.

cases.title: An override replays the task of a project that does not reach the overridden package
cases.why: An override changes only the projects whose dependency tree contains the package it forces. `a` never reaches `z`, so its installed code is the same as before. A runner that treats any change to the root manifest as a change for every project rebuilds the whole workspace for a fix that touches one tree.

cases.title: Respelling an override so it resolves the same package replays every task
cases.why: What a task loads is the package an override resolves to, not how the override is written. `file:./vendor/z2` and `file:vendor/z2` install the same directory. A runner that keys on the manifest text reruns every task after a cosmetic edit. Keying on the resolution keeps the cache, and still sees a real change.

cases.title: A workspace package the root depends on builds before a project that reads it through the root
cases.why: The root installs a workspace package where every project resolves it, whatever that project’s own manifest says. Here `app` reads `lib`’s build through the root, so `lib` must build first. A runner that orders tasks only by each project’s own manifest may run `app` first, and it then reads a missing or old `dist`.

cases.title: A change to a workspace package the root depends on runs a project reading it through the root again
cases.why: A package the root depends on is reachable by every project, so a project that reads it depends on it even without naming it. When `lib`’s source changes, `app`’s output changes too. A runner that leaves the root’s workspace dependencies out of `app`’s key replays `app`’s old build.

cases.title: A package the root depends on that itself depends on another workspace forms no cycle
cases.why: `util` can reach `lib` through the root, but `lib` depends on `util`. Adding the root’s dependencies as an edge from every project would give `util` an edge back to `lib`, a cycle no manifest wrote. The runner would then refuse to build or pick an order at random. The root’s edge must not point a package at what depends on it.

cases.title: A committed change to a workspace package the root depends on selects a project reading it through the root
cases.why: A changed-projects check must see the same dependencies a build does. `app` reads `lib` through the root, so a change to `lib` reaches `app`. If the check only reads each project’s own manifest it selects `lib` alone, and CI never tests `app` against the change, which then breaks on main.

cases.title: An edit inside a `file:` dependency beside the repository runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: The dependency lives beside the repository, so no git status shows the edit and the lockfile names only its path. The task still reads its files through the install. A key built only from the repository misses the change and replays a result built from the old code.

cases.title: An edit inside a `file:` dependency beside the repository replays the projects that do not depend on it
cases.why: Only the projects that depend on the outside folder read its files. An edit there cannot change the output of a project that never installs it. Running those projects again for a change they do not read spends a full build on each, every time the shared folder moves.

cases.title: Pointing a `file:` dependency at another directory beside the repository runs the task again
cases.why: Pointing the dependency at another folder changes the code the task installs and reads, even if the name stays the same. The manifest and lockfile record the new path. A key that does not follow the new folder’s content replays a result built from the old folder.

cases.title: An edit inside a `link:` dependency beside the repository runs the task of the project depending on it, with no install
cases.why: node_modules holds a link to the folder, so an edit there is what the task reads at once, with no install. Nothing in the repository changed, and git sees nothing. A key that only looks inside the repository replays the old output while the code it read has moved.

cases.title: A file added to a `link:` dependency beside the repository runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: A linked folder is read live, so a file added there is part of what the task can import, with no install. Adding a module is as much a change as editing one. A key that only hashed the files present at install time misses it, and the build replays without the new file.

cases.title: An edit inside a `link:` dependency beside the repository replays the projects that do not depend on it
cases.why: Only the projects that link the outside folder read its files. An edit there cannot change the output of a project that does not depend on it. Running every project on such an edit spends builds that produce the same bytes and makes a shared folder cost the whole workspace.

cases.title: Pointing a `link:` dependency at another directory beside the repository runs the task again
cases.why: Pointing the link at another folder changes the code behind the same name, though the name is unchanged. The task reads the new folder’s files from then on. A key that keeps hashing the old target, or only the name, replays a result built from code that is no longer installed.

cases.title: Installing again with a `link:` dependency beside the repository unchanged replays the task
cases.why: Installing again with nothing changed leaves the same link to the same folder with the same files. The task reads exactly what it read before, so its result is already on disk. Running it again because an install touched node_modules costs a full build for nothing.

cases.title: A file added to a `link:` directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it, with no install
cases.why: A linked folder is read live, so a file added to it is something the task can now import, with no install step. Adding a module is as much a change as editing one. A key that only covers files known at install time replays the old build without the new file.

cases.title: An edit inside a `link:` directory dependency replays the projects that do not depend on it
cases.why: Only the projects that link the folder read its files. An edit inside it cannot change the output of a project that does not depend on it. Running those projects again spends a build each on bytes that cannot differ, on every save in the shared folder.

cases.title: Pointing a `link:` dependency at another directory in the repository runs the task again
cases.why: Pointing the link at another folder in the repository changes the code behind the same name. The task reads the new folder from then on. A key that keeps hashing the old folder, or only the dependency’s name, replays a result built from code that is no longer linked.

cases.title: An edit to a `link:` dependency kept inside another project’s directory runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: The edited folder sits inside another project’s directory, but the dependant links it and reads its files. Which project owns the folder on disk does not decide who reads it. A key that charges the edit only to the owner replays the dependant with code it no longer reads.

cases.title: Swapping which `link:` directories two dependency names point at runs the task again
cases.why: The same two folders are linked as before, but each name now points at the other one. The task imports by name, so it now reads different code. A key that only collects the set of linked folders sees no change and replays a result built from the old pairing.

cases.title: Pointing a dependency name at another package, the import name unchanged, runs the task again
cases.why: The task imports the same name either way, but that name now resolves to a different package. What the task reads has changed even though its source has not. A key that sees only the import name, not what it installs to, replays a result built from the old package.

cases.title: An edit behind a dependency installed under another name, linked from beside the repository, runs the task again
cases.why: The dependency is installed under another name and linked from beside the repository, so neither git nor the name shows the edit. The task still reads the linked files. A key that follows only repository files, or the package’s own name, replays an output built from the old code.

cases.title: A task with caching off runs on every run
cases.why: Turning caching off is an explicit request to run the command every time. Such tasks often have effects beyond their outputs, such as a deploy, a migration or a fetch of fresh data. Replaying one would skip that effect while reporting success. The cost of running again is the price the user chose.

cases.title: Changing a task’s command runs it again
cases.why: The command produces the output as much as the source files do, so it is part of the key. Changing a flag or a script line and getting the old result back makes the edit look like it did nothing. A developer then debugs a config that is already right while the cache serves output from the old one.

cases.title: Changing a dependency’s command rebuilds the projects that read its output
cases.why: A dependency’s new command produces new output, and projects built from that output must rebuild. If only the dependency reruns, its dependants keep the output they built from its previous result. The tree then holds a library built one way and an app built against the other, under a green run.

cases.title: Declaring a new output runs the task again so the cache holds it
cases.why: An entry saved before an output was declared does not hold that output, so it cannot be replayed as if it did. A hit here would restore a tree without the newly declared files, and anything that reads them fails or reads leftovers. Running once more stores the full set of outputs for later hits.

cases.title: Committing a change keeps the entry the uncommitted run saved
cases.why: A cache entry belongs to the content a task reads, not to whether that content is committed. Running a build and then committing the same files changes nothing the task reads. Missing here would make every commit pay again for work done minutes before, which is most of the time a developer spends waiting.

cases.title: An edit that keeps a source’s length, right after a run, runs the task again
cases.why: A cache key must come from a file’s bytes, not its size or timestamp. An edit that keeps the length, right after a run, can leave both the size and a coarse mtime unchanged. A runner that trusts them replays the old output, and the developer tests or ships a build that does not match the source.

cases.title: Writing a source again with the same bytes replays the task
cases.why: A key built from content does not change when a file is written again with the same bytes. Formatters, branch switches and code generators often touch files without changing them. If a moved mtime alone reran the task, the cache would miss after every checkout or save, and CI would redo work whose result is already stored.

cases.title: Adding an empty file under the inputs runs the task again
cases.why: Which files exist under the inputs is input too, even when a file is empty. A command such as `ls`, a bundler’s glob or a test runner looking for test files reads the list of names. If an empty file changed no key, the runner would replay output that misses the new file, and nothing would warn.

cases.title: Changing one byte in the middle of a binary input runs the task again
cases.why: Inputs are bytes, and a binary file must be hashed as bytes. A runner that reads it as text, stops at a zero byte or normalises its encoding can see two different files as one. A changed image, font or compiled asset would then replay the old output, and the shipped build would carry the old file.

cases.title: Changing the last byte of a 2 MB input runs the task again
cases.why: A key must cover the whole of every input, not a prefix or a sample. Hashing only the start of a large file is cheaper, but a change at its end, such as an appended record or a data table’s last row, goes unseen. The runner replays output built from the old file, and the change never reaches the build.

cases.title: A declared variable set to its own name is not the same as the variable unset
cases.why: A declared variable’s key must tell an unset variable apart from every value it can take. A key that writes the name in place of a missing value makes `MODE=MODE` and no `MODE` look the same. The second run then replays `unset` where the command should print `MODE`. Name and value must be encoded so that no value can stand in for absence.

cases.title: A task reading every project file replays though a sibling task wrote its gitignored output: ignored in the workspace’s .gitignore
cases.why: A gitignored file is local state, not source, so it is not an input even of a task that reads every project file. Here the build writes `dist`, ignored in the workspace’s .gitignore. cases.title: A task reading every project file runs again when the build it depends on changes
cases.why: Leaving an ignored output out of the key must not hide a change behind it. The reader depends on the build, so its key folds in the build’s own inputs. When `src/a.txt` changes, the build’s key changes and the reader must run again on the new output. Otherwise the test passes against the old build while the source has moved on.

cases.title: A task stopped by SIGTERM mid-run fails the run and is run again next time, never replayed
cases.why: A task stopped part way never finished its outputs, so there is no result to keep. An entry saved for the stopped run would replay a partial tree as a success: a half-written bundle, a missing file, under a green run. The stop must also fail the run, so CI that cancels a job does not report it as passed. The next run must do the work again.

cases.title: With `* text=auto` in .gitattributes, a same-size edit to a CRLF file runs the task again
cases.why: Under `* text=auto` git may store a CRLF file with LF, but the task reads the CRLF bytes on disk, so those bytes are the input. An edit that keeps the size, with a future mtime, can look clean to git. A runner that trusts git’s stored blob replays the old build, though the file the task reads has changed.

cases.title: With `* text` in .gitattributes, a same-size edit to a CRLF file runs the task again
cases.why: Under `* text` git treats every file as text and stores it with LF, while the CRLF bytes stay on disk. The task reads the disk, so those bytes are the input. A runner that hashes git’s normalised form, or trusts a stat that did not move, misses a same-size edit and replays output built from the old file.

cases.title: With `*.txt text eol=crlf` in .gitattributes, a same-size edit to a CRLF file runs the task again
cases.why: With `eol=crlf`, git writes CRLF on checkout but stores LF, so what is on disk and what git holds differ by design. The task reads the disk, so those bytes are the input. A same-size edit that git’s stat does not catch must still run the task again, or the runner replays output built from the old text.

cases.title: Under a project’s own `*.md text` rule, a same-size edit to a CRLF file runs the task again
cases.why: A project can set its own line-ending rules in its own `.gitattributes`, and they apply to its files as the root’s do. Under `*.md text` git may store a CRLF file with LF, yet the task reads the CRLF bytes on disk. A runner that trusts git’s stored form, or reads only the root’s rules, can miss a same-size edit and replay the old build.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, rewriting a file holding a lone CR from LF to CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: Whether git calls a file text or binary, a rewrite from LF to CRLF changes the bytes the task reads. A lone CR makes git’s guess about the file uncertain, and in text mode it may store both versions as the same blob. A runner that trusts that blob replays output built from the LF file, so the CRLF version never reaches the build.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, rewriting a file holding a NUL past its first 8000 bytes from LF to CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: Git looks only at a file’s first 8000 bytes to decide if it is binary, so a NUL past them leaves it text. Rewritten from LF to CRLF, the file on disk changes while git may store the same normalised blob. A runner that trusts that blob replays the old build, though every line the task reads is different.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, rewriting a file holding a control byte from LF to CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: A control byte does not make git call a file binary, so under `* text=auto` it is normalised like text. Rewritten from LF to CRLF, the bytes on disk change while git may store the same blob. A runner that trusts git’s stored form replays output built from the LF file, and the task’s real input never counts.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, rewriting a file holding plain text from LF to CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: Under `* text=auto`, git stores plain text with LF whatever is on disk. A rewrite from LF to CRLF then leaves git’s blob the same while every line the task reads changes. A runner that keys on that blob replays the old output, and a tool that cares about line endings, such as a shell script or a snapshot test, sees the wrong file.

cases.title: Under `* text=auto`, dropping the CR from a binary file’s CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: Under `* text=auto` git decides by content whether a file is text, and a file holding NUL bytes is binary. Dropping a CR from it changes the bytes the task reads, even though a text-mode view of it might not. A runner that normalises line endings before hashing would see no change and replay output built from the old file.

cases.title: An edit to a committed input with a non-ASCII name runs the task again
cases.why: A committed file with a non-ASCII name is an input like any other. Git quotes such a path in its output unless asked not to, and a quoted path names no file on disk. A runner that reads git’s list as-is drops the file from the key, so editing it replays the old build. Names are bytes and must be read as git meant them.

cases.title: An input `src/*:bar.txt` keys `foo:bar.txt` and `foo::bar.txt`: a `:` is part of a name
cases.why: In a glob, a `:` is an ordinary character of a file name, not syntax. A runner that reads `src/*:bar.txt` as something else, such as a prefix or a path list, matches no file, and the task is keyed on nothing. Edits to `foo:bar.txt` then replay the old output. Both `foo:bar.txt` and `foo::bar.txt` match and must count.

cases.title: An input `src/a,b.ts` keys the file named so: a `,` outside braces is part of a name
cases.why: A `,` means something in a glob only inside braces; elsewhere it is part of the name. A runner that splits `src/a,b.ts` into two patterns keys on `src/a` and `b.ts`, neither of which exists, so the file named `a,b.ts` is no input. Editing it then replays the old output, and the build ships stale code.

cases.title: Inputs through `@scope`, `a+b` and `(marketing)` directories key the files under them
cases.why: Paths with `@scope`, `a+b` and `(marketing)` are common: package scopes, and route groups in web frameworks. A glob engine that reads `+`, `@` or `( )` as pattern syntax matches nothing under them. The task is then keyed without its pages or modules, and an edit there replays the old build. These characters must match themselves.

cases.title: Inputs named with a `$`, quotes, a space or a tab, committed or not, each rerun the task when edited
cases.why: File names may hold `$`, quotes, spaces or tabs, and route files such as `$id.tsx` are common. If the runner passes names through a shell, or splits a list on white space, such a file is mangled or lost. Its edits then replay the old output. Names must be handled as bytes from the file system to the key, committed or not.

cases.title: A file or directory whose name holds a newline is an input, untracked or committed
cases.why: A newline is a legal byte in a file or directory name. A runner that reads git’s or the file system’s list one line at a time splits such a name in two, and neither half names a file. The file then drops out of the key, and an edit to it replays the old output. Git’s NUL-separated output keeps each name whole.

cases.title: An input `src/[invalid` keys the file named so, or is refused, never left unkeyed
cases.why: An unclosed `[` opens no character class, so `src/[invalid` is the name of a file. A runner may key that file, or refuse the glob as malformed; both tell the truth. What it must not do is match nothing and run with the input silently left out, since an edit to the file would then replay the old build.

cases.title: Only a file named .gitignore holds ignore rules: `foo.gitignore` and `.ignore` do not
cases.why: Git reads ignore rules only from files named `.gitignore`, plus `.git/info/exclude` and the user’s global file. A file named `foo.gitignore` or `.ignore` is just a file. A runner that treats them as rules drops inputs git would track, and edits to those files replay the old output. The ignore set must match git’s.

cases.title: An uncommitted .gitignore edit that stops ignoring a file, then ignores it again: an edit it ignores replays the task
cases.why: Ignore rules decide what is local state, and the rules in force are the ones on disk now, committed or not. While `gen.txt` is ignored, editing it changes nothing the key holds, so the task replays. A runner that reads ignore rules from the last commit keys a file the developer has just ignored, and reruns after every regeneration.

cases.why: A nested .gitignore ignores only below its own directory. `src/b/x.txt` has the same name as the file `src/a/.gitignore` ignores, but lies outside its scope, so it is an input. A runner that applies the rule by name across the project drops it from the key and replays output that misses the file.

cases.title: A FIFO under an input glob does not hang the run
cases.why: A FIFO is not a file with content: opening it to read waits for a writer that never comes. A runner that hashes everything under a glob hangs there, and a CI job runs until its timeout. Tools and test servers create FIFOs in project trees, so a runner must skip them, or treat them by type, and finish the run.

cases.title: Staging and then committing an edit keeps the entry the unstaged run saved
cases.why: Staging and committing change git’s view of a file, not its bytes. The run before staging already stored a result for those bytes. A runner that keys a dirty file differently from a clean one misses after `git add` and again after the commit, so every edit is built three times before it is pushed.

cases.title: A same-size edit right after a commit runs the task again
cases.why: Right after a commit, git cannot always tell a same-size edit from its stat, since both can fall in the same second (racy git). A runner that trusts git’s index there keys the new bytes as the committed blob, and replays the old build. The bytes on disk must be read whenever the stat cannot prove them unchanged.

cases.title: Staging and committing a deleted input replays what the run after the deletion stored
cases.why: Deleting a file, then staging and committing the deletion, leaves the same files on disk at each step. The run after the deletion stored a result for that tree. A runner that keys on git’s state, not the files, misses at each git step and rebuilds the same tree, which costs CI time on every pull request that deletes a file.

cases.title: A file added with `git add -N` keys its bytes: an edit to it runs the task again
cases.why: `git add -N` records a path in the index with the empty blob, before its content is staged. That blob says nothing about the bytes on disk. A runner that trusts the index for the file keys every version of it as empty, so edits replay the old build. Such a file must be hashed from disk, like an untracked one.

cases.title: In a repository with no commit yet the run caches, and the first commit keeps that entry
cases.why: A new repository with no commit is a normal place to start a project, and its tasks still have inputs. A runner that needs a HEAD should not refuse to cache there, and the first commit changes no file a task reads. If the commit made every key change, the first push would rebuild the whole workspace for nothing.

cases.title: A task stored by a run of every project replays when the run names its project, or excludes another
cases.why: Which projects a run selects is not an input of a task: the same task on the same tree is one entry. A developer who builds everything, then only `lib`, should get a replay. A runner that folds the selection into the key misses whenever the filter differs, so local runs and CI jobs with other filters never share results.

cases.title: A task an affected run selects replays what a run of every project stored
cases.why: A run limited to changed projects asks for the same tasks on the same files as a full run. The full run already stored them, so the affected run should replay. A runner that keys on how a task was selected misses here, and CI rebuilds work that a full run on the same commit has already done.

cases.title: A task keyed on a root file and no project file runs again when the root file changes
cases.why: A task may depend on a file at the workspace root, such as a shared config, and declare it explicitly. That file is then part of its key even when no project file is. A runner that ignores root inputs when the project lists none replays the old output after the root file changes, and the new config never reaches the build.

cases.title: Moving a value from one declared variable to another, or swapping two, runs the task again
cases.why: A variable’s value means something only with its name. A key that folds values without their names cannot tell `A=1` from `B=1`, or `A=1 B=2` from `A=2 B=1`. The runner then replays a build made for one environment in the other, such as a staging URL in a production build. Each name and value must be keyed as a pair.

cases.title: A declared value holding `=`, newlines, a tab and non-ASCII reaches the task byte for byte
cases.why: A declared variable must reach the task exactly as the shell set it. Values with `=`, newlines, tabs or non-ASCII text are common: keys, certificates, multi-line settings. A runner that splits on `=` or a newline, or re-encodes the value, hands the task a different value from the one that is keyed, and the build is wrong under a matching key.

cases.title: A PATH with one more directory, not declared, replays the task
cases.why: PATH differs on almost every machine and changes with each tool installed. If an undeclared PATH were keyed, no two machines would share an entry, and a remote cache would never hit. The trade-off is that a tool found through PATH is not in the key; a task that depends on a tool’s version can declare that explicitly.

cases.title: TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP reach a task as set, and what a task exports reaches its children
cases.why: TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP tell a task where it may write temporary files, and the host sets them for a reason, such as a larger or private disk. A runner that drops or rewrites them sends the task’s temp files where the host never pointed it, filling a small disk or sharing files between jobs. A task’s own exports must also reach its children.

cases.title: Other forwarded args run a cached task again, and the first args again leave their output
cases.why: Forwarded args change what a task does, so they are part of its key. A run with new args must run the task again, or it replays output made for other args, such as tests for another filter. Going back to the first args must leave their own output, whether run again or replayed, never the output of the args in between.

cases.title: A bare `--` with no args replays what a run without it stored
cases.why: A bare `--` with nothing after it passes no args, exactly as a run without it. The command the task runs is the same, so the stored result is the same. A runner that keys the separator itself misses whenever a script or alias adds `--` by habit, and rebuilds work it has already done.

cases.title: New forwarded args for a task replay its dependency, which never sees them
cases.why: Args go to the task that was asked for; a dependency never sees them. A dependency keyed on them would miss on every new argument, though its command and output are the same. Running a test task with a new filter would then rebuild every library it depends on, for no change in what they produce.

cases.title: A dependency’s bin named `sh` does not become the shell of a long-running task either
cases.why: A long-running task, such as a dev server, is started the same way as any other, so the same rule holds. The task’s PATH decides what its command resolves, not which shell parses it. If a dependency’s bin named `sh` became the shell, a package could take over the server, and the tests run against it would test something else.

cases.title: An output that is a directory, a file or a link in turn comes back in each build’s own shape
cases.why: A replay must leave the output exactly as the build that stored it, whatever was there before. When `dist/out` is a directory in one build, a file in the next and a link in a third, each replay lands on another shape’s tree. Merged into it, the result is neither build’s output, and the next step reads a mix of both.

cases.title: A directory where a replayed output file goes, or a file where its directory goes, is replaced
cases.why: A replay can find a stray directory where its output file goes, or a stale file where its directory goes. Writing around it, or failing on it, leaves a tree that is not the stored one. A runner must replace what is in the way, since the declared output path is the task’s to own, and the run must not fail over leftovers.

cases.title: An output link to a directory, or a dangling one, comes back as the link
cases.why: A link is an output in its own right: what it points to, not a copy of the target. A link to a directory, or one whose target does not exist, must come back as that link. A runner that follows links when storing copies a whole directory or fails on the dangling one, and the restored tree differs from what the build made.

cases.title: Through an output directory that is a link inside the project, a deleted output comes back
cases.why: Builds often make their output directory a link into another folder of the project. When the files behind it are deleted, a replay must restore them where the link leads. A runner that stores only the link, or writes through it to the wrong place, leaves `dist/out.js` missing while the run reports success.

cases.title: Through an output directory link, each build leaves only its own files
cases.why: Each build’s output is exactly the files it wrote, also when the output directory is a link. A replay of `one` must remove `two.js` that another build left behind it, and the other way round. A runner that only adds files through the link leaves both, and a bundler or deploy step then ships files from a build that is not current.

cases.title: An output list ["dist"] naming a directory link brings back the file behind the link once it is deleted
cases.why: An output named `dist` means what the build wrote there, also when `dist` is a link to another folder. A runner that stores only the link, and not the files behind it, has nothing to restore once `real-out/out.js` is deleted. The replay then reports success while the file the next step reads is missing.

cases.title: An output list ["dist/","real-out/**"] naming a directory link brings back the file behind the link once it is deleted
cases.why: Naming both the link `dist/` and its target `real-out/**` declares the same files twice, which must not confuse a restore. The replay must bring back `real-out/out.js` once, and keep `dist` pointing at it. A runner that writes the files through the link and then replaces the link, or the other way round, can leave the output missing.

cases.title: A root output that links to another file of the same output comes back as the link
cases.why: A task can declare an output at the workspace root, and a link inside it that points to another file of the same output. Such a `latest` link is a common pattern for generated assets. On replay it must come back as the link, not as a copy or a missing file, or tools that follow it read the wrong version.

cases.title: A rebuild whose output turns from a directory into a file finds no stale directory in its way
cases.why: Declared outputs belong to the task, so the runner clears them before a run, as a replay would. If the old `dist/out` directory stays, a build that now writes `dist/out` as a file fails, or writes beside stale files. The result then depends on what earlier builds left, and a clean CI checkout would build something else.

cases.title: An output named outright, `dist/out`, turns from a directory to a file and back, run and replayed
cases.why: An output named outright, such as `dist/out`, is the same path whether it is a file or a directory. Run or replayed, the runner must leave it in the shape this build made. A runner that matches the name only as a file, or only as a directory, stores or restores nothing in the other shape, and the next step finds no output.

cases.title: A task that exits non-zero fails the run
cases.why: A non-zero exit is how a command says it failed, and the run’s exit code is what CI and scripts read. A runner that reports success over a failed task lets a broken build merge and deploy. The task’s own output is shown so the developer can see what failed without running it again.

cases.title: A failed task is not replayed as a success next time
cases.why: Only a successful run is a result worth keeping. A stored failure would replay the same error without trying again, so a flaky test or a fixed environment could never pass. A failure saved as a pass would be worse: a broken build hidden behind a green run. So a failed task runs again every time.

cases.title: A failed dependency stops the projects that need it from running
cases.why: A task that depends on another reads what that one produced. If the dependency failed, its output is missing or half written, and a dependant built on it either fails with a confusing second error or passes on stale files. Skipping the dependants keeps the first real error in front of the developer and saves the time spent building on a broken base.

cases.title: Fixing a failed task’s input makes the next run pass and build
cases.why: A fix to an input is a new input, so the task must run again on it and succeed. A runner that remembered the failure by task name, not by input, would keep failing after the fix and push the user to wipe the cache. The output on disk is the one the passing run wrote.

cases.title: A task killed by a signal fails the run and is not cached
cases.why: A task killed by a signal never finished, so whatever it wrote is partial. Treating the death as success, or caching it, would replay half-written output as a green result on every later run. The run fails so CI sees it, and the next run tries the task again from scratch.

cases.title: A task that writes to stderr and exits 0 succeeds
cases.why: Many tools print warnings, progress and deprecation notes to stderr while succeeding. The exit code is the only contract a command makes about failure. A runner that failed on stderr output would break builds over harmless warnings and push users to silence useful diagnostics.

cases.title: Asking for a task no project declares fails the run
cases.why: A task name no project declares is almost always a typo or a stale script. If the run exits 0 having run nothing, CI reports green while no test or build ran at all. Failing loudly turns the typo into a message the developer sees at once, instead of a gap found weeks later.

cases.title: Tasks that depend on each other in a cycle fail the run before any runs
cases.why: A cycle has no valid order: each task waits on the other, so neither can correctly go first. Starting one anyway means it runs without the input it declared it needs. Refusing before anything runs points at the config mistake, rather than leaving a half-run graph or a run that waits forever.

cases.title: Ctrl-C (SIGINT) ends the run, its task, and what the task backgrounded
cases.why: Ctrl-C means stop everything this run started, and start nothing new. A non-interactive shell runs a backgrounded job with SIGINT ignored, so the signal alone does not end it. Unless the runner takes down the whole process tree, the job runs on under init, holding ports and files after the prompt is back.

cases.title: SIGTERM ends the run, its task, and what the task backgrounded
cases.why: SIGTERM is how a CI system, a container runtime or a process supervisor asks a run to end. Unless the runner ends the whole task tree, a job the task backgrounded keeps running after the run has exited. On a shared CI machine that orphan can hold a port, keep writing files or use CPU into the next job.

cases.title: A hang-up (SIGHUP) ends the run, its task, and what the task backgrounded
cases.why: A closed terminal or a dropped SSH session sends SIGHUP, and the work started there should end with it. A runner that passes it only to the task’s shell leaves what the task backgrounded running, unseen, with no terminal to show it. Such orphans pile up and hold the ports and locks the next run needs.

cases.title: Ctrl-\ (SIGQUIT) ends the run, its task, and what the task backgrounded
cases.why: The quit key is a harder stop than Ctrl-C, and a user who presses it wants everything gone. A shell runs a backgrounded job with SIGQUIT ignored, so the signal alone does not end it. The runner must end the whole tree, or the job runs on under init with nothing left that will stop it.

cases.title: SIGINT to the run reaches a running task as SIGINT
cases.why: A task should receive the signal the user sent, unchanged. Cleanup code is often bound to one signal, such as a Node `process.on("SIGINT")` handler or a shell `trap ... INT`. If Ctrl-C is forwarded as SIGTERM or SIGKILL, that handler never runs, and temp files, locks or child processes are left behind.

cases.title: SIGTERM to the run reaches a running task as SIGTERM
cases.why: A supervisor’s SIGTERM should reach the task as SIGTERM. Containers and CI agents send it to ask for a graceful shutdown, and programs bind their shutdown code to it. Forwarded as SIGINT or SIGKILL, that code is skipped, so connections are not drained and partial state is left on disk.

cases.title: A task that exits 0 on Ctrl-C does not start its dependants
cases.why: Once the user asks a run to stop, nothing new should start. A task that handles Ctrl-C by exiting 0 is shutting down cleanly, not reporting that its work is done. Starting its dependants would launch new work after the stop, on output that may be incomplete, and keep the terminal busy after Ctrl-C.

cases.title: Ctrl-C ends a run whose task ignores SIGINT and SIGTERM
cases.why: A stop must end the run even when a task ignores the polite signals. Some programs trap or ignore SIGINT and SIGTERM, by design or by bug. Without escalating to SIGKILL after a grace period, the run hangs at Ctrl-C, or exits and leaves the task running in the background.

cases.title: A run stopped by SIGTERM exits only once its tasks have
cases.why: A run should exit only after its tasks have. If the runner returns the prompt while tasks are still running their shutdown code, they keep printing over the next command and writing files the user thinks are settled. A script that starts the next step once the runner exits would race those late writes.

cases.title: One Ctrl-C lets a task finish its cleanup
cases.why: One Ctrl-C should reach a task once. Many cleanup handlers run once and then reset, like `process.once` or a trap that clears itself, so a second copy of the signal kills the task in the middle of its cleanup. A runner that signals the process group and then the task again leaves the cleanup half done.

cases.title: A process a task backgrounded gets to clean up on SIGTERM after the task’s shell has died
cases.why: Every process in a task’s tree deserves the same chance to shut down cleanly. A task’s shell often dies on SIGTERM at once, while a process it backgrounded is still running its handler. A runner that sends SIGKILL to the rest of the tree as soon as the shell exits cuts that cleanup short and leaves lock files or temp state behind.

cases.title: A task that traps Ctrl-C and exits 0 is not cached with its partial outputs
cases.why: An exit 0 after a stop does not mean the work finished. A program that traps Ctrl-C and exits 0 to shut down gracefully may have written only part of its outputs. Cached, that partial tree would replay as a success on every later run with the same inputs, so the next run must run the task again.

cases.title: A task that finished before Ctrl-C is replayed by the next run
cases.why: A task that finished before the stop produced a complete, valid result. Throwing it away because a later task was interrupted makes the next run redo work that was already done. Only the interrupted tasks need to run again; the finished one replays from the cache.

cases.title: A run started with SIGHUP ignored (nohup) runs on when the terminal closes
cases.why: `nohup` sets SIGHUP to ignored so that a long job survives a closed terminal or a dropped SSH session. The ignore is inherited, and a runner that installs its own SIGHUP handler over it stops the run anyway. The user asked for the job to keep going, so the run finishes and exits 0.

cases.title: A dependency killed by a signal mid-write leaves no dependant cached from its partial output
cases.why: A dependency killed mid-write leaves partial output, and nothing built from it may be kept. The kill came from something that is not an input, so a later healthy run derives the same cache keys. If a dependant had been cached from the partial file, that run would replay the wrong bytes under a green result.

cases.title: A concurrency of 0 is refused or read as a limit, never a run that waits for good
cases.why: A concurrency of 0 lets no task start, so a run that takes it literally waits forever. In CI that is a job that hangs until its timeout, with no error to explain it. The runner may refuse the value with a clear message or read it as some valid limit, but it must never sit idle.

cases.title: A second Ctrl-C kills a task still in its cleanup at once, and leaves nothing running
cases.why: The first Ctrl-C asks tasks to clean up and stop. Pressing it again says the user will not wait for that cleanup. A runner that keeps waiting ignores the user, and one that exits while leaving the task running hides a process that may still hold a port or write files.

cases.title: A task that reads its input stream sees it end, though the runner’s own stays open, and the run finishes
cases.why: A task that reads its input stream must see it end, or it waits forever for input nobody will type. The runner’s own input may stay open, as a terminal or a supervisor leaves it. Handing that stream on to the task turns a finished build into a run that never ends.

cases.title: A task past its time limit is killed, fails the run, and is not cached
cases.why: A time limit exists so a hung task cannot hold a run, or a CI job, forever. A task that hits it did not finish, so it fails the run and its partial output is never cached. If it were cached, the next run would replay a half-written result instead of trying again.

cases.title: A task that finishes inside its time limit succeeds
cases.why: A time limit is an upper bound, not a schedule. A task that finishes inside it must succeed exactly as it would with no limit. A runner that killed it early, or read the limit in the wrong unit, would fail healthy builds at random and teach users to remove the limit.

cases.title: A timed-out task that traps SIGTERM and exits 0 still fails, and its partial output is not cached
cases.why: A timeout is a failure, whatever exit code the task gives back. Many programs trap SIGTERM and exit 0 as their graceful shutdown, so the exit code after the kill says nothing about the work. Read as success, the partial output would be cached and replayed as a finished build on later runs.

cases.title: A timed-out task that ignores SIGTERM is killed anyway, and the run does not hang
cases.why: A time limit only bounds a run if the task actually dies. A task that ignores SIGTERM would keep the run, and the CI job, waiting well past the limit. After a short grace period the runner must send SIGKILL, so the limit means what it says.

cases.title: A timeout kills what the task backgrounded, not only its shell
cases.why: A timeout ends the task, and the task is its whole process tree, not only its shell. A command like `sh -c "server & wait"` starts a process that outlives its shell if only the shell is killed. That orphan keeps running after every timeout, holding ports and CPU into the next run.

cases.title: A timeout kills a backgrounded child that ignores SIGTERM after its shell has died
cases.why: A timeout must end every process the task started, even one that ignores SIGTERM. The shell dies on SIGTERM at once, so a runner that stops escalating when the shell exits never sends SIGKILL to the child. The child then runs on with no parent, holding resources after the run has failed.

cases.title: A time limit no timer can hold is refused, not turned into an instant kill
cases.why: A limit the runner cannot honour should be refused, not silently changed. Timers have a maximum, and a value past it often fires at once, so a limit of hundreds of years kills the task within milliseconds. That is the opposite of what the user asked for, and the cause is hard to see from the failure.

cases.title: A task that fails once and passes on its retry passes the run, and the passing attempt is what is cached
cases.why: A retry exists to absorb a transient failure, so a task that passes on its retry passes the run. What is cached is the output of the passing attempt, because that is the result the run reported. Caching the failed attempt’s files would replay the wrong bytes; caching nothing would redo the work next time.

cases.title: A task that fails every attempt runs once plus its retries, then fails the run
cases.why: Retries are a bounded number of extra tries, not a way to hide a real failure. The task runs once plus each retry, and if every attempt fails, the run fails. Running fewer attempts ignores the config, and running more stretches a broken CI job for nothing.

cases.title: A task with retries that passes first time runs once
cases.why: A retry is for a failure. A task that passes on its first attempt is done, and running it again would spend CI time and could repeat side effects such as a publish, an upload or a database migration. The retry count bounds attempts after failures; it is never a number of runs.

cases.title: A task killed by a signal the run did not send is retried like any failure
cases.why: A task killed by a signal the user did not send has failed like any other. The out-of-memory killer, a crashed tool or the task’s own script can kill it, and that is the kind of transient failure retries exist for. Only a stop the user asked for should end the retries.

cases.title: Ctrl-C during a task with retries does not attempt it again
cases.why: When the user stops the run, the task’s failure is the stop itself. Retrying it would start the work again right after the user asked it to end, and Ctrl-C would seem not to work. The run ends after the one attempt, as asked, and reports the stop rather than a run of failed retries.

cases.title: A retry does not remove the output directory a task beside it is writing into
cases.why: Before a retry, a runner may clean the failed attempt’s own outputs, and only those. Removing a shared directory, or pruning one that looks empty, can delete what a task running beside it has just made there. The sibling then fails, or its output vanishes, for no fault of its own.

cases.title: `^build` runs the dependency’s build, not the builds that build itself never names
cases.why: `^build` means the build of each nearest dependency that has one, not every build further down. Here b’s own build declares no dependency on c’s build: c is in b’s package graph but not in this task graph. Running c’s build anyway does work nobody asked for, on every run.

cases.title: `^build` reaching one build through two projects without a build runs it once
cases.why: `^build` passes through dependencies that have no build to reach the builds beyond them. When two such paths lead to the same project, its build is still one task and runs once. Running it twice wastes time and can race two writers on the same output directory.

cases.title: Two tasks of one project on `^build` each wait for the dependency’s build
cases.why: Each task that lists `^build` needs its dependencies built before it starts. When two tasks of one project both list it, each must wait, not only the first. If the second loses its edge, it reads the dependency half built and produces output from stale or missing files.

cases.title: Each entry of a dependsOn list runs first: three of the project’s, two `^` names
cases.why: Every entry in a dependsOn list is a separate requirement. A runner that honours only the first entry, or lets one `^` entry stand for the others, starts the task before some of what it needs exists. The task then reads missing files, or old ones from an earlier run.

cases.title: `^test` and `^lint` through a project with no tasks reach each project beyond that declares them
cases.why: A project that declares no tasks still sits in the package graph. `^test` and `^lint` must each pass through it to the projects beyond that declare them, and the order they are listed in must not matter. Stopping at the empty project, or letting one name’s walk decide the other’s, runs the task before its real dependencies.

cases.title: `^build` where only a project off the dependency path declares build runs the task alone
cases.why: `^build` asks for the builds of this project’s dependencies, and none of them has one. Some other project declares build, so the name is not a typo and the run should not fail. The task runs alone, and the unrelated project’s build is not pulled in.

cases.title: A task that depends on the requested builds is not run with them
cases.why: A run builds what was asked for and what that needs, not what happens to depend on it. A task that depends on the build tree is a consumer of the builds, not part of them. Running it too adds work, and possibly side effects such as a deploy, that the user did not request.

cases.title: dependsOn naming another project’s task that does not exist fails before any runs
cases.why: A dependsOn entry is a promise that the named task runs first. If that task does not exist, the promise cannot be kept, and dropping the edge in silence runs the task without what it said it needs. Failing before anything runs points at the typo or the renamed task.

cases.title: dependsOn naming a task its own project lacks fails before any runs
cases.why: A same-project name the project does not declare, such as `lnt` for `lint`, is a typo. Running the task without it quietly skips the check the user meant to run first. Failing before any task runs shows the mistake in the config where it was made.

cases.title: `^biuld`, a name no project declares, fails the run instead of passing with no edge
cases.why: A `^name` some project declares may simply have no holder among this project’s dependencies, which is fine. A `^name` no project anywhere declares, like `^biuld`, can only be a typo. Passing the run with no edge hides that the dependency the user wanted is never built.

cases.title: `^build` around a ring of four projects fails before any build runs
cases.why: A ring of `^build` edges has no valid order: each build needs another that needs it back. Starting any of them means it reads its dependency’s output before that exists. Failing before any build runs names the cycle, instead of a run that hangs or builds from stale files.

cases.title: A `^build` ring that passes through a project without a build still fails
cases.why: `^build` reaches past a project without a build to the builds beyond it. Around this ring that walk comes back to the start, so each build waits on itself through the empty project. It is a real cycle, and the run must refuse it before any build runs, as it would a direct one.

cases.title: A package ring whose other projects declare no build is no task cycle: `^build` runs the build
cases.why: A cycle in the package graph is not a cycle in the task graph unless tasks close it. Here walking past the projects without a build leads back to the project that asked, and a task is never its own dependency. Refusing would break a valid repo over a package loop that holds no task cycle.

cases.title: A package cycle between a project with a build and one without orders and runs
cases.why: app1’s build reaches app3’s build through app2, which has none. app3’s own walk back through app2 meets only itself, so there is no task cycle. The builds have a valid order and run; refusing them would fail a repo over a package loop its tasks never close.

cases.title: A cycle the requested task only leads into fails the run before any task runs
cases.why: A cycle anywhere below the requested task makes its graph impossible to order, even if the task itself is not in the cycle. Starting what can start would leave the run stuck, or run tasks before their inputs exist. Failing before any task runs names the cycle so it can be fixed.

cases.title: `build.*` on a task named `build.all` runs the other matches, not itself
cases.why: A pattern like `build.*` names the other tasks in its family. It also matches the name of the task that declares it, and read as an edge, that is a cycle the user never wrote. The declaring task is left out, so the pattern means what it plainly says.

cases.title: A dependsOn pattern that matches no task runs the task alone
cases.why: A pattern names a family of tasks that may be empty in a given project. A shared preset can list `codegen.*` for every project, including ones with no codegen. Failing there would force each project to opt out by hand, so the task simply runs alone.

cases.title: A `^` pattern no project’s task matches runs the task alone
cases.why: A `^` pattern names a family of tasks that dependencies may or may not have. When no project matches, there is nothing to wait for, and the task runs alone. Unlike an exact name nobody declares, a pattern that matches nothing is a normal case for shared config, not a typo.

cases.title: `^build.*` runs every match of the nearest dependency holding one, and stops there
cases.why: `^build.*` runs the matching tasks of the nearest dependency that has any, as `^build` does for one name. It runs every match there, since each may produce something the task needs. It does not reach further down, where the dependency’s own config decides what its tasks need.

cases.title: `^build.*` passes through a dependency with no match to the one beyond it
cases.why: A dependency with no matching task is a step on the way, not the end of the walk. `^build.*` passes through it to the project beyond that has matches, as an exact `^build` would. Stopping there would run the task before the build it needs, on missing or stale files.

cases.title: `^build.*` across a package cycle does not wrap back to the asking project’s own tasks
cases.why: `^` means the tasks of dependencies, never of the asking project itself. Across a package cycle, walking a’s dependencies leads back to a, but its own `build.inner` is still no dependency’s task. Including it would add an edge the user never wrote and run work nobody asked for.
