cases.title: The `.` in `build.x*` is a dot: it never matches `buildAx1`
cases.why: In a task pattern the `.` is a plain character; task names use it to group families like `build.x1`. Reading it as a regular-expression wildcard would also match `buildAx1` and run a task the pattern was never meant to reach. Only `*` is a wildcard.

cases.title: A task named both exactly and by a pattern in one dependsOn runs once
cases.why: A task named twice in one dependsOn, once exactly and once by a pattern, is still one task. It runs once, before the task that needs it. Running it twice wastes time and lets two copies race on the same outputs, so the result depends on which copy finishes last.

cases.title: A task named like a route, `t--src/app/[id]/page`, is one name in dependsOn
cases.why: An exact name in dependsOn is matched as written, whatever characters it holds. Generated task names often follow file routes and contain `[`, `]` or `/`. Reading such a name as a pattern links the wrong task or none, and the dependant runs without what it needs.

cases.title: In `t--src/app/[id]/*` the brackets are characters, not a class
cases.why: Only `*` is a wildcard in a task pattern; brackets are plain characters. Routes like `src/app/[id]/page` are common in task names, and reading `[id]` as a character class would match `i/page` instead. The pattern then links the wrong task, and the one the user meant runs late or not at all.

cases.title: Asking for `constructor`, a task no project declares, fails the run
cases.why: A task exists only if a config declares it. A name every JavaScript object carries, like `constructor`, must not be found by accident in a lookup table. Otherwise the run would pass or crash on a task nobody declared, instead of reporting the unknown name.

cases.title: A task the config names `constructor` runs like any other
cases.why: A task name is just a string, and `constructor` is as valid as `build`. A runner that keeps tasks in a plain object may confuse it with the object’s own property and fail or run the wrong thing. The declared task must run like any other.

cases.title: `^build:prod` runs the dependency’s `build:prod` first and reruns on its change
cases.why: Names with colons, like `build:prod`, are common for task variants and must work in `^` edges. The dependency’s `build:prod` runs first, and a change to its inputs reaches the dependant’s cache key. Otherwise the dependant could replay output built from the old dependency.

cases.title: A task named `a:b:c` runs as one name, not as `a` with more after it
cases.why: Some runners read a colon as a separator, such as between project and target. A task named `a:b:c` must still be one name, run as declared. Splitting it would run a different task, here `a`, and report a result for work nobody asked for.

cases.title: A git worktree checked out inside the workspace adds no project to a run
cases.why: A git worktree checked out inside the workspace holds copies of the same projects under the same names. Those copies are another checkout, not part of this workspace. Read as projects, they clash on names or build everything twice, and files from the other branch mix into this run.

cases.title: A task switched to never cached runs, instead of replaying what it saved while cached
cases.why: When the user turns caching off for a task, the task must run every time. The entry saved while it was cached is exactly what they no longer want replayed. Replaying it would skip a task the user has marked as needing to run, such as one with side effects.

cases.title: An uncached task over a cached dependency finds the dependency’s deleted outputs back
cases.why: An uncached task still needs its cached dependencies’ outputs on disk. When those outputs were deleted and the dependency is a cache hit, the runner must restore them before the dependant runs. Otherwise the dependant reads nothing and fails, or ships an empty deploy.

cases.title: A cached task run with other forwarded args runs again instead of replaying
cases.why: Arguments passed through to a command change what it does. The output saved for `--a` is wrong for `--b`, so the args must be part of the cache key. Without that, a different command line replays the earlier result, and the user gets output for flags they did not pass.

cases.title: A concurrency of 1 runs independent tasks one at a time
cases.why: A concurrency of 1 is how a user says tasks must not overlap, often because they share a port, a database or a lot of memory. Independent tasks then run one at a time. Running two at once breaks that promise and causes failures that depend on timing.

cases.title: A directory selector selects the same projects from a subdirectory as from the root
cases.why: A directory selector names paths in the workspace, so it means the same thing wherever the command runs. A runner that reads the path from the current directory, or adds the project it was started in, selects different projects by cwd. The same command then gives different results in a script and in a terminal.

cases.title: SIGINT to the run reaches a server past its ready line as SIGINT
cases.why: A server past its ready line should still receive Ctrl-C as SIGINT. Its shutdown hook is often bound to that one signal, to close connections and remove temp files. Forwarded as SIGTERM or SIGKILL, the hook never runs, and the server’s state is left behind while its dependants are torn down.

cases.title: SIGTERM to the run reaches a server past its ready line as SIGTERM
cases.why: A ready server should receive a supervisor’s SIGTERM as SIGTERM. Servers bind their graceful shutdown, such as draining open connections, to that signal. Forwarded as another signal, that code is skipped, and requests in flight are cut off instead of drained while the run shuts down.

cases.title: SIGTERM ends a run whose ready server and the task using it are both running
cases.why: SIGTERM ends the whole run: every task in it, not only the one that started first. Here a ready server and the task using it are both running, and both must end. A run that stops one and waits on the other hangs the supervisor that asked it to stop.

cases.title: SIGTERM ends the child of a ready server that traps TERM, INT and HUP
cases.why: A stop must end every process the run started, even a server’s child that traps TERM, INT and HUP. Without escalating to SIGKILL, that child outlives the run and keeps its port and its output pipe. The next run then fails to bind, or the current one never exits.

cases.title: One Ctrl-C lets a ready server finish its cleanup while its dependant is stopped
cases.why: One Ctrl-C should reach a ready server once. Many servers read a second signal as a request to force quit and skip their cleanup. A runner that sends the stop twice, once to the group and once to the server, leaves lock files and temp state behind.

cases.title: Ctrl-C while a command that keys a task is still running ends the run and the command
cases.why: A command that computes part of a task’s key is part of the run and must end with it. If Ctrl-C leaves that probe running, the stopped run stays open until the probe finishes on its own. To the user, the run seems to ignore Ctrl-C.

cases.title: A dev server starts after its dependencies’ builds and runs until Ctrl-C, which ends it
cases.why: A dev server serves what its dependencies built, so it starts only after those builds finish. It then runs until the user stops it, because a server has no natural end. Ctrl-C ends it, and the run with it, so the port is free for the next start.

cases.title: A task that needs a server runs while the server is up, and the run ends when the task does
cases.why: Depending on a server means the task needs it running, as an e2e suite needs a dev server. The server stays up while the task runs, and the run ends when the task does, since nothing else needs the server. Killing the server when the dependant starts, or refusing the edge, leaves no way to express the most common use of a server.

cases.title: A run whose task fails beside a server fails promptly and stops the server
cases.why: Once the task that needs a server fails, the server has nothing left to serve. The run should fail at once and stop the server, not keep going until someone notices. In CI, a server left up after a failure holds the job open until its timeout and buries the real error under a cancelled job.

cases.title: A server the run no longer needs is asked to stop politely, so its cleanup runs
cases.why: When a run no longer needs a server, the server should be asked to stop with a catchable signal before anything harsher. That gives it the chance to remove a lock file, flush its log and release its port. A server killed outright with SIGKILL leaves that state behind, and the next start may refuse to run.

cases.title: A server that ignores SIGTERM does not keep a finished run from exiting
cases.why: A finished run must exit even if a server it started will not stop politely. A server that ignores SIGTERM would otherwise hold the run open after its work is done. After a grace period the runner kills it, so CI moves on and no server is left behind.

cases.title: A server’s own child that ignores SIGTERM does not keep a finished run from exiting
cases.why: A run is not over until every process it started has ended. With `server & wait`, the shell dies on SIGTERM, but the server it started ignores the signal and keeps the output pipe open. A runner that waits for that pipe to close hangs, and one that never kills the child leaves it running.

cases.title: A server that exits non-zero as it starts fails the run instead of hanging it
cases.why: A server that exits non-zero as it starts has failed, and the run should say so. Waiting for a server that is already gone hangs the terminal or the CI job with no visible cause. Failing at once shows the server’s own error output while it is still on screen.

cases.title: A server whose shell exits leaves nothing it started holding its port
cases.why: When a server’s shell exits, everything it started must end with it. A process left behind keeps the port bound, so the next `dev` fails with an address-in-use error that has no visible cause. The run fails, and nothing from it is left running.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 1 a server’s dependant still runs
cases.why: A server never exits on its own, so it cannot hold a concurrency slot the way a build does. A scheduler that keeps the only slot for the server until it ends never starts the task that needs it, and the run hangs. Servers run beside the limit so their dependants can still run within it.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 1 the tasks behind a running server still run one at a time
cases.why: A concurrency limit is often set to protect a machine or a shared resource, such as a database the tests use. Once a server is up, its dependants must still run within that limit, one at a time at a concurrency of 1. Releasing them all together breaks the limit and can make tests that share state fail.

cases.title: A server that depends on another server starts after it, and both stay up while a task needs them
cases.why: An app’s dev server on top of a library’s watcher is a common setup. The app’s server must start after the server it depends on, and both must stay up while a task uses them. Refusing the edge, or starting the app before its upstream, leaves the developer starting the two by hand.

cases.title: Every server a run selects starts, at a concurrency below their count
cases.why: Servers never finish, so they cannot wait in line for a concurrency slot that will never free up. If they count against the limit, some of the servers a filter selects never start, and the app that needs them waits forever. Every selected server starts, whatever the limit.

cases.title: A server only cached tasks need is not started when they all replay
cases.why: A server is started only to serve the tasks that need it. When all of those tasks replay from the cache, nothing runs against it, so booting it wastes its whole start-up time. Here the server declares it reads no files, so its dependant can be keyed without it, and an edit to the dependant brings the server back.

cases.title: A server that dies mid-run keeps the tasks that need it from starting, and fails the run
cases.why: A task that needs a server cannot give a real result once the server is gone. Run anyway, it either fails with an unrelated connection error or passes against nothing. The run should skip what still needs the server and fail, so the server’s death is the error the developer sees.

cases.title: Ctrl-C before a server’s turn leaves it unstarted
cases.why: After Ctrl-C, no new task should start, servers included. A server spawned after the stop comes up after the teardown has run, so nothing ends it. It then holds the run open, or keeps running in the background with its port taken.

cases.title: SIGINT to the run reaches a running server as SIGINT
cases.why: A server should receive the signal the user sent, unchanged. Dev servers often bind their shutdown to SIGINT, the Ctrl-C signal, to close connections and remove temp files. If the runner forwards it as SIGTERM or SIGKILL, that hook never runs and the server’s state is left behind for the next start.

cases.title: SIGTERM to the run reaches a running server as SIGTERM
cases.why: A server should receive SIGTERM as SIGTERM. Containers and CI agents send it to ask for a graceful shutdown, and servers bind their drain and cleanup code to it. Forwarded as another signal, that code is skipped, and open connections, lock files or temp files are left as they were.

cases.title: Ctrl-C ends a server’s own child that traps every signal it can
cases.why: Ctrl-C must end everything a server started, even a child that traps every signal it can. Such a child would otherwise outlive the run, keep its port and keep printing into the terminal. After a grace period the runner kills it with SIGKILL, which cannot be trapped.

cases.title: A task that needs a server starts only once the server prints its ready line
cases.why: A server is useful to its dependants only once it accepts connections, and the ready line is how it says so. Starting the dependant as soon as the process spawns sends e2e tests to a port that is not open yet. That gives failures that come and go with machine speed, the worst kind to debug in CI.

cases.title: A server that exits non-zero before its ready line fails the run and starts no dependant
cases.why: A server that exits non-zero before it is ready has failed to start. Its dependants need it, so they must not start, and the run must fail rather than wait for a line that can never come. Otherwise CI either hangs until its own timeout or runs tests against nothing.

cases.title: A server whose command does not exist fails the run at once, not after waiting for its ready line
cases.why: A command that does not exist fails at once, and the run should report it at once. Waiting for a ready line from a process that never started hides a clear error, like a missing install or a typo, behind a hang or a timeout. The developer should see the real cause in seconds.

cases.title: A server-style task that finishes with exit 0 before its ready line lets its dependants run
cases.why: A task that exits 0 before its ready line did its work and ended cleanly. Some setup steps, like seeding a database, are declared like a server but finish on their own. There is no server left to wait for and nothing failed, so its dependants run; failing or hanging would punish a task that succeeded.

cases.title: Ctrl-C while a server is still starting ends it and starts none of its dependants
cases.why: Ctrl-C during a server’s start-up means the user no longer wants the run. The starting server must be ended, not left booting in the background, and none of its dependants may start. Otherwise the stop launches the very tests it was meant to cancel.

cases.title: A server that prints its ready line as Ctrl-C stops it does not start its dependants
cases.why: Readiness only counts while the run is still going. A server may print its ready line from its shutdown handler, after the user pressed Ctrl-C. Starting dependants on that line would launch new work after the stop, against a server that is about to exit.

cases.title: A server that never prints its ready line fails at its time limit, and is killed
cases.why: A server that is alive but never prints its ready line will never be useful to its dependants. Without a limit it holds the run open for good, and in CI that is a job that hangs until it is cancelled. At its time limit the run fails with a clear reason, and the server is killed, not left running.

cases.title: A server that is ready inside its time limit keeps running past it
cases.why: For a server, the time limit bounds the wait for its ready line, not its life. A dev server is meant to keep running while the tasks that use it do. Killing it once the limit passes would pull it from under the tests mid-run and fail them for no fault of their own.

cases.title: A never-ready server that ignores SIGTERM is killed at its time limit anyway
cases.why: A time limit must hold even for a server that ignores SIGTERM. Without escalating to SIGKILL, the server stays up and the run waits on it past its limit, which is the hang the limit was set to prevent. The run fails at the limit and leaves nothing running.

cases.title: A never-ready server that exits 0 on its time limit’s SIGTERM still fails
cases.why: A server that never became ready has failed, however it exits. Many servers exit 0 on SIGTERM as their graceful shutdown, so the exit code after the time limit’s kill says nothing about readiness. Read as success, the run would go green with its dependants never run and nothing tested.

cases.title: A never-ready server’s backgrounded child that ignores SIGTERM dies with it at its time limit
cases.why: At its time limit a never-ready server must die with everything it started. Its shell exits on SIGTERM at once, while a child that ignores SIGTERM keeps running unless the runner kills the whole tree. That child would hold the server’s port into the next run, which then fails to bind.

cases.title: A never-ready server’s SIGTERM cleanup runs to its end at the time limit
cases.why: Killing a server at its time limit should still let its cleanup finish. Many handlers run once and reset, so a second SIGTERM arriving during cleanup kills the server half way. A runner should send the signal once, wait a grace period, and only then use SIGKILL.

cases.title: A committed change selects its project and every project that depends on it
cases.why: A change can break any project built on top of it, so an affected run must reach every dependent, not only the project that was edited. If dependents are left out, a pull request that breaks `app` through a change in `lib` passes CI. The break then shows up on main or in production, far from the commit that caused it.

cases.title: A change in a project nothing depends on selects only that project
cases.why: Selecting by change exists to run only what the change can reach. A project nothing depends on cannot pass its edit to anyone else, so only its own tasks need to run. Running its siblings or its dependencies as well spends CI minutes on work whose result is already known.

cases.title: With nothing changed, an affected run runs nothing and succeeds
cases.why: When no file changed, no task’s result can differ from last time, so the right answer is an empty run that succeeds. Failing would turn a no-op pull request, such as a merge of an empty commit, into a red build. Running everything would waste the whole CI budget on work nothing asked for.

cases.title: An uncommitted edit counts as a change
cases.why: A developer runs the affected tasks before committing, to check the edit they are making. The working tree is what the tasks will read, so an edit on disk is a change whether or not it is committed yet. Comparing only commits would report nothing to run and let the developer commit untested work.

cases.title: A new file git does not track yet counts as a change
cases.why: A new file is read by any task whose inputs match it, even before git tracks it. Ignoring untracked files would skip the project where a developer just added a source or a test. The run would look clean, and the new file would only be checked after it is committed and pushed.

cases.title: A deleted file counts as a change to its project
cases.why: Removing a file changes what a task reads as surely as editing it: an import can now fail, a test can vanish. The project that lost the file and every project built on it must be selected. Treating a delete as no change lets a pull request that breaks the build by removing a file pass CI.

cases.title: A change to a root file no task reads selects nothing
cases.why: A file at the root that no task names as an input cannot change any task’s result. Selecting every project on such an edit, for example a notes file or a README, makes a one-line docs change cost a full CI run. The tool has the inputs declared, so it can tell that nothing reads the file.

cases.title: An uncommitted edit selects its project and every project that depends on it
cases.why: An uncommitted edit changes what dependents build against just as a commit does. A local affected run must reach every dependent, not only the edited project. Otherwise the developer sees a green check while `app`, built on the edited `lib`, was never tested.

cases.title: Changing a project’s task definition selects it and its dependents
cases.why: A task’s definition is what it runs: a new command, flag or dependency is a change as much as a new source. Its project and every dependent must be selected. Comparing only source files misses a config change that breaks the build, and CI stays green.

cases.title: Removing every task of a dependency selects the projects depending on it
cases.why: When a dependency loses its tasks, what its dependents built against has changed: the build they waited on is gone. The dependents must run to show whether they still work. Treating the removed tasks as nothing to select hides a broken dependency chain.

cases.title: A base several commits back selects what every commit since changed
cases.why: A base several commits back must cover every commit since then, not only the latest. Each commit may touch a different project. Comparing only HEAD with its parent leaves earlier changes on the branch untested, so a pull request with many commits passes with gaps.

cases.title: A branch base selects what this branch changed, not what the base branch did since
cases.why: Comparing against a branch means comparing against where this branch left it, the merge base, as a pull request does. Commits main gained since then are not this branch’s change. Comparing directly with main’s tip selects projects only main touched and reruns their tests on every pull request.

cases.title: On a merge commit, the first parent as base selects what the merge brought in
cases.why: CI often checks out the merge of a pull request into its base. On that merge commit, the first parent is the base branch, so comparing with `HEAD^1` gives exactly what the merge brought in. Main’s own commits must not be counted, or each pull request reruns unrelated tests.

cases.title: A tag works as a base, as a branch does
cases.why: Releases are often compared against the last tag, so a tag must work as a base just as a branch does. Rejecting it, or resolving it to the wrong commit, forces users to look up commit hashes by hand. Selecting everything instead makes every release run a full rebuild.

cases.title: An annotated tag works as a base: the commit it points at is compared
cases.why: An annotated tag points at a tag object, which in turn points at a commit. The comparison must use that commit. Diffing against the tag object fails or resolves to nothing, and the release check either errors or reruns every project.

cases.title: In a depth-2 clone, the previous commit as base selects the change and its dependents
cases.why: CI often fetches only the last few commits. When the base is within that history, the tool can compute the diff normally and must do so. Bailing out because the clone is shallow, or selecting everything, throws away the affected run in exactly the place it saves the most time.

cases.title: In a depth-1 clone, the previous commit as base is fetched and selects the change
cases.why: CI checks out a single commit by default, so the previous commit is not on disk but is on origin. The tool should fetch what it needs and select only the change. Failing breaks the default CI setup; selecting everything makes affected runs cost a full run in CI.

cases.title: In a depth-1 clone of a branch, the base branch on origin selects what the branch changed
cases.why: A pull request job usually checks out one commit, with the base branch and merge base only on origin. Comparing with `origin/main` must fetch the history needed to find the merge base. Failing breaks the job; selecting everything turns each pull request into a full run.

cases.title: In a depth-1 merge checkout, the first parent as base selects what the merge brought in
cases.why: A common pull request checkout is the merge commit fetched alone, with neither parent present. Its first parent is the base, so comparing with `HEAD^1` must fetch it and select what the merge added. Failing or selecting everything loses the affected run on every pull request.

cases.title: An edit to a file marked assume-unchanged in git’s index selects its project
cases.why: Marking a file assume-unchanged tells `git status` not to look at it; it does not freeze the file for the build. A task reads the file on disk, so an edit there changes its result. Trusting the flag hides the edit, and the project’s tests do not run on code it now reads.

cases.title: An edit to a file marked skip-worktree in git’s index selects its project
cases.why: Skip-worktree hides a file from git’s view of the working tree, often to keep a local config edit. The task still reads the edited file, so the project must be selected. Trusting the flag means the edit is never tested, though it changes what the task produces.

cases.title: Deleting a file marked assume-unchanged selects its project
cases.why: A file marked assume-unchanged can still be deleted from disk, and the task then cannot read it. git’s status does not report the delete, so the tool must check the disk. Missing it leaves a project untested after a source it needs is gone.

cases.title: A skip-worktree file absent from disk, as a sparse checkout leaves it, selects nothing
cases.why: A sparse checkout leaves files out of the working tree on purpose and marks them skip-worktree. A file absent for that reason was not deleted by anyone. Counting it as a change would select every project with unmaterialised files on each run in a sparse checkout.

cases.title: An edit to the file an input link points at selects the link’s project
cases.why: A task reads the content behind a file link, wherever in the workspace that content lives. git reports the edit at the target’s path, outside the project holding the link. The link must be followed, or the project that reads the file is not selected.

cases.title: An edit inside the directory an input link points at selects the link’s project
cases.why: A directory link makes the target directory part of the project that holds the link. git reports an edit there at the target’s path, which belongs to no project. Without following the link, the project that reads the file is skipped and its tests do not run on the new content.

cases.title: A new file in the directory an input link points at selects the link’s project
cases.why: A new file in a linked directory is a new input for the project holding the link, as an input glob through the link now matches it. git reports it at the target’s path, not the project’s. Not following the link skips the project that now reads one more file.

cases.title: An edit to a git-ignored file an input link points at selects the link’s project
cases.why: A link may point at a file git ignores, such as a local config. git’s diff cannot see that file, so it cannot say the file did not change. The tool must check what the link reads, or the project is skipped after an edit that changes its result.

cases.title: A dangling link, or a link whose target did not change, selects nothing
cases.why: Following links must stay precise. A dangling link reads nothing, and a link to an unchanged file reads the same bytes as before. Selecting every project that holds a link whenever anything nearby changes reruns work whose result cannot have changed.

cases.title: When only a project without the task changed, the run succeeds and runs nothing
cases.why: In an affected run, which projects are in scope depends on what changed. If only a project without the requested task changed, the correct result is an empty run that succeeds. The task exists elsewhere, so this is not a typo, and failing would turn a harmless change into a red build.

cases.title: A changed project lacking the task, depending on one that has it, runs nothing and succeeds
cases.why: A changed project that lacks the requested task has nothing to run, and the change cannot flow back into a project it depends on. The run should succeed and run nothing. Failing makes a change in a project without tests break a test job; running the dependency’s task wastes time.

cases.title: When only a project declaring no tasks at all changed, the run succeeds and runs nothing
cases.why: A project may declare no tasks at all, for example a folder of shared assets. A change there selects nothing for a task no project in scope has. The run should succeed with nothing to do; failing turns an edit in a task-less project into a red build.

cases.title: An affected run of a task no project declares fails, whatever changed
cases.why: A task no project declares can never run, whatever changed. The run must fail, so a typo like `tset` is caught at once. Exiting 0 because the change happened to select nothing turns a broken CI step into a green one that silently tests nothing.

cases.title: A project that is a clean submodule is not selected
cases.why: A project can be a git submodule. When the submodule is clean and still on the recorded commit, nothing in it changed. Selecting it just because it is a submodule, or because git reports it as a special entry, reruns its tasks on every affected run for no change.

cases.title: An edit inside a submodule project selects it
cases.why: A submodule’s files are read by its project’s tasks like any others. git’s diff of the outer repository reports a dirty submodule, not the file inside it. The tool must still map the edit to the project, or the submodule’s tests do not run on the change.

cases.title: A new untracked file inside a submodule project selects it
cases.why: A new file inside a submodule is a new input for the tasks that read that project, even before it is tracked. The outer repository sees only that the submodule is dirty. Not looking inside skips the project and lets the new file go untested.

cases.title: Moving a submodule to another commit selects it, committed or not
cases.why: Moving a submodule to another commit swaps every file its project reads. The project must be selected whether the move is still in the working tree or already committed in the outer repository. Once compared against the commit that already holds the move, it must stop being selected.

cases.title: A submodule `.gitmodules` tells git to ignore still selects its project when it changes
cases.why: Setting `ignore = all` for a submodule in `.gitmodules` quiets `git status`; it does not stop tasks from reading the files. An edit inside the submodule still changes what its project produces. Trusting the setting hides the change, and the project’s tests do not run.

cases.title: An edit inside a submodule nested in a project selects that project
cases.why: A submodule can sit inside a project, for example a vendored library. Its files belong to the project that holds it, and an edit there changes what that project’s tasks read. The outer diff only marks the submodule dirty, so the tool must map it to the holding project.

cases.title: A new git repository created inside a project selects that project
cases.why: A git repository created inside a project, for example by a tool or a clone, is untracked content of that project. Its files are on disk and an input glob over the project reads them. git may hide its contents behind one path, so the project must be selected all the same.

cases.title: Edits in two projects select both
cases.why: A change set is the union of every file it touched, so each project with an edited file must be selected. Stopping at the first project found, or picking one, leaves the other untested. The project left out is then free to ship broken from the same pull request.

cases.title: A change staged in git’s index but not committed counts as a change
cases.why: Files staged with `git add` are on disk and about to be committed, so tasks read them like any other edit. A comparison that looks only at the working tree against the index, or only at commits, misses them. A developer who stages before checking would see an empty run and commit untested work.

cases.title: A file deleted from the working tree, not committed, selects its project
cases.why: A file removed from the working tree is gone for every task that reads the project, even before the delete is committed. Its project must be selected, since an import or fixture it held may now be missing. Seeing only edits and new files would let a breaking delete pass a local check.

cases.title: A file renamed inside a project selects that project alone
cases.why: A rename changes the project’s file set: a task over `*` sees a new name, and an import of the old path now fails. The project must be selected, but nothing outside it changed, so other projects stay out. Missing the rename hides a broken import; selecting everything wastes the run.

cases.title: A file moved from one project to another, not yet committed, selects both
cases.why: Moving a file out of one project and into another changes both: one lost an input, the other gained one. git may report the move as a single rename, but its two paths belong to two projects. Selecting only the target leaves the source untested after it lost a file it may still need.

cases.title: A committed move of a file from one project to another selects both
cases.why: Once committed, a move between projects still changes both: one lost an input, the other gained one. git’s diff may fold the move into a single rename entry, but both of its paths must be checked against projects. Counting only the new path leaves the project that lost the file untested.

cases.title: A new file with a non-ASCII name selects its project
cases.why: A file name with accented or other non-ASCII letters is as much a source as any other. By default git quotes and escapes such names in its plain output, so a reader that takes them literally gets a path that matches no project. The change is then dropped and the project’s tests do not run.

cases.title: A changed file whose name holds a quote or a backslash selects its project
cases.why: A quote or a backslash in a file name is legal and does occur, for example in generated test fixtures. git escapes these characters in its plain output, so a naive reader sees a path no project owns. The edit is then silently dropped, and a broken project passes as unaffected.

cases.title: New files git ignores, an install among them, select nothing
cases.why: Files git ignores, such as an installed `node_modules` or a local build cache, are local state, not changes to the source. Counting them would select a project after every install, on every machine differently. Affected runs would then select much more than the change touched, and their selection would depend on whose machine ran them.

cases.title: An edit to a file committed under a `node_modules` directory selects its project
cases.why: A file committed to the repository is a source, even if it sits under a directory named `node_modules`, as test fixtures often do. Only an untracked install there is the package manager’s local state. Skipping the committed file by its path would hide an edit that its project’s tests read.

cases.title: A change in `app-e2e` selects it, not `app` or `app-e2e-utils` beside it
cases.why: A project owns a path only when the path continues with a `/` after the project’s directory. Matching on a bare string prefix makes `packages/app` claim `packages/app-e2e/x`, so an edit there also selects `app`. Worse, a longest-prefix bug can give the file to the wrong project and skip the one that changed.

cases.title: A project nested in another owns its files: an edit there selects it, not its parent
cases.why: When one project sits inside another, each file belongs to the innermost project that holds it. An edit in the inner project should not select the outer one, and the reverse holds too. Otherwise every change to the inner project reruns the outer project’s tasks, which never read those files.

cases.title: A base spelled like a git option is never passed to git as one

cases.title: A base naming a directory inside a commit (`HEAD:packages`) selects nothing unchanged

cases.title: When git cannot diff the base, the run fails or runs everything, never nothing
cases.why: If git cannot read the diff, for example because an object is missing from a damaged clone, the tool does not know what changed. An unreadable diff is not an empty one. It must fail or run everything; running nothing turns a broken checkout into a green job that checked nothing.

cases.title: An edit or a bump in a submodule selects its project though git is set to ignore it
cases.why: A user may set `diff.ignoreSubmodules` to quiet git’s diff, but the task still reads the submodule’s files. An edit inside the submodule, or a bump to a new commit, changes what the task sees. Trusting the quieted diff skips the project, and its tests do not run on the new code.

cases.title: An edit to a file only the project’s own `test` reads leaves its dependents’ tests out
cases.why: Dependents reach a project only through the tasks they wait on, here its `build`. When the edited file is one only the project’s own `test` reads, and `build` excludes it, nothing a dependent builds on changed. Rerunning the dependents’ tests on every test-file edit wastes CI time for no new result.

cases.title: A change no requested task reads runs nothing and succeeds
cases.why: An affected run answers which of the requested tasks the change can reach. If the change only touches files those tasks do not read, the right answer is an empty run that succeeds. Running the tasks anyway wastes time; failing turns a harmless change into a red build.

cases.title: An affected project’s build gets its unchanged dependency’s build first, from cold
cases.why: Selection decides which tasks the user asked for; it does not remove the tasks they need first. An affected build reads its dependency’s output, so that dependency must be built, or restored, before it even though it did not change. Leaving it out fails the build on a clean machine, or reads a stale output left on disk.

cases.title: An input glob spelled `./src/**` selects on an edit under src/
cases.why: Users write input globs as `./src/**` as often as `src/**`, and both mean the same files. A matcher that compares the changed path with the literal pattern finds no match for the `./` form. The edit is then missed, and the task and its dependents do not run on the new source.

cases.title: A file an input’s `!./src//**` exclude leaves out selects nothing
cases.why: An exclude is part of what a task declares it reads, whatever its spelling. `!./src//**/*.test.txt` excludes the same files as `!src/**/*.test.txt`, so an edit to one of them reaches nothing. Failing to apply the exclude reruns the task and its dependents for a file it does not read.

cases.title: An input naming a bare directory (`src`) selects on an edit under it
cases.why: Naming a directory such as `src` as an input means the files in it, and the cache key already reads it that way. Selection must use the same meaning, or an edit under the directory selects nothing. The task and its dependents would then not run, even though their cache key changed.

cases.title: A task that only aggregates others runs when a task it depends on is affected
cases.why: A task with no command of its own often groups others, like an `all` or `ci` task. It is affected whenever a task it waits on is affected. Dropping it because it reads no files would leave the grouped work out of the affected run, and CI would not check what the change reached.

cases.title: A task that only aggregates others is left out when nothing it depends on changed
cases.why: A task that only groups others is affected only through them. When nothing it waits on can see the change, it has nothing to do. Selecting it anyway, because it reads no files of its own, runs all the grouped work on changes that never reach it.

cases.title: A task named `toString` is declared only where it is written
cases.why: A task can be named anything, including `toString` or `constructor`. Looking it up on a plain object finds the inherited member in every project, so projects that never declared the task appear to have it. The run then schedules tasks that do not exist, or fails on them.

cases.title: Any change in a project selects its task that is never cached
cases.why: A task that is never cached declares no inputs, so the tool cannot know which of its project’s files it reads. Any change in its project must select it, since any file may matter. Guessing a narrower set would skip a lint or check that the edit can make fail.

cases.title: A dependent whose task waits on nothing of the change is left out
cases.why: A project dependency alone does not make every task depend on the other project. If the dependent’s build declares no edge to the dependency’s build and reads none of its files, the change cannot reach it. Selecting it anyway reruns work whose result is already known.

cases.title: A task with no edge to other projects runs only where the change is
cases.why: A task with no edge to other projects reads only its own project’s files. A change in `lib` cannot alter what `app`’s `style` sees. Running it in every dependent project because of the package graph spends CI time on checks whose result is already known.

cases.title: A task reaches a change through either arm of a diamond of task edges
cases.why: Task edges can form a diamond, where a task reaches a changed one through only one of two paths. The task must be selected if any path leads to the change. Following just one arm, or stopping at the first visited node, misses the task and leaves its result unchecked.

cases.title: A task whose edges never reach the changed task is left out
cases.why: A task is affected only if one of its edges leads to a changed task. Tasks that share a project or a parent with the change are not enough. Selecting all of a project’s tasks when one of them changed reruns work that cannot see the edit, here `side`, `left` and `base`.

cases.title: A change to a root file a task names as an input selects that task
cases.why: A file at the workspace root belongs to no project, but a task that names it as an input depends on it. Shared config and schemas often live there. If a change to it selects nothing, the tasks that read it are skipped and their output stays built against the old file.

cases.title: A file in one project that another names as a root input selects both
cases.why: A task may read a file inside another project, declared as a root input. A change to that file affects both the project that owns it and the task that reads it. Selecting only the owner leaves the reading task built against the old content.

cases.title: Editing the root package.json in a way no task reads selects nothing
cases.why: An edit to the root `package.json` that no task reads, such as its description, changes no input, no dependency and no command. Treating every root manifest edit as a change to everything turns small housekeeping commits into full runs. Inputs are declared, so the tool can tell nothing reads the change.

cases.title: A root file one task reads does not select its project’s other, never-cached task
cases.why: A root input belongs to the task that names it, not to every task in that task’s project. A never-cached `lint` reads its own project, so a root file only the `build` names does not reach it. It must still run when its own project changes, which the case checks after.

cases.title: Each task’s own root config file selects that task, not its sibling
cases.why: Each task declares its own root inputs, so a root config file selects only the task that names it. Lumping all of a project’s root inputs together reruns `build` when only the test config changed. A root file no task names, like `other.cfg`, selects nothing.

cases.title: An edit inside a nested repository a root input reaches selects the task naming it
cases.why: A nested git repository appears in the outer one as a single path, or not at all, so its diff never lists the files inside. A task whose root input reaches into it still reads those files. Trusting the outer diff alone misses the edit and leaves the task built against the old content.

cases.title: An edit behind a directory link selects a task whose `src/**/*.txt` reaches through it
cases.why: A directory link inside a project makes the files it points at part of what an input glob like `src/**/*.txt` reads. git sees an edit there under the link’s target path, not the project’s. Without following the link, the task that reads the edited file is not selected.

cases.title: An edit behind a directory link leaves out a task whose glob stops above it
cases.why: Following links must stay as precise as the glob itself. `src/*.md` reads only files directly in `src/`, none inside `src/v/`, so an edit behind that link does not reach it. Selecting every task in the project whenever a linked file changes reruns work for no reason.

cases.title: An edit behind a root directory link selects a task whose root input reaches through it
cases.why: A root input such as `shared/**/*.txt` reads the files behind a directory link under `shared/`. git reports an edit there at the link’s target, outside the glob’s literal path. The link must be followed, or the task that reads the file is not selected.

cases.title: An exclude alone keeps the workspace-root project, as it keeps every other member
cases.why: An exclude filter removes what it names and keeps everything else. The workspace-root project is a project like any other, so excluding `c` keeps it. Dropping it silently skips root tasks such as code generation or a lint over shared config.

cases.title: Running a task in a named project that does not declare it fails
cases.why: Naming a project and a task is an explicit request. If that project does not declare the task, nothing can satisfy it, and the run must fail. Exiting 0 after running nothing hides a typo in the task or project name, and CI reports a check that never ran.

cases.title: Running a task in named projects runs it where declared; one that lacks it is no error
cases.why: Across several named projects, the task runs where it is declared; one project lacking it is normal in a mixed workspace. Failing the whole run for that forces every project to declare every task. The run fails only when the task exists nowhere in scope.

cases.title: Asked to continue, a run goes on past a failed task and still fails
cases.why: Asked to continue, the run should go on with every task the failure does not block, so the user sees every error at once. The run as a whole still failed, though. A green exit would let a pipeline merge or deploy with a broken task the log mentions only in passing.

cases.title: A task that ran past its dependency’s failure is not replayed once the dependency is fixed
cases.why: When the run continued past a failed dependency, the task after it ran on whatever the failure left, which is not a valid build. Saving that result lets it replay after the dependency is fixed. The task must run again on the fixed dependency, or the stale output outlives the fix.

cases.title: A forced run runs every task past its cache entry, and the next run replays what it saved
cases.why: Forcing a run asks for every task to run regardless of what the cache holds, often because the user suspects an entry. The fresh results must then replace the saved ones. A force that saves nothing leaves the doubted entry in place for the next run to replay.

cases.title: A run that only reads the cache replays a hit, and saves nothing for a miss
cases.why: A read-only cache lets a run use what others built without writing, as an untrusted branch build should. A hit must still replay, or the mode saves nothing. A miss must run and leave the cache as it was, so the next normal run builds it again instead of replaying it.

cases.title: A planned run runs no task, writes no output, and saves nothing
cases.why: A planned run shows what would run without running it. No command may start, no output may be written and no cache entry may be saved. A plan that runs tasks surprises the user with side effects, and one that saves entries can later replay results nothing ever built.

cases.title: A variable passed through reaches the task
cases.why: A pass-through variable is one the task needs to run, such as a token or a path, but whose value does not change the output. It must reach the command, or the task fails or behaves differently. Keeping it out of the key is a choice about caching, not about whether the task sees it.

cases.title: A change to a variable passed through, not keyed, replays the task
cases.why: The user declared that this variable reaches the task but does not change its output, such as a log level or a token. Changing it therefore leaves the result as it was. Running the task again ignores that declaration and costs a full build on every machine where the value differs.

cases.title: A task ordered after a dependency, but not keyed on it, replays when only the dependency changes
cases.why: The task was told to run after its dependency but not to key on it, because it never reads what the dependency produces. A change only in the dependency leaves this task’s inputs as they were. Running it again ignores that declaration and costs a build that gives the same bytes.

cases.title: A linked git worktree of the same commit replays what the main checkout built
cases.why: A linked git worktree at the same commit holds the same files as the main checkout. The task’s inputs are identical, so the result already built is right here too. Building again because the path differs makes every extra worktree start cold, which is the cost a shared cache should remove.

cases.title: A run started through a link to the workspace replays what the real path built
cases.why: Opening the workspace through a link leaves every file and the commit the same; only the path the shell shows differs. The task’s inputs are identical, so the saved result is right. Building again because of the path makes the same tree cost twice depending on how the user reached it.

cases.title: A run reports that a task missed the cache
cases.why: Knowing which tasks missed the cache is how a user finds what broke caching. A key that changes on every run looks like a slow build until the report shows the miss. Without it, a team cannot tell a cold cache from one that never hits, and cannot find the input that keeps changing.

cases.title: A run reports that a task was replayed
cases.why: A report of each hit tells the user what was replayed rather than run. When a result looks wrong, the first question is whether the task ran at all. It is also how a team checks that CI gets the reuse it expects, and notices when a change quietly turns hits into misses.

cases.title: A run reports how long each task took
cases.why: Per-task time is the number a build is tuned with. Without it, a user cannot find the slow task on the critical path or tell whether a change made a task slower. The total time of a run alone hides which task to fix, since many tasks run at once and overlap.

cases.title: A run reports how long a replay took, not the original run
cases.why: A replay’s time is the time to restore it, not the original command’s time. Reporting the original time makes a hit look as slow as a miss and hides whether the cache helps at all. It also hides a slow restore, such as a large artifact from a slow store. The original time belongs to the run that paid it.

cases.title: A run reports each task’s CPU time
cases.why: CPU time shows how much work a task does, apart from how long it waited. A task that waits on the network and one that compiles for the same span look alike by wall time. CPU time tells a user which tasks gain from more cores and which from less waiting, and whether parallel runs are starved.

cases.title: A run reports each task’s peak memory
cases.why: Peak memory decides how many tasks fit on a machine at once. Without it, a user sizing CI runners or a concurrency limit guesses, and a run can be killed for running out of memory with no hint of which task caused it. Per-task numbers show which task needs the larger machine.

cases.title: A run reports the size of what each task wrote
cases.why: The size of what a task writes is what the cache must store and move. Large outputs make saves and restores slow and fill a remote cache. Reporting it per task shows which outputs to trim, split or leave uncached, instead of guessing from the size of the whole cache.

cases.title: A run reports the size of what a replay restored
cases.why: On a replay, the bytes restored are the cost of the hit. A hit that pulls a large artifact over the network can take longer than running the task. Reporting the restored size lets a user see when that happens and narrow what the task declares as output.

cases.title: A variable the task does not declare never reaches it
cases.why: A variable that reaches the command but not its key can change the output while the key stays the same. A later run with another value then replays the wrong result. Keeping undeclared variables out of the task makes that mistake fail loudly now instead of silently later.

cases.title: An isolated task that reads its inputs and writes its outputs succeeds
cases.why: Isolation exists to catch what a task did not declare, not to break tasks that declared everything. A task that reads only its inputs and writes only its outputs must run as it would without isolation. A sandbox that fails it makes isolation too costly to turn on.

cases.title: An isolated task that reads a project file it never declared fails
cases.why: A file the task reads but never declared is outside its key. An edit to that file would leave the key the same, and a later run would replay a stale result. Failing the read now shows the missing input at once, while it is cheap to add, instead of after a wrong replay.

cases.title: An isolated task may read a file it is granted beyond its inputs
cases.why: Some files a task must read are not inputs, such as a tool’s config outside the project, and the user grants them on purpose. A granted read is a decision the user made, not a mistake to catch. Failing it forces users to turn isolation off for tasks that are already correct.

cases.title: An isolated task that reads another project’s source fails
cases.why: Reading another project’s source ties this task to files outside its key and its own folder. An edit there changes the output while nothing reruns. Failing the read makes the hidden link visible, so the user can declare the dependency instead of shipping a stale build.

cases.title: An isolated task that writes outside its outputs fails, and the file is not left behind
cases.why: A file written outside the outputs is never stored with the task. A later replay restores the outputs but not that file, so the tree differs depending on whether the task ran. Failing the write, and leaving nothing behind, keeps a run and a replay producing the same tree.

cases.title: An isolated task that writes into another project fails, and leaves that project as it was
cases.why: Writing into another project changes files that project owns and keys on, behind its back. Its next run may replay or rerun on content no one edited. Failing the write and leaving that project as it was keeps each project’s files under its own control and key.

cases.title: An isolated task that rewrites its own source fails, and the source is kept
cases.why: A task that rewrites its own source changes its inputs while it runs, so its key no longer matches what it built from. A replay then hides the rewrite, or the next run loops on it. Failing the write and keeping the source protects the user’s code from a build step.

cases.title: An isolated task cannot read the user’s SSH key
cases.why: An SSH key in the user’s home is a secret no build should read. A task that can reach it can leak it through a log, an output or a cached artifact shared with others. An isolated task must see none of the home it did not declare, so a compromised script cannot take the key.

cases.title: An isolated task with no network grant cannot reach a server the run started
cases.why: A response from the network is an input no key holds. The next run replays the saved result whatever the server says now, and two machines can build different bytes under one key. A task without a network grant must fail to connect, so that hidden input shows up at once.

cases.title: An isolated task cannot read an undeclared file through a link inside its inputs
cases.why: A link inside the inputs can point at a file the task was never granted. Following it reads that file as surely as opening it directly, and the key does not cover it. Isolation must check where the link leads, or one symlink turns every grant into a way around it.

cases.title: Editing a source file while watching rebuilds with the new content
cases.why: Rerunning a task when what it reads changes is the whole point of watching. The output must hold the new source, not the one the watch started with. A watch that misses the edit leaves a stale build that looks fresh, so the user tests old code and trusts the result.

cases.title: Editing a file the task does not read reruns nothing
cases.why: The task said which files it reads, and the edited file is not one of them. Running it again would build the same output from the same inputs. Work done for a file nobody reads only delays the result the user is waiting for, and in a large project that wait comes with every save.

cases.title: Saving a file without changing it reruns nothing
cases.why: An editor that saves on focus loss, or a formatter with nothing to fix, writes the same bytes again. The task reads the content of its files, and the content did not change. A rerun here repeats work whose result is already on disk, and it happens on every idle save.

cases.title: Undoing an edit while watching brings back the earlier result without rebuilding
cases.why: After the undo the inputs are exactly the ones an earlier run already built. That result can be put back as it was, which is both correct and immediate. Building it again gives the same bytes and only costs the user time, on the edit people make most while trying things out.

cases.title: A new file matching the task’s inputs rebuilds with it included
cases.why: Inputs given as a pattern also cover files that do not exist yet. Adding a source file changes what the task reads as surely as editing one does. A watch that only follows the files present at the start misses one of the most common edits of all, a new module, and the build quietly leaves it out.

cases.title: Deleting a source file rebuilds without it
cases.why: A deleted file is no longer part of what the task reads, so the output built with it is now wrong. Keeping that output would ship code the user just removed. A deletion is a change to the inputs exactly as an edit is, and the next build must show the tree as it now stands.

cases.title: A file added in new folders under the inputs rebuilds with it, and so does its next edit
cases.why: A pattern over a folder covers its subfolders, including ones made after the watch started. Creating folders and a file in them is a normal edit while adding a feature. A watch that only follows the folders it saw at the start misses the file, or its next edit, and the build goes stale.

cases.title: Creating an empty folder under the inputs reruns nothing
cases.why: An empty folder holds no file the task could read, so the task’s output cannot change. Version control does not even record an empty folder. A rerun for it is work that produces the same bytes again, and it happens every time a tool or an editor makes a scratch folder.

cases.title: A change to a git-ignored file among the sources reruns nothing
cases.why: Ignored files are scratch: logs, editor swap files, local caches. They are not part of what the task builds from, and a cache key does not see them. A rerun on each of their writes is busy work, and when the task itself writes such a file it can keep the watch busy forever.

cases.title: A build’s own output does not start it again
cases.why: The task writes its output after reading its inputs, and the output is not one of them. Treating that write as a new change would build once more, or loop for good. After one edit the task should run exactly once, and then the watch should go quiet until the user changes something.

cases.title: A build writing a declared output folder that git does not ignore does not loop
cases.why: Some projects keep their built files next to the sources, where version control does not ignore them. They are still declared as the task’s output, not its input, and only inputs decide whether to run again. Rerunning on its own output turns every edit into a loop that never settles.

cases.title: A build that rewrites an ignored side file every run does not loop
cases.why: A process id file or a timestamped log differs on every run, so its bytes never settle. It is ignored by version control, so no input can depend on it. A watch that follows it reruns the task on its own leftovers without end, and the machine never goes idle between edits.

cases.title: Many files changed at once, as a checkout does, rebuild once
cases.why: Switching branches or pulling rewrites many files within a moment. Together they are one change, and one build over all of them gives the final result. Building once per file repeats the same work many times and shows results for trees that never existed in between.

cases.title: An editor’s save by renaming a temporary file over the source rebuilds
cases.why: Many editors write a temporary file and rename it over the original, so the file is replaced rather than edited in place. The source still changed, and the build must hold the new content. A watch that only follows edits in place misses every save from such an editor.

cases.title: A source folder deleted and made again, as a checkout does, rebuilds from the new files
cases.why: Tools that restore a tree, such as a checkout or a stash, often remove a folder and write it again. The new folder holds new content, and the build must reflect it. A watch that kept following the deleted folder hears nothing from then on, and every later edit is lost too.

cases.title: An edit made while the build is running is built right after
cases.why: The running build read the source before the edit, so its output is already stale when it finishes. The edit must lead to one more build, or the result shown is older than the code. Dropping changes that land mid-run is the usual way a watch drifts out of date without saying so.

cases.title: A build that fails while watching is built again once the source is fixed
cases.why: Breaking the code halfway through an edit is the normal state of work in progress. The watch should report the failure and keep going rather than exit. The fix is an edit like any other, and it must produce a fresh build without the user having to start the watch again.

cases.title: Editing a library rebuilds it, then the app that depends on it
cases.why: The app’s build reads what the library’s build produces, so it must run after it, on the new output. Building the app first, or not at all, leaves it built against the old library. Order matters under a watch exactly as much as it does in a plain run.

cases.title: Editing the app rebuilds only the app, not the library it uses
cases.why: The library reads nothing from the app, so its output cannot change when the app does. Only the edited project and those that depend on it need to run. Rebuilding the library on every app edit adds its whole build time to each save, for a result that is already on disk.

cases.title: Editing one project reruns nothing in an unrelated one
cases.why: Two projects with no dependency between them share no inputs. An edit in one cannot change the other’s output. Rebuilding every project on any edit makes watching a large workspace as slow as building all of it, which is the cost watching was supposed to avoid.

cases.title: Watching one app also rebuilds it when a library it depends on changes
cases.why: Selecting the app means its build and everything that build needs. A library edit changes what the app is built from. A watch that only follows the selected project’s own folder leaves the app built against the old library, and the user sees a result that no longer matches the code.

cases.title: Watching one app reruns nothing when a project outside it changes
cases.why: The user asked to watch the app, and the edited project is neither the app nor something it needs. Its build was not requested at the start, so the edit does not request it either. Running it anyway spends time on work nobody asked for and fills the output with noise.

cases.title: Editing a shared file at the root that the task reads rebuilds it
cases.why: A shared settings file outside the project is still one of the task’s declared inputs. Changing it changes the output as much as a source edit does. A watch that only follows project folders leaves the build on the old settings, though a plain run would have rebuilt it.

cases.title: Changing a task’s command while watching runs the new command

cases.title: Adding a new task to the config while watching does not rebuild the existing one

cases.why: A test run or a dev server can write dozens of ignored logs in the moment the user saves a source. The logs are noise, but the source edit among them is a real change. A watch that drops the burst with its noise leaves the build stale; one that answers each write rebuilds many times.

cases.title: Edits to two projects, one after another, each rebuild their project and the last wins
cases.why: A watch stays up for many edits, not one, and each must be answered as the first was. After the first rebuild the watch has to listen again, in every project it follows. One that hears only the first change, or only its first project, leaves later edits unbuilt while it still looks alive.

cases.title: Two tasks with no edge between them run at the same time
cases.why: Tasks with no dependency between them can run side by side, and a run that has cores to spare should use them. Here each task waits a while for the other to start, so run one after the other they each wait out the full delay. Running independent work in turn makes a monorepo’s wall time the sum of its tasks instead of its longest path.

cases.title: A task that closes its output and keeps working is waited for until it exits
cases.why: A process can close its output streams and go on working, as a daemonizing tool or a quiet build step does. The task ends when its process exits, not when its output ends. A runner that takes the closed stream as the end starts the dependant on a half-written output, or ends the run with the task still running behind it.

cases.title: Putting back the outputs a task first declared replays the entry saved for them
cases.why: An entry is saved under the task’s config as it was, so going back to that config finds it again. A team that tries a wider output set and reverts it should get its old hits back, not rebuild. The entry still holds every output the restored config names, so replaying it leaves the right tree.

cases.title: Switching a declared variable back and forth replays each value’s own result
cases.why: Each value of a keyed variable has its own entry, and a new value must not push out the old one. Builds that switch between modes, such as dev and prod or two targets, go back and forth all day. A cache that keeps only the latest value rebuilds on every switch, though both results are already known.

cases.title: Running a task with one set of args, then another, then each again replays both
cases.why: Forwarded args are part of the key, so each set of args has its own entry. Running tests for one file, then another, then the first again is ordinary work. A cache that keeps only the last args reruns work whose result it already had, while keeping both costs nothing in correctness.

cases.title: A project whose package.json does not parse fails the run
cases.why: A manifest that does not parse leaves the project’s name, dependencies and tasks unknown. Skipping the project lets the run go green with its tasks never run and its dependants built in the wrong order. Failing at once names the broken file while the mistake is fresh.

cases.title: Replaying an older build over a tree holding the same directory link restores through it
cases.why: A store layout such as `dist/pkg -> store/pkg` is common in package builds, and the link is already there when an older entry is replayed. The restore must put the old files back and leave the link as a link to the same directory. A restore that trips over the existing link fails a run that should replay, and one that follows or flattens it leaves the newer build’s bytes or a copy where a link belongs.

cases.title: Forwarded args such as `--help`, `--version` and `-v` reach the task, not the runner
cases.why: Args after the task belong to the task’s command, whatever they look like. `--help`, `--version` and `-v` are also flags of every runner, and a runner that reads them itself prints its own help or version and runs nothing, often with exit 0. The user asked the task for its help or a verbose run and got neither, with a green exit hiding it.

cases.title: A dependency reached by `^build` and by `b#build` builds once, first
cases.why: Naming one task twice, once through the package graph and once by its full name, asks for the same work twice. It must run once and finish before the task that needs it. Two runs of it waste time and can rewrite its output while the dependant reads it; dropping either edge can start the dependant early.

cases.title: Explicit `project#task` edges chain: each one’s own edges run first, and nothing else
cases.why: An explicit edge names a task, and that task brings its own dependsOn with it. deploy needs utils#lint, which needs core#build and utils#build, so all of them run first, in that order. A runner that follows only the first hop lints against a core that was never built; one that pulls in core#clean or the tests runs work nobody named.

cases.title: A negation with a trailing slash, `!src/gen/`, takes that directory’s tree out of the key
cases.why: A trailing slash only says the path is a directory: `!src/gen/` takes back every file under it, as `src/` keys every file under src. Read as a bare pattern, it matches nothing and the generated files stay in the key. Each regeneration then reruns a task the user excluded them from, while edits outside it must still rerun.

cases.title: A command of multi-byte characters runs byte-exact, and changing its last character runs it again
cases.why: A command is text of any script, and `echo ああ` must print exactly that. A runner that counts characters as bytes cuts the command inside a character or drops its tail, so the shell runs something else, or two commands differing only at the end share one key. The edit then replays the old output under a green run.

cases.title: A forwarded arg of multi-byte characters reaches the command byte-exact and keys the task
cases.why: Args forwarded to a task are its input as much as its files are. An emoji must reach the command as the same bytes the user typed, and a different emoji is a different run. A runner that mangles or truncates the arg feeds the command something else, or replays the result of one arg for another.

cases.title: Two excludes alone each take their project out of every project
cases.why: An exclude given with no include takes from the whole workspace, and a second exclude takes from that same set. A runner that lets the second exclude replace the first, or reads it as an include, runs a project the user ruled out. That can be the slow or broken project the excludes were there to skip.

cases.title: An exclude alone that names no project runs every project, or refuses
cases.why: Excluding a project that does not exist leaves the whole workspace: nothing was taken out. Refusing the run as a likely typo is also fair, before anything starts. Running nothing and exiting 0 is not: CI goes green having checked no project at all.

cases.title: The three tasks one task releases run at the same time, and the task over them reads all three
cases.why: When a shared dependency finishes, every task waiting only on it is ready at that moment and can start together. Here each of the three waits a while for the other two to start, so run one at a time they each wait out the full delay. A runner that releases ready tasks one by one turns a wide graph into a chain, and the wall time becomes the sum of the branches instead of the longest one.

cases.title: Either of a dependency’s two output trees, deleted alone, is back before a rebuilding dependant reads it
cases.why: A task that writes two trees, as a build writing `dist` and `types` does, is only present when both are. Deleting one and keeping the other is what a partial clean or a tool that prunes one directory leaves. A runner that sees one tree on disk and calls the dependency done lets the dependant build against a missing file, and fail or ship without it.

cases.title: A `!**/*.bak` input still keys a file named plain `bak`
cases.why: An exclusion by suffix means files ending in `.bak`, not every name holding those letters. A file named plain `bak`, with no dot, is a source like any other, and the user never took it back. A tool that matches the suffix loosely replays a stale result when that file changes, under a green run.

cases.title: A read-only output file left by a newer build is replaced by the cached one, still read-only
cases.why: Some tools write their outputs read-only, as generated sources or vendored files often are. When the inputs go back to an earlier state, the cache must put the earlier file back over the read-only one on disk. A restore that cannot overwrite it either fails the run or leaves the newer file under a green replay. The file comes back as the task wrote it, read-only.

cases.title: Six thousand output files, half empty and half with the same content, all come back on a hit
cases.why: A bundler can write thousands of chunks, many empty or byte-identical. A cache that stores each content once must still put every path back, and an empty file is a file, not a missing one. A restore that drops the empty files, writes one copy of a shared content, or stops at a size limit leaves a partial tree under a green replay.

cases.title: A forced run after an input edit saves under the new inputs, and the old inputs never replay its result
cases.why: Forcing a run after editing a source must file the fresh result under the edited inputs, so the next run with those inputs replays it. Filing it under the entry the last run used means that putting the source back replays the result of the edit: a stale hit under a green run. A force that saves nothing leaves the next run to build the same thing again.

cases.title: A change to a file another task of the project reads does not select its task that reads no files
cases.why: A task that declares empty inputs says no file in the project changes its result, as a task that only prints a version does. Here the changed file is one the project’s `test` declares, so the tool knows what reads it, and it cannot make `build` stale. Selecting `build` anyway reruns work on every commit that touches the project, while the task in another project that reads its own changed file is still selected.
